en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Section of Eights.
1. The First Fifty-Section (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga) 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Loving-kindness (Mettāsuttavaṇṇanā)
1. In the first [sutta] of the *Aṭṭhakanipāta*: "By one who has increased" means by way of the fulfillment of development (*bhāvanā*), that is, by having brought it to full growth.
"By one who has practiced repeatedly" means by performing the development again and again through its frequent cultivation.

"By one who has made it like a harnessed chariot" means that just as a harnessed chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses, when controlled by a skilled charioteer, proceeds according to his wish, so too [the mind] proceeds according to one's wish.
"Bringing it to the state of being ready for its function. "In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of being the foundation for all success.
"Presented" means established repeatedly and not abandoned through frequent cultivation.
"Heaped up on all sides" means brought to an accumulation in every respect according to the mode of cultivation; hence he said, "accumulated. "Well undertaken" means exceedingly...

[It is] for one who has been reborn in exactly that way. Regarding the passage beginning "And whoever develops loving-kindness," anyone at all—whether a householder or one gone forth [into homelessness]. "Loving-kindness" (*mettā*) refers to the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*).
It is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) both by way of its cultivation and by way of its object; for unlike the cultivation of the foul (*asubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth, it is immeasurable.
It is "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) because it does not grasp only a single portion of the object, but rather pervades it entirely and without limitation;

and because, through its immeasurable object, it is a familiar cultivation. "The fetters become thin" means that for one who takes loving-kindness as a basis, reflects upon it, and attains the lower noble paths, the fetters such as aversion are easily abandoned.
The meaning here should be understood as: "being abandoned, they become thin.
Having thus shown the abandonment of defilements and the attainment of Nibbāna as the culminating benefits of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the passage beginning with "Even if one...
is now stated to show other benefits as well. In that context, "one of uncorrupted mind" refers to one who, by the power of loving-kindness...

Because he has thoroughly suppressed ill-will (*vyāpāda*), his mind is untainted by ill-will. "He practices loving-kindness" (*mettāyati*) means he performs loving-kindness by way of pervading [others] with welfare.
"Virtuous" (*kusalī*) means one who is exceedingly skillful and possesses great merit; he is secure (*khemī*) through the departure of harm such as aversion.
In the phrase "and all living beings," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates a distinction. "Compassionate in mind" (*manasānukampī*) means feeling compassion with the heart. This is what is meant:
It is so: even loving-kindness directed toward a single being is a great mass of wholesome merit;

but for one who, with a mind that extends welfare as if toward their own child, compassionately feels sympathy for all living beings, the noble one of purified heart is capable of producing a vast, abundant, immeasurable, and boundless stream of karmic fruition for himself, sufficient to continue for sixty-four great aeons—such is the sublime merit.
"The person alone makes [it] and brings it to completion. "Filled with beings" means not sparse with beings; the meaning is "crowded with people.

"Bases of sympathy" (saṅgahavatthu) are the causes for winning over the world. When nine parts of the harvested crop have been given to the farmers, the king's taking of one part or a tenth part is called the "tenth-part levy" (dasama-bhāga).
Thus, the farmers, joyful and satisfied, [plant] the crops...
"He brings about success" means "he is wise in bringing about the success of the crops. It is said that from that time onwards, the practice of taking a sixth share arose.
"Six-monthly" (*chammāsika*) means sufficient for every six months. "He entices" (*pāseti*) means he acts as if [the prey] were caught in a snare.
"Pleasant speech" (*vācāpiya*) is speech that is pleasant; the action of that is "pleasantness of speech" (*vācāpeyya*). This is because the entire kingdom is in a state of prosperity and so forth.

Secure. "Nirabbuda" (free from boils) because of the absence of thieves; for a kingdom where there are no thieves is indeed prosperous. It is called "niraggaḷa" (boltless) because its houses are left open.
"Having uprooted" means having pulled out by the roots. "By two sacrifices" refers to the period preceding the Great Sacrifice.
And by the two subsequent offerings of attendants that were to be performed. "Seven... pe... terrifying" means:
[it was] terrifying because of the slaughter of five hundred and ninety-seven domestic animals, bringing fear to those who are afraid of evil. For thus they say:
"Six hundred animals are yoked; in the middle, one is slain."
“In the horse-sacrifice, it was deficient by three animals.
“Sammanti” means that which should be inserted into the opening of the yoke. “Pāsanti” means they throw. “Saṃhārimehi” means by means of carts capable of being drawn.
It is said that formerly, while a certain king was performing the Sammāpāsa sacrifice on the bank of the river Sarassatī, in a fissure of the earth—

He sank down as soon as he was given [the offering]. The blind, foolish brahmins, following one another like sheep, established the Sammāpāsa sacrifice there under the impression that "this is the path for his journey to heaven.
Therefore it is said: "starting from the place where he sank," and so forth. An *ayūpa* is a sacrifice performed over a few days;
a *sayūpa*, however, is a *satrayāga* (a sacrificial session) to be accomplished over many days. [This refers to] those things fashioned by the words of the mantras.
Clarified butter and honey are conventionally termed "vāja. Gold, bullion, cows, buffaloes, and so forth constitute the seventeenfold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Because there are no bolts (*aggaḷa*) on the inner chambers, storehouses, and other such structures, it is called *niraggaḷa*.
It is said that at such a sacrifice, one's own property is offered up entirely, without concealment.

"Candappabhā" means by the radiance of the moon itself. "All like the hosts of stars" means that just as all the hosts of stars do not equal even a sixteenth part of the moon's splendor, so too those sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (assamedha) do not equal even a sixteenth part of a mind of loving-kindness well-developed according to the characteristics described;
they do not reach it, they do not equal it—this is the meaning.

Now, in order to show further benefits of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) pertaining both to the present life and to future lives, the passage beginning with "He who does not kill" was spoken.
In this context, "he" refers to the person devoted to the cultivation of the sublime abode of loving-kindness.

"Does not kill" means that, by the very power of that cultivation of loving-kindness, because ill-will (*byāpāda*) has been suppressed from afar, he does not harm any living being nor does he afflict them with clods of earth, sticks, or other such means.
"Does not kill" means that having encouraged another, he does not cause beings to be killed, nor does he cause them to be harmed.
"Does not conquer" means that by way of contentious or quarrelsome speech and the like, he does not conquer anyone because of the very absence of contention;
or, by way of causing a dispute, such as through legal litigation and so forth, he does not conquer anyone. Therefore it is said: "He does not himself bring about a dispute with another. Does not...

Having engaged others in gambling, one should not cause others to suffer the loss of their wealth. Therefore he said: "One does not cause another to suffer the loss of another's [wealth] by means of another.
Or, the "part" (aṃsa) of loving-kindness is a constituent part in the sense of non-harming; thus it is "the part of loving-kindness" (mettāṃsa).
The commentary on the Mettā-sutta is finished.
2–4. Commentary on the Discourse on Wisdom, etc. (Paññāsuttādivaṇṇanā) 2–4.

Regarding the phrase "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyikā*) in the second [verse]: that which pertains to the beginning of the holy life is simply "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life. Therefore, he said: "That which has become the beginning of the holy life of the Path" (*maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāya*).
"Noble" (*ariya*) means faultless and completely pure. "Silence" (*tuṇhībhāvo*) does not refer to the adoption of a vow of dumbness by the followers of other sects (*titthiya*).
The noble silence is "as if impure" [in comparison]. It is called the "fourth jhāna" by way of a description of the highest;

however, even the first jhāna and the others are reckoned simply as the noble silence. Regarding the word "knows," he says "it knows that which is to be known" because this is an accusative construction (kamma-sādhana).
Or, just as someone who grasps things erroneously does not know even though they are knowing, [so it is here].
Even one who passes by does not see; it is not like this. Rather, it should be understood here thus: "This one, knowing, knows; seeing, sees.
The third and subsequent sections are easy to understand.
The commentary on the Paññāsutta, etc., is concluded.

5. Commentary on the First Discourse on Worldly Conditions (Paṭhamalokadhammasutta-vaṇṇanā) In the fifth [discourse], "worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) refers to those conditions that are inevitably encountered by the world of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said:

"There are none who are free from these," and so forth. "Gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of food, clothing, and so on; or rather, it is the very things themselves, because they are what is to be acquired.
The absence of that is "non-gain. Here, by the mention of "gain," attachment toward its object is included; by the mention of "non-gain," aversion is included.
Since, when there is blood, attachment finds its opportunity just as pus does through the injury caused by it, therefore it is said:
"When gain has arrived, non-gain has surely arrived. This same method applies to fame and the rest as well. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the First Discourse on Worldly Conditions is finished.
6–8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Worldly Conditions, etc. 6–8. Regarding the sixth:

that by which one applies oneself further is *adhippāyo* (intention); it is an action to be performed with distinction. Therefore, he said, "the application of the additional. There is nothing further to be said regarding the seventh and eighth.
The commentary on the second *Lokadhamma-sutta* and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Nanda-sutta*.

In the ninth [sutta], there are two kinds of sons of good family: those who are sons of good family by birth and those who are sons of good family by conduct. Regarding that, "Then indeed... [and so forth].

By this [definition], those sons of noble families who have come forth—such as the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, who was the son of the head of a prominent family in that very town of Thullakoṭṭhika—are "sons of noble birth" by way of lineage.

However, those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, even if they are born into any kind of family whatsoever, are called "sons of noble family" by way of conduct. Here, however, it refers to being born into a high-ranking family.
He said, “a son of good family,” because the Blessed One spoke with reference [to Nanda], saying: “Monks, one who speaks rightly of Nanda may say, ‘he is a son of good family.
However, his status as a son of good family is due to both of these reasons. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Nanda Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Kāraṇḍava Sutta In the tenth [verse], "he moves by concealing" (*paṭicarati*) means he moves—that is, proceeds—by way of concealment.

Alternatively, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word "moves" (*carati*) has the sense of "concealing"; thus it is said, "he conceals" (*paṭicchādeti*). Furthermore, the phrase "one thing by another" (*aññenāññaṃ*) is a demonstration of the manner of concealment.
He said, "By another reason," and so forth. In this context, "another reason" means either a statement;
that is, he conceals with a different reason or statement whatever reason or statement was spoken by the accuser to reveal the fault of the one being accused.
"By reason" means by a logical argument (*yutti*) that demonstrates the groundlessness of the accusation or its lack of foundation. "By statement" means...
By means of speech that conveys that meaning. After answering the charge with "Who has fallen [into an offense]? and so forth, to fall into evasion is to evade by talking about something else.

What is called "diverting the conversation to external matters" is the same as answering the charge—when it is said, "You have fallen into such-and-such an offense"—with "I have gone to Pāṭaliputta," and so forth; this alone is the distinction. For whoever...
When told, “You have committed an offense,” he says, “Who has committed it? What has been committed? In what has one committed it?
Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying? Or, when told, “You have seen such a thing,” he either says, “I did not hear it,” or turns his ear away;
this is called evading one matter with another. But as for one who is told, “You have committed such-and-such an offense,” [and so on].
When questioned, he says, "I have gone to Pāṭaliputta. When told again, "We do not ask about your going to Pāṭaliputta;
we ask about the offense," he then says, "I have gone to Rājagaha.
Whether you go to Rājagaha or to the brahmin's house, you have committed an offense. I obtained pork there," and so forth. This is *bahiddhā* (external).
How indeed does he drive it away? "The refuse of recluses" means that by wearing the dress of a recluse and merely resembling a recluse, one has become like refuse among recluses.
"Sweep away the *kāraṇḍava* weed" means that one should sweep away, without regard, a person who—due to their ruined virtue—is like refuse, just as one sweeps away actual refuse.
"Take it away! Cast out the chaff! means: pull him out like a Caṇḍāla who has become like chaff—having broken out in open, oozing leprosy while standing in the midst of Kṣatriyas and others.
For what reason? Because the Saṅghārāma was established for those possessing virtue, not for those lacking virtue.
It is with reference to this very point that he said: "Therefore, winnow away the chaff—the non-recluses who pride themselves on being recluses. Just as chaff...

Just as rice grains devoid of internal essence and lacking the kernel are seen only by their outer husks, so too do evil monks, though inwardly devoid of virtue, appear like monks by means of their external requisites such as the saffron robes; therefore, they are called "chaff.
Drive out that chaff, winnow it away, and scatter it—those who are in the ultimate sense not ascetics, yet who pride themselves on being ascetics merely by wearing the guise of an ascetic.

"Kappayāvho" means "you should fashion it"; it is said, "make it. "Patissatā" means "possessing mindfulness. The meaning is: "You will make an end of the suffering of saṃsāra; you will attain parinibbāna.
The commentary on the Kāraṇḍava Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mettāvagga is finished.
2. Mahāvagga 1.
Commentary on the Verañjasutta.
11. Regarding the first [case] of the second [sutta], "He was dwelling at Verañjā": here, *Verañjā* is a designation for that city; [the phrase] means "in that Verañjā.
The locative case is used in the sense of proximity (*samīpatthe*). Regarding "at the foot of the Naḷerupucimanda tree": here, *Naḷeru* is the name of a *yakkha*.
*Pucimanda* is a *nimba* tree. *Mūle* means "nearby. For this word *mūla* [is used in the sense of proximity, as in]: "one should pull up the roots..."
In such passages as “even as much as a stalk of usīra grass,” it is seen in the sense of the root of a root. In such passages as “greed is a root of unwholesomeness,” it refers to a non-common cause.
In such passages as “as long as the shadow extends at midday, and leaves fall in a windless place, to that extent is the vicinity of the tree’s root,” it refers to proximity.
Here, however, proximity is intended; therefore, by the nāḷeru-yakkha—
The meaning here should be understood as "in the vicinity of the Pucimanda tree that had been taken possession of.
It is said that this Pucimanda tree was delightful and beautiful, acting like a sovereign over many other trees, and it stood not far from that city in a place well-suited for coming and going.
Then the Blessed One, having gone to Verañjā, dwelt in a suitable location.
He dwelt in the lower part near that tree. Therefore it is said: “He was dwelling at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree.

Regarding “rising from his seat,” this means rising from the seat; thus he says, “he does not rise from his seat. The meaning is that he does not rise from the seat where he is sitting. And here, in the phrase “the old man...
having reached old age,” the accusative case is used in relation to the action of rising from the seat.
It does not exist. Therefore, the meaning should be understood by supplying the words “having seen [him] when he is old... having reached the stage of decline.
Alternatively, the accusative case is used in relation to the action of going out to meet;
therefore, the meaning of “he does not rise to meet him” should be understood as “he does not rise and go out to meet him,” for even going out to meet is called rising to meet.
For this has been said: "But rising upon seeing a teacher from afar and going forward to meet him is what is called 'rising'.
However, it should be understood that by the phrase "emerges from his seat," the absence of going forward to meet him is merely indicated as an illustration.
"In the sense of manifestation" means in the sense of what is termed the manifestation of the natural state (*pakati*). "Or does not pay homage" means...
It is said that he does not perceive [the person] as one who should be saluted.
That is ignorance (*aññāṇa*); it is the ignorance occurring by way of not knowing, [thinking]: "This person is not of a nature worthy for me to perform salutations and so forth.
Regarding "looking": "Indeed, it is suffering to dwell without respect and without deference; what now..."
He looked with the eye of knowledge by means of the very same sutta beginning with, "I would honor and revere either a recluse or a brahmin.
*Nipaccakārārahan* means worthy of prostration. *Sampatijāto* means born just a moment ago;
it is said that this was immediately after birth. *Uttarenamukho* means facing the northern direction. "Having walked seven steps... [the rest of the passage follows].
“...he surveyed the ten-thousandfold world system”— this refers to the following:
“It is the natural law, monks, that as soon as he is born, the Bodhisatta stands with his feet firm on even ground,
walks seven steps facing north, and while a white parasol is held over him, surveys all the directions.”
"He utters a bull-like cry"—
this was stated in the text because it describes looking toward all directions as if he were standing in the middle of the seven strides;
however, it should not be understood in this way, for he had already performed the surveying of the directions even before the seven strides.
For the Mahāsatta, having escaped from the hands of men, looked toward the eastern direction; thousands of world-systems became a single open space.
There, gods and humans, worshipping with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said:
"Great Being, there is no one even equal to you here, much less anyone superior. In this way, he looked toward the four directions and the four intermediate directions.
It should be understood that after surveying the ten directions—below and above—and seeing no one equal to himself, he proceeded with the seven-step stride, thinking, "This is the northern direction.

"He looked" means: when the miracle of the opening of the world occurred through the power of his merit, he looked with his own physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) at the thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*) that was becoming manifest; such is the meaning.
A “Great Man” (mahāpurisa) is a great person by virtue of birth, lineage, family, country, and so forth. “Foremost” (agga) means preeminent among all in terms of qualities.
“Eldest” (jeṭṭha) means, by virtue of qualities alone, the most senior among all; what is meant is that he is the most venerable in terms of his qualities.
“Best” (seṭṭha) means, by virtue of qualities alone, the most praiseworthy among all. As for the meaning, however, the latter two are synonyms for the first.
It should be understood. *Tayā* is the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
*Uttaritaro* means more excellent. *Patimānesi* means he honored. *Āsabhiṃ* means supreme. *Mayhaṃ abhivādanādiraho puggalo* means a person worthy of my acts of salutation and so forth;
that is, a person suitable for such actions as saluting me. Here, however, a compound should be seen due to the constant requirement of the genitive. *Tathāgata* means...
“From the Tathāgata, in the presence of the Tathāgata”—this is what is meant. “Of such a kind” refers to the nature of salutation and so forth.
“With bonds loosened by ripening” means that the bonds have become slack through ripening.

“That speech” refers to the speech beginning with, “I am not that, O Brahmin. If he were to say, “I am not one who lacks flavor, nor are those like me ones who lack flavor,” the Brahmin might become arrogant; therefore it is said, “for the purpose of producing softness of mind.”

"But what is 'he'?"—this is a masculine designation requiring a correlative; the meaning is, "What is that method? "By way of birth" means by way of birth as a kṣatriya and so forth. "By way of rebirth" means by way of rebirth among the devas.

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even those regarded as best," he shows that this applies even more so to those not regarded as best. "Rejoicing" means by way of craving accompanied by delight.

“Of those who are rejoicing”: of those who are being impassioned by way of powerful lust. The feeling of joy associated with craving that arises through the enjoyment of visible forms is called the “taste of form” because it is produced from form and gladdens the heart, just as the juices of mangoes and other fruits do.

“They draw forth” means they attract. “In the combination of the basis, object, and so forth” means in the combination of causes such as the physical basis and the objective field. “Thrusting forward” means...
Not exalting himself—that is, not praising himself—because he was unsuitable for the brahmin’s discourse spoken by way of self-praise.

However, in this context, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, in the phrase "by the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatassa*) in the sense of "abandoned" (*jahitā*), the genitive is used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "abandoned by the Tathāgata.
"Root" (*mūla*) refers to the root of existence (*bhava-mūla*). Although one should have said "made like a palm stump" (*tālavatthukatā*), [the text uses the form *tālavatthukātā*].
In expressions such as “oṭṭhamukho,” the middle word is elided and the vowel *a* is lengthened; thus, it is said “tālāvatthukatā.
Therefore, he says: “Their basis (vatthu) has been made like the base of a palmyra tree (tālāvatthu), hence they are ‘tālāvatthukatā’. In that context, the base of a palmyra tree is “tālavatthu.
Just as a place that was formerly the site of a monastery is called “ārāmavatthu” when the monastery is no longer there, [so too here].

It is said thus: when a palm tree has been uprooted along with its roots and only a mere spot remains, it is called a "palm-tree site" (*tālavatthu*) because that place was formerly the site of a palm tree.
"Of these" refers to visible forms, tastes, and so forth. But how is their site like a palm-tree site?

To this he says, "For just as... and so on. [This refers to] visible forms, tastes, and so forth, which are comprised of the feeling of joy associated with craving arisen through the enjoyment of visible forms and the rest.
It is said, “When the mere continuity of consciousness has been made their basis by virtue of having previously arisen,” because the continuity of consciousness serves as the foundation for them.
In that context, “previously” (*pubbe*) means earlier; it refers to the time when [the mind] was accompanied by lust.

They are called “made like the base of a palmyra tree” (*tālāvatthukatā*) because, like the base of a palmyra tree, they have been made the basis for themselves, such as visible forms, tastes, and so forth.
...are so called. By this, the non-recurrence of abandoned defilements is shown.

"By way of having the nature of not growing" means by way of having the characteristic of not growing. A palmyra tree with its top cut off is "a palmyra stump" because it has become a place where leaves, fruit, and so forth no longer have a basis;
thus he said, "made like a palmyra tree with its top cut off. By this, [it is meant that] "it is made like a palmyra stump..."
The analysis (*viggaha*) shown here is: "made into a palmyra-tree stump" (*tālāvatthukatā*).

In this context, however, it should be understood that although one ought to say "made into a stump like a palmyra tree" (*avatthutālakatā*), the word *tāla* (palmyra) has been placed last as an adjective, hence it is expressed as "made into a palmyra-tree stump" (*tālāvatthukatā*).
By this meaning, he shows that by the expression "the nature of having the quality of ripening" (*vipākadhammadhamma*), [it refers to] the states of form, taste, and so forth.
Previously, wholesome and unwholesome states that had arisen were grasped;

although they had arisen, because they were severed by the army of the Path—the craving and ignorance which are like the crown of a palm tree—they became incapable of producing resultant aggregates in the future that are like palm leaves.
Therefore, the visible forms, tastes, and so forth are said to be "made into a palm stump" (tālāvatthukatā). In this sense, [the phrase] "for those who delight" (*abhinandantānaṃ*)...

They say that by this term, wholesome joy (*kusalasomanassa*) is also included. Regarding the phrase "having brought them to non-existence" (*anabhāvaṃ katvā*), the prefix *anu-* has the same meaning as the word *pacchā* (afterwards);
thus he says, "so that there is no subsequent state for them," and so forth.
As for the statement, "The method you have in mind does not exist," this refers to that which is characterized by the absence of the essence of harmony consisting of veneration and the like.
You state that the reason is his lack of the flavor of courtesy; however, that reason is not so, meaning it does not exist.

But surely this brahmin spoke thus, "Master Gotama is devoid of the flavor of courtesy," with reference to a figurative expression (pariyāya) consisting in the absence of the flavor of such things as salutation?
When it is said, "That figurative expression does not exist," does it not follow that the Blessed One performs salutations and the like?
Pointing out this undesirable consequence, he said, "But is it not so," and so forth.
"In all the modes" means in all the sections. "Merely spoken with reference to" refers to that which the brahmin had in mind when he said, "Venerable Gotama is without enjoyment," and so on;
and that which the Blessed One had in mind when he admitted to himself such things as being without enjoyment.
This was said with reference to that alone. "Enjoyment through desire and lust" means enjoyment by way of desire and lust.
"Another way" means another reason.
"Family custom and action" means action characterized as family conduct; the meaning is "family behavior. "Non-performance" means...

The state of non-doing. Although there is the general statement, “of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states,” one should understand that the remaining unwholesome states—excluding those already mentioned—are to be taken by way of the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*). Thus he says, “having set aside those states,” and so forth;
the meaning is: having set aside those unwholesome states previously mentioned, such as bodily misconduct and the rest. “Various kinds” means of many types.
“This world-tradition” means this worldly custom characterized by such acts as saluting the elders.

Since the arising of lust occurs through attachment to ornaments and the like in the case of non-returner Brahmās, and through attachment to robes and the like in the case of non-returner bhikkhus, it should be understood that the abandonment of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure alone is effected by the path of non-returning;
thus he said, “of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Regarding forms and so forth...

The lust arising toward the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), which are portions of objective sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), should be understood as "lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Here, the word *guṇa* denotes a "portion," as in such expressions as "the qualities of youth (*vayoguṇā*) are gradually abandoned.
"Associated with two types of unwholesome consciousness" means associated with the two types of consciousness accompanied by mental displeasure (*domanassa*). Of delusion...
Because it is common to all unwholesome states, he said, "of the origin of all unwholesome states. "Of the remainder" refers to personality view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth.
"He feels disgust, as it were" means he feels as if he were disgusted, thinking, "I am well-born, handsome, and wise;
how could I possibly perform such acts as saluting others? Or, "he feels disgust" means he observes [them with aversion]. Being disgusted by unwholesome states...
"He feels disgust even for their state of possession" means "he feels disgust for the attainment (*samāpatti*) of unwholesome states.

"Attainment" is a synonym for this very term; it refers to the act of attaining (*samāpajjana*) or the state of being possessed (*samaṅgibhāva*). "Of a decorative nature" (*maṇḍanajātika*) means having a decorative character, that is to say, having the habit of decorating.
"Disgustingness" (*jegucchita*) refers to the quality of having a disposition toward disgust.
“World-preeminent action” (*lokajeṭṭhakakamma*) means the action to be performed by those who are world-preeminent, or action that is regarded as the best in the world.

“Therein” (*tattha*) refers to both of those two alternative meanings. “Meaning expressed by a word” (*padattha*) is the meaning conveyed by a word; what is meant is the meaning of the phrasing (*byañjanattha*). Or, regarding the phrase “it deserves discipline” (*vinayaṃ vā arahati*):
here, “discipline” (*vinaya*) is the act of disciplining (*vinayana*), which means subduing (*niggaṇhana*). Therefore he said: “subduing” (*niggahaṃ*).

“It is said that he ‘deserves’ (arahati). But surely, among the two alternative meanings stated first—the sense of self (sakattha) and the sense of deserving (arahattha)—a taddhita suffix is observed according to the characteristics of grammar;
however, it is not [observed] in this sense of “teaching the Dhamma for the sake of discipline” (vinayāya dhammaṃ deseti).
Therefore, how can there be a taddhita suffix here? To this he replied: “For the application of taddhita suffixes is manifold.”

And here, the variety [of these formations] is to be understood from the perspective of worldly convention. For instance, in whatever sense the application of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs in the world, in each such case the function of that secondary derivative is established by worldly usage; thus, the function of secondary derivatives is manifold.

Therefore, just as one who says, "Do not make a sound," is called "one who makes no sound" (*māsaddika*), so too one who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the Vinaya is called "one who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the Vinaya."
The intended meaning is that it is called "vinayika" (pertaining to discipline).
"A wretched man" refers to a person who is miserable due to being devoid of virtuous qualities.

"Without investigating the phonemes" means that, as in the case of words such as *tissadatta*, one does not perform an investigation of the phonemes by thinking, "In this sense, this is the suffix"; what is meant is that it is done by way of an unestablished nominal base (*pāṭipadika*).

Although it was said, “By the attainment of a womb in the world of the gods,” since the taking of a womb does not occur among the remaining devas—excluding the earth-dwelling devas—it should be understood that here "attainment of a womb" refers specifically to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Demonstrating this very point by explaining it further, he said: “It leads to the acquisition of rebirth-linking in the world of the gods. “Assa” means of the respectful service consisting of prostration and so forth.
"Showing the fault in taking rebirth in a mother’s womb" means showing the impurity regarding the mother;
just as one wishing to revile someone might revile them by pointing out the fault of being born from the womb of a slave-woman, saying "you are the son of a slave," so too,
even while reviling the Blessed One by showing the fault in his taking rebirth in his mother’s womb, he spoke thus.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "From the womb" means from the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the world of the gods. For this very reason he said: "The intended meaning is that he is incapable of reaching rebirth in the world of the gods.
Regarding the analysis (*viggaha*) "one who has no womb is *apagabbha*," while showing the intended meaning through one particular method, he said:
"Because he is excluded from the womb of the world of the gods, he is subject to obtaining a lowly womb in the future."
The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because he is one who partakes in obtaining a low womb even in the future, therefore the intention is:

"he may have a low womb," thus he is called *apagabbha*. Again, showing the intention for that same analysis (*viggaha*) by adapting it to the method stated below—"displaying [himself] through anger... etc."—he said: "Or [he is so called] because of his lowliness within the mother's womb..."

The intention is that "there was dwelling in a womb. The word *gabbha* has two senses: it is a synonym for the mother’s womb, as in "the young man dwells in the womb" (*gabbhe vasati māṇavo*), and so forth;
and it is a synonym for a being born within the mother’s womb, as in "down to the causing of a miscarriage," and so forth.
Taking the sense of the mother’s womb here, he spoke thus to show the meaning: "In the future..."
“Womb-dwelling” (*gabbhaseyyā*): dwelling in a womb is *gabbhaseyyā*. “By the unsurpassed path” means by the supreme path.

Because the defilements of karma have been destroyed by that path, he says, “because it is the cause of destruction. “The other three as well” refers to the egg-born, the moisture-born, and the spontaneously born.

And here, although only “womb-dwelling” should be mentioned in accordance with the term “one who is not subject to rebirth in a womb” (*apagabbho*), it is mentioned [here] by way of incidental connection.
However, since it is appropriate to state everything that can be obtained, it should be understood that the "re-arising of renewed existence" (punabbhavābhinibbatti) is also mentioned.
Now, demonstrating the various types of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) by means of the word *gabbha* in its sevenfold sense, he says: “Moreover,” and so forth.
In this alternative interpretation, both “lying in the womb” (*gabbhaseyyā*) and “the re-arising of renewed existence” (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) are [treated] solely by way of lying in the womb.

They also say that it is so stated. But surely, since it is said, “The lying in a womb in the future has been abandoned,” it follows that only the *seyyā* (lying) in the womb has been abandoned, not the *gabbha* (womb) itself; thus he says, “And just as...,” and so forth.
Furthermore, why is the term “renewed existence” (*punabbhava*) used instead of merely saying “rebirth” (*abhinibbatti*)? To this he says, “And what is called ‘rebirth’...,” and so forth.
"Non-rearising" refers to the manifestation of phenomena that arise moment by moment.
"The element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*): herein, it is called the element of phenomena because it holds all phenomena without exception and examines them as they truly are;
it is the nature of awakening to phenomena according to their true individual essence. This is a designation for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Having penetrated" means...
"Having realized" means having attained; what is meant is "for the sake of attainment. "He has reached the elegance of teaching" (*desanāvilāsa*):
the "elegance of teaching" is the capacity to demonstrate [the Dhamma] by way of turning it over according to one's inclination; the meaning is that he has reached or acquired that.
"The expansion of compassion" (*karuṇāvipphāra*) is the pervading of all beings with great compassion. Furthermore, the characteristic of suchness (*tādilakkhaṇa*)...
Having clarified it by means of a simile, he says, “even-mindedness like the earth.

Just as the earth does not waver and does not fall into favor or aversion when clean or unclean things are placed upon it, or when it is cut or broken, so too, because one has abandoned favor and aversion toward the desirable and undesirable, or gain and loss, the state of having an unwavering mind is called “even-mindedness like the earth. Regarding the term *akuppadhamma*: here, *akuppadhamma*...

Some say that it is called "attainment of fruition" (*phalasamāpatti*). However, our own view is that its meaning here should be understood as "the state of being unshakable by nature, due to a mind equal to the earth even when others are reviling.
"Pervaded by old age" means enveloped by old age. "Death is near for the Brahmin because of his advanced age" is said by way of esteem (*sambhāvana*).
“Having died today,” and so forth, was said. “But with great exertion” means with such great exertion as was produced by thinking, “It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
“An incomparable state of priority” means a state of priority that is not shared by any other.
It is “incomparable” (appaṭisama) because there is no equal (paṭisama) to it; it is the state of priority.
"Flapping their wings" means moving their feet. "Of those emerging" is a genitive used for the purpose of selection (*niddhāraṇe sāmivacana*); the meaning is "among those who have emerged.
"He is to be called the eldest" means that the chick which emerges first from the eggshell is to be called the eldest;
the sense is that he would be so designated. "Arranging them together" means bringing them into alignment. Even those included within the three planes...
"Beings have entered into the shell of ignorance" means they are enveloped by ignorance that has not been abandoned here and there;
thus he said, "among beings who have entered into the shell of ignorance. "The eggshell" refers to the seed-vessel.

"In the world-dwelling" (*lokasannivāse*): the world itself, in the sense of being a place where [beings] gather and dwell together, is the world-dwelling—the community of beings (*sattanikāya*). "Perfect enlightenment" (*sammāsambodhiṃ*)...
In this context, *samma* has the sense of "unperverted" (*aviparīta*), while the prefix *sam-* indicates the meaning "by oneself" (*sāma*).

Therefore, because one awakens to and penetrates the four truths by oneself in an unperverted manner, it is called "perfect self-enlightenment" (*sammāsambodhi*); thus, the Path is so designated. Hence he said:
"Perfect and by oneself enlightenment," the meaning being "that which is perfectly and by oneself awakened. Alternatively, *samma* is a word signifying "praiseworthy."
The word *saṃ* means "beautiful"; thus he said, "Alternatively, *bodhi* is praised and beautiful.

Regarding the phrase "because it does not bestow all qualities": this means because it does not bestow every single quality. For one who does not give all qualities is called "one who bestows non-all-qualities" (*asabbaguṇadāyaka*);

this is an *asamattha-samāsa* (a compound where the members are not semantically equivalent) used for the sake of clarity, just as in the expression "mouths that do not see the sun" (*asūriyapassāni mukhāni*). "The three knowledges" refers to [the knowledge] of one who possesses the necessary support (*upanissaya*).
Together with the fruit of arahantship itself, it bestows the three types of clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*). Now, one might ask:

since among these three types of clear knowledge the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) is included within the path, how is it appropriate to say that "the path bestows the three types of clear knowledge"? This is not a fault.
Even though the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is indeed included within the path, when the eightfold path exists, [it is bestowed] together with the knowledge of the path.
"The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) become fulfilled" means that it is said, "the Path bestows the three knowledges.

Regarding the "six direct knowledges" (cha abhiññā), the same principle applies here as well. "The knowledge of the disciple’s perfection" (sāvakapāramiñāṇa) refers to the mundane and supramundane knowledge that must be acquired by the foremost disciples.
Regarding "the knowledge of private enlightenment" (paccekabodhiñāṇa), the meaning should be understood in this very same manner. "He fully understood" (abbhaññāsi) means he knew.
And since this knowing is not by way of hearsay and so forth, he said, "I have penetrated" (*paṭivijjhi*); the meaning is that he made it directly manifest before his eyes.
Furthermore, this penetration is not like the penetration of characteristics from a distance; thus he said, "I have attained" (*pattomhi*); the meaning is that he reached it.
And this reaching is not by going there oneself; thus he said, "I have realized" (*adhigatomhi*); the meaning is that he acquired it by way of its arising within his own mental continuum.
“Applying the simile” means the correct application of the meaning of the simile to the object of comparison (*upameyya*).

“By way of the meaning” means by way of the meaning of the object of comparison. Just as the performance of the threefold action upon the eggs by a hen is the primary cause for the chicks emerging from their eggshells, so too is the performance of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta.
He said, "The threefold practice of contemplation is the primary cause for emerging from the eggshell of ignorance," because [the text] states, "Just as that hen...
and so forth. Because it is said "in the continuity" (*santāne*), the continuity is like an egg; the Buddha-qualities are like the chick that has emerged from outside.
And in meaning, the Buddha-qualities are the Buddha himself, as it is said: "Vāseṭṭha, this belongs to the Tathāgata..."
Because of the statement, "The 'Dhamma-body' is also a designation.

"The thinning of the eggshell of ignorance" means the thinning of the eggshell of ignorance by way of powerful insight; and ignorance is similar to an eggshell due to their common characteristic of obscuring.
"Hardness and rigidity" is stated in order to exclude the possibility that what has become soft might again attain a state of hardness. "Sharpness, hardness, clarity, and courage" [is stated].

Herein, when formations are being comprehended, the penetration of bliss by insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) through the power of the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) is its sharpness;
and even after having penetrated them, its non-dulling and unblunted nature is due to not overstepping [the object] by means of the faculty of mindfulness (*sati-indriya*).
For some arrows, though sharp, become blunted upon hitting the target; this [insight-knowledge] is not like that. And even while possessing this unblunted nature, it functions with subtlety.
The state of clarity by way of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) should be understood as being free from the agitation caused by the active manifestation of defilements;

and even while possessing that clarity, the state of heroism by way of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) should be understood as the thorough overcoming of the enemies that are the defilements without wavering in the interim.
Thus, it should be seen that by these modes, it is precisely the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) that is being referred to. Of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
"The time of transformation" refers to the attainment of the state of leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminibhāva*) through insight (*vipassanā*).
And at that time, she is as if bearing the embryo of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*); thus it is said, "the time of conceiving the embryo.

"Having caused her to conceive the embryo" means having caused her to conceive the embryo immediately after equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), by way of the culmination of conformity-insight (*sikhāppattānulomavipassanā*), for the purpose of giving birth to the Path (*magga*).
"On the side of direct knowledge" (*abhiññāpakkhe*) means on the side of mundane direct knowledge (*lokīyābhiññā*). For supramundane direct knowledge has already shattered the eggshell of ignorance.
However, it should be understood that where some manuscripts write "on the side of the six direct knowledges" (*chābhiññāpakkhe*), that is not the correct reading.
"Eldest" (*jeṭṭha*) means eldest by virtue of being most senior; "best" (*seṭṭha*) means most praiseworthy because of being supreme in all qualities.
Now, showing the connection (*anusandhi*) for the teaching beginning with “But energy was aroused by me, brahmin,” he said, “Thus the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Therein, “from the prior stage onwards” means starting from the arousal of energy belonging to the prior stage of meditation.
“With muddled mindfulness” (*muṭṭhassati*) means with ruined mindfulness; the meaning is “devoid of mindfulness. “With an agitated body” (*sāraddhakāya*)—

"With a noble body of chariots. "At the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) means at the place where the state of being the "essence" (*maṇḍa*) of the knowledge known as "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) was attained.

For "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is said to be wisdom (*paññā*). Since that [wisdom] became the essence—that is, clear and settled—here, that location is designated as the "seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
"Exerted" means grasped by way of the quality of endurance known as firm effort, without making the undertaking slack.
Therefore he said, "set in motion without slackness. "Unshrunk" means not contracted, having not fallen into contraction through indolence.
"Established" means having approached the object by way of non-floating, which is known as plunging; therefore he said, "by way of being directed toward the object.
It does not forget because it proceeds by way of destroying forgetfulness.

Unconfused. Although the mind itself is tranquilized by way of mental tranquility (*cittappassaddhi*), and the body becomes tranquilized by way of bodily tranquility (*kāyappassaddhi*), nevertheless, because bodily tranquility arises only together with mental tranquility and not apart from it, it is said: "by way of bodily and mental tranquility. Regarding bodily tranquility...
Because it brings about the calming of both bodies, it is said: "The material body also becomes calmed.
And that, indeed, is the body. "Free from distress" means free from the distress of the defilements.

For when the mental body (nāmakāya) is free from distress, the material body also has its distress and fever subsided. "Well-placed" refers to [the mind] which was previously characterized by wandering among various objects.
Having cut off distraction, it is properly applied and established by bringing about a state of non-distraction upon a single object alone.
Therefore he said, "well-established," and so forth. The mind's state of non-unification is its flickering due to distraction;
since that does not occur when there is one-pointedness, he said, "one-pointed, immovable, unwavering. "To this extent" means: "undertaken..."

By the passage beginning with “But indeed...,” the accomplishment of the functions of energy (*vīriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), and concentration (*samādhi*) is demonstrated. [Objection:
Is it not the case that the accomplishment of the functions of faith (*saddhā*) and wisdom (*paññā*) must also be desired as part of the preliminary practice for *jhāna*? [Reply: True;

however, because that [accomplishment] is established even without being explicitly stated due to its immediate proximity [to the others], it was not included. For in the absence of faith, the initiation of energy and so forth are simply impossible; and when there is the embracing of wisdom (*paññā-pariggahe*), [the rest follow].

Furthermore, it should be understood that if these [qualities] were absent, there could be no undertaking of the method (ñāya) and so forth; likewise, since qualities such as non-slackening and non-confusion belong to energy and the rest, the accomplishment of the function of wisdom (paññā) is included here by the very mention of non-slackening and the other qualities.

Alternatively, it should be seen that the path preliminary to jhāna concludes with concentration (samādhi) in order to show that the function of concentration is required in excess for the development of jhāna.
"It is said" is how it should be understood.
Since the aggregates in past existences, as well as the names and clans associated with them, are all included under "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*), he asked, "What does it make known? Past lives.
Ignorance (*moha*) is called "darkness" (*tama*) because it is like darkness in its quality of concealing.
He said: "It is delusion itself. It is called "making manifest" (*obhāsakaraṇa*) because it must be made; the manifestation itself is the making, hence "making manifest. The meaning is:
in the sense of being produced as a state of manifestation by its own conditions.

The remainder is a term of praise, so it is said because it makes known the specific modes of activity that dispel their opposites. By the phrase "ignorance has been dispelled," in the sense of discerning...

It should be understood that this meaning of "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) is also illustrated here. Why? Because by the phrase "since true knowledge has arisen," it is shown that ignorance (*avijjā*) is the opposite of true knowledge;
and its being the opposite is demonstrated by the fact that ignorance is to be abandoned while true knowledge is the factor that abandons it.
This same method applies to the other two phrases as well: "darkness is dispelled, destroyed. Why? Since light... [has arisen].
This refers by extension to the meaning "arisen. In the sense of burning away and tormenting the defilements (*kilesa*), energy (*vīriya*) is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*);

thus he said, "ardent through the ardor of energy," which means "possessed of energy. "Of one whose mind is directed" (*pesitattassa*) means of one whose mind has been released toward the accomplishment of the intended goal.
Just as [in the phrase] "dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute," so too for another...
The intention is: "of anyone like me. "Of one devoted to the exertion" means of one intent upon the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

"Encompassed by the knowledge of review" means that it is not merely [the attainment] as in the case of the acquisition of the first two knowledges; this is the intention. "Showing" means showing by way of a conclusion, for its essential nature has already been shown previously.
By the phrase "born three times," however, he shows this: "I, Brahmin, am indeed born through the first knowledge..."
“Because he lacks anyone born before him or born simultaneously with him, he is the eldest and most senior among all;

how much more so, then, since he has been ‘born’ three times through the three types of higher knowledge (vijjā). Regarding the phrase “by means of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa), there is knowledge of the past”:

this should be construed as having manifested the knowledge of the past by means of the knowledge of past lives, due to their commonality in having the past as their object and because of the latter’s nature as a manifestation of the former. In that context:
"Knowledge of the past" means unimpeded knowledge regarding the past categories (koṭṭhāsa) comprised of the past aggregates, bases, and elements.
Since the divine eye knowledge has the present as its object, and since the knowledge of rebirths according to karma and the knowledge of the future also succeed by way of the divine eye,
they are considered ancillary knowledges to the divine eye and are thus included within the divine eye itself.
And because the knowledge of others' minds is established for one who is thus stationed, it is said: "The knowledge of the present and future portions by means of the divine eye.

In this context, "by means of the divine eye" refers to the divine-eye knowledge together with its peripheral range. "The present portion and the future portion" constitute "the present-and-future portions";
the knowledge therein is "knowledge of the present-and-future portions. [This occurs] precisely through the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

Because other unique qualities of a Buddha—such as the remaining six uncommon knowledges, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha—just like the knowledge of omniscience, are accomplished through the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), it is said: "by the destruction of the taints, all mundane and supramundane qualities.
Therefore, he said: "having manifested all the qualities of omniscience."

"Pītivipphāraparipuṇṇagattacitto" means one whose body and mind are filled by the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*). "Aññāṇaṃ" has the sense of "of ignorance" (*aññāṇassa*); for due to its connection with the particle *dhi*, this is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Verañja Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sīha Sutta.
12. Second, a *saṇṭhāgāra* is simply one large hall.
For on occasions such as the time of military mobilization, kings sit there and make arrangements—determining boundaries by saying, "Let so many go forward, let so many stay behind," and so forth;
therefore, that place is called a *saṇṭhāgāra*. And from the point of view of being a place of mobilization...
It is called a *santhāgāra* because when they arrive, those kings remain there for one or two days while their houses are being prepared with cow-dung plaster and other such treatments;
or it is a *santhāgāra* because it is the house (*agāra*) where those kings deliberate together on affairs of state.
For they are republican kings (*gaṇarājāno*), and therefore a matter that has arisen cannot be decided by one person alone.
Success is achieved; it is necessary for all to have the desire [to act], and therefore everyone, having assembled there, gives instruction.
Hence it is said: “The household along with the instruction in its purpose.

Or rather, because they assemble there and deliberate upon the duties of domestic life in such a manner as, “It is appropriate to plow at this time; it is appropriate to sow at this time,” and so forth.
Therefore, it is called a *santhāgāra* because they spread out a household life that is both full of gaps and without gaps.
The relinquishing of requisites such as children, wife, and wealth constitutes the *pāramīs*. The relinquishing of one’s own limbs constitutes the *upapāramīs*.
The relinquishing of one’s own life constitutes the *paramattha-pāramīs*. Conduct for the benefit of kinsmen is *ñātatthacariyā*. Conduct for the benefit of the world is *lokatthacariyā*.

The practice for the welfare of the world (*lokatthacariyā*). The range of knowledge (*ñāṇacāra*) consisting in the knowledge of the ownership of one’s actions (*kammassakata*), the mastery of blameless spheres of action, spheres of craft, and branches of science;
the mastery of the aggregates, bases, and so forth; and the investigation of the three characteristics—this is the practice of a Buddha (*buddhacariyā*).
[This is accomplished] by one who relinquishes the five great renunciations through the relinquishing of limbs, vehicles, wealth, kingdom, children, wife, and retinue.

Although generosity (*sati*) is included within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) as one of the great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*), it is mentioned separately among the five great renunciations both to demonstrate its specific nature as a particular form of renunciation and to show that it is extremely difficult to perform.
For that very reason, the renunciation of the eyes is mentioned separately from the renunciation of limbs.
Furthermore, even though they share the common quality of being renunciations, the renunciation of wife and children is mentioned separately from the renunciation of wealth and kingdom.
It has been said: "The brief summary is just the going forth.

Regarding "the seven contemplations": these are the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*), the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*), the contemplation of dispassion (*virāgānupassanā*), the contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*), and the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*).

"Having investigated" (*anuviccakāraṃ*) means having made an investigation. To show the two reasons why they support those who have entered discipleship under them while remaining in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, the passage beginning with "Why? (*kasmā*) was stated.
“Gradual discourse” means a discourse that should be told in a gradual sequence. What, then, is it? It is the discourse on giving and so forth.

Among these, the discourse on giving is spoken first because it occurs even among ordinary people, because it is common to all beings, because it is easy to perform, and because it serves as the means for establishing oneself in virtue (*sīla*).
For a person whose nature is one of relinquishment, due to their state of non-attachment toward objects of possession...

One undertakes the precepts with ease and becomes well-established therein. Following the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue is presented because virtue purifies both the donor and the recipient;
because it speaks of benefiting others while prohibiting the harming of others; because it speaks of the nature of action (kiriya-dhamma) while implying the nature of non-action (akiriya-dhamma);
and because, after speaking of the cause for the attainment of wealth, it speaks of the cause for the attainment of existence (bhava). Thus, the discourse on virtue follows the discourse on giving.
It was said [thus] for the purpose of showing that "this virtue is dependent on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), and this prosperity of existence is its fruit.
And by means of these bases of meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue— which are distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior—
these immeasurable prosperities of divine enjoyment, distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior, [are attained] among the Cātumahārājika devas and so forth.
Following that, the discourse on heaven (*saggakathā*) is for the purpose of showing that [heaven] is to be attained.
Following heaven, the discourse on the Path (*magga*) is for the purpose of showing that while this heaven is defiled by lust and so forth, the Noble Path is entirely undefiled.
And when teaching the Path, for the purpose of demonstrating the means for its realization, all sensual pleasures (*kāmā*)—let alone those included within heaven—are shown to be such.
The danger of sensual pleasures is that they have many disadvantages, are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. Their contemptuousness and baseness is expressed by the description:
"They are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unconnected with the goal. The corruption therein is that all states of existence (bhava) serve as the basis for the defilements (kilesa).
And the benefit in renunciation (nekkhamma) should be explained as Nibbāna, which is entirely free from corruption.
Regarding the phrase "this meaning is being sought," it should be understood that the word *iti* here is used in the sense of "beginning with.
"The source of all happiness" means the cause of all happiness—whether pertaining to this life, the future life, or associated with Nibbāna.
For whatever is called the happiness of wealth in the world, all of that is dependent upon giving; this point is well known.
Furthermore, giving is indeed a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) even for that happiness associated with jhāna, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
It is called "the root of prosperities" because it is the source of all human prosperities— such as the various types of success in this world including regional sovereignty, glory, power,

and the excellence of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) resplendent with the seven treasures— as well as the divine prosperities belonging to the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth, or whatever else [there may be].
Furthermore, there are other prosperities as well, and this is the root cause of them all. Regarding "of enjoyments" (*bhogānaṃ*):

it is the foundation for those things called "enjoyment" in the sense that they are to be enjoyed—namely, pleasant and agreeable forms and so forth, or the pleasures of use based upon them—by virtue of providing a stable basis.
Regarding "of one who has gone astray" (*visamagatassa*): it means one who has met with calamity. "Refuge" (*tāṇaṃ*) means protection, because of the act of guarding from that [calamity].
“Leṇa” (a shelter) means a place of retreat for one being overwhelmed by calamities. “Gati” (a destination) means a place to be gone to. “Parāyaṇa” (a refuge) means a resort.
“Avassaya” (a support) means a reliance that prevents one from falling into ruin. “Ārammaṇa” (an object) means an object of attachment.
“Like a lion-throne made of jewels” means like a great seven-limbed lion-throne made of all kinds of gems. For it is thus [for him].
Having become of great value, it is shown to have the sense of providing total protection against falling into the lower realms.
Because it causes one to find a firm footing in whatever place one goes, like the great earth;
and just as a supporting rope is a prop for a weak man when he is rising up or standing still, so too is giving a support for the rebirth of beings in a state of prosperity.
And because it is a condition for stability, he said: "In the sense of being an object, it is like a supporting rope.

"In the sense of crossing over suffering" means in the sense of crossing over the states of suffering in the miserable destinies (*duggati*). "In the sense of providing consolation" means in the sense of providing consolation from the danger posed by enemies such as greed and stinginess.

"In the sense of protection from fear" means in the sense of guarding against the fear of poverty. "By the stains of stinginess, etc."... [text fragment] ...means by the stains of stinginess and so forth.
By means of the mental impurities such as stinginess, greed, hatred, pride, envy, wrong view, and doubt. "In the sense of being unsullied" means by way of being undefiled.

"Of these" refers to the impurities of stinginess and so forth. "In the sense of being difficult to assail" refers to those very same [impurities]. "In the sense of being without trepidation" means by way of the absence of any cause for fear.
For a donor, a master of giving, does not tremble before anyone even in this present life, much less [in the future].

In the future. "In the sense of being powerful" means by way of great strength. For a donor, as a master of giving, is powerful through the strength of his faction in the present, but in the future he is powerful even through physical strength and so forth.

"In the sense of being esteemed as an auspicious blessing" means by way of being universally recognized as a cause for prosperity. Leading from a state of misfortune to a state of success is the bringing [beings] to the land of safety.
Now, in order to demonstrate the quality of giving even through the practice of the Great Awakening (*mahābodhicaryā*), it is said: "This so-called giving," and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase "by one who delivers oneself," it is shown that "Great Beings, seeing the fruit of giving correctly, relinquish even their own lives;
therefore, what wise person indeed would form an attachment to external objects, let alone [to lesser things]."
He gives advice. Now, showing that all the worldly and supramundane excellences in their highest degree proceed from giving alone, he said, "For giving," and so forth.

Therein, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are for one's own benefit alone, whereas the attainment of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) is for both one's own benefit and the benefit of others; thus, to show this, it is placed after them.

The prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) has been described. To show that those [prosperities] are mundane (*lokiya*), whereas these are supramundane (*lokuttara*), the passage beginning with "the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections" (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) was stated.
Furthermore, to demonstrate the progressive degree of excellence—superior, more superior, and most superior—among them, the threefold knowledge (*ñāṇattaya*) was stated in sequence.

Moreover, the fact that giving (*dāna*) serves as the condition for those [knowledges] has already been explained below. By this very [explanation], its [status as a condition] for the prosperity of a Brahmā (*brahmasampatti*) is also [established].
It should be understood that the state of being a condition is thus illustrated.
Now, what is called "giving" (dāna) is the relinquishing of one's own possessions to others out of a desire for their welfare or a desire for their honor;
therefore, it is not the case that a donor, as a person, kills others or takes away what belongs to others.

"This is impossible" he said, [meaning] "one who gives a gift is able to undertake virtue. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, because virtue brings about a particular excellence of beauty.
The same principle applies here when it is said, "there is no flower like the flower of virtue.
Regarding the statement, "there is no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue," there is the verse beginning with "Sandalwood or tagara... and so forth.
One should speak by citing Jātaka verses such as: “The fragrance of seers who have long since gone forth, having departed from the body, travels with the wind.
For morality is indeed the ornament, the decoration, and the perfumed unguent of sentient beings; it brings about the state of being worthy of being seen by others.
Therefore, he said: “By the ornament of virtue,” and so forth.
"This heaven is attained" was said with reference to the virtue undertaken by those of middle capacity. For this very reason, Sakka, the King of the Gods, said:
"By an inferior holy life one is reborn among Khattiyas;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified."

*Iṭṭha* means pleasant. *Kanta* means desirable. *Manāpa* means that which increases mental delight. To demonstrate its state of being "pleasant" and so forth, it is said: "Herein, play is constant," and so on.
*Dosa* refers to the state of being corrupted by impermanence and so forth, and by having little gratification and so forth, because of which they do not please the minds of the wise.
Alternatively, it is called *ādīnava* because it proceeds (*vāti*) from the beginning (*ādi*), namely, extreme wretchedness. And thus are sensual pleasures in their true nature.

They present themselves to those who reflect upon them. "The state of being base" means a lowly condition that is practiced by the inferior and not practiced by the superior. "Corruption" means the quality of being oppressive and tormenting.
"The advantage in renunciation" means that here, "as many as are the dangers in sensual pleasures, so many are their opposites in renunciation."
Furthermore, he proclaimed the advantages of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) in this manner: “Moreover, this renunciation is unconfined and undefiled;

it has gone forth from sensual pleasures, gone forth from the perception of sensual pleasure, gone forth from thoughts of sensual pleasure, gone forth from the fever of sensual pleasure, and gone forth from the perception of ill-will,” and so on.
He also made manifest and praised the virtues of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), etc.

"Wholesome mind" (*kalla-citta*) means a workable mind; because the mental defects such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) have been removed by the teaching that proceeded previously, it is a mind capable of action through its attainment of the state of being a fit vessel for the subsequent teaching.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it says "healthy mind" (*aroga-citta*) because lack of faith and the other defects are like diseases of the mind, and at that time they have departed.
The mind is pliant through the departure of defilements such as views and conceit. It is free from hindrances through the departure of sensual desire and the like.
It is uplifted through the possession of sublime rapture and gladness in right practice. Therein, it is confident through the perfection of faith.
"When the Blessed One knew"—this is the connection. Alternatively, "the fit mind" means a healthy mind due to the departure of sensual desire.
"Soft mind" means a mind that is not rigid due to the departure of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) through the influence of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Unobstructed mind" means a mind that is not covered by that [rigidity] because it is free from distraction due to the departure of restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*).

"Exalted mind" means a mind that is not dejected due to being uplifted by the departure of sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*). "Serene mind" means a mind that is resolutely intent upon right practice due to the departure of doubt (*vicikicchā*).
In this way, the meaning of the remaining phrases here should be understood.
With the words "Just as," etc., he demonstrates by means of a simile both the lion’s abandonment of defilements and the arising of the Noble Path.
"Apagatakāḷakaṃ" means free from blackness. "Sammadeva" means quite well indeed. "Rajanaṃ" refers to the various kinds of dye, such as blue, yellow, red, and so forth.
"Should accept" means he would take it up; he would become radiant. "On that very seat" means on that very sitting posture.

By this, his state of being a swift practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*), his possession of sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññatā*), and his state of having a pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññatā*) are demonstrated.

"Dustless" (*virajaṃ*) means dustless through the disappearance of the dust of lust and so forth that leads to rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*). Through the removal of the stains of views and doubt without remainder...

"Stainless" (*vītamala*). Or, it is "dustless" (*viraja*) by virtue of being free from the dust of defilements (*kilesa*) to be abandoned by the first path; it is "stainless" by virtue of the departure of the stain of the fivefold misconduct (*dussīlya*).

Why was it said, "for the purpose of showing the mode of its arising"? This is stated in response to the objection: "Is it not the case that path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) has the unconditioned dhamma (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*) as its object?
Regarding the phrase "penetrating" (*paṭivijjhantaṃ*) therein, it means by way of penetration through non-delusion (*asammoha-paṭivedha*).
[He is] penetrating [the truth]. Therefore he said, "by way of function. Herein, this is the correlation with the simile: the mind is like the cloth;
the state of the cloth being soiled by adventitious stains is like the state of the mind being defiled by the stains of lust and so forth;
the stone slab for washing is like the progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā); the water is like faith; and having moistened it with water, [using] ash, cow dung, chaff, and lye...

Just as one applies a washing process to a cloth after rubbing out black stains, so too, having moistened it again and again with the moisture of faith, one loosens the defects by means of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
then, through the method of hearing and so forth, one exerts energy in purifying the mind.
By that application, just as the removal of black stains occurs from the cloth, there is the suppression of defilements through the exertion of energy, and the Noble Path is like the dye.
Just as a clean cloth possesses a radiant quality, so too the mind, from which the defilements have been suppressed, is purified by the Path.

Having said "one who has seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*), the term "one who has attained the Dhamma" (*pattadhammo*) is stated in order to exclude the possibility that there might be some other kind of seeing besides the vision of knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*).
Since there also exists a kind of attainment other than the attainment of knowledge, it is stated [as "attained"] for the purpose of distinguishing it from that.

It is said, “one who has understood the Dhamma. However, since this state of having understood the Dhamma may exist even with respect to only a portion of the Dhammas, in order to show the state of having understood them without exception, it is said, “one who has thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma.

By this, he illuminates precisely the full awakening to the Truths. For path-knowledge, by accomplishing its functions such as full understanding through a single act of clear comprehension, [penetrates] the Dhamma of the Four Truths without exception.
It is called "plunged all around. Therefore he said: "The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by this one; thus, he is one who has seen the Dhamma (diṭṭhadhammo).
"Crossed over doubt" means that doubt—consisting of sixteen or eight bases and resembling a fearful wilderness—has been crossed over, has been transcended.
"Gone beyond perplexity" means that regarding the process of existence and so forth, the state of "Is it thus? Is it not thus? has departed.
Thus, the occurrence [of doubt] has vanished and uncertainty has been cut off.

Because of the abandoning of those evil qualities that cause trepidation and because of being established in the virtues such as virtue (sīla) which are their opposites, he has attained self-confidence (vesārajja), the state of being confident (visāradabhāva), and proficiency (veyyattiya).
Since he has seen this for himself through direct personal experience, he does not rely on another, nor is there anything for another to rely upon.
"It exists" means it is not dependent on another.
"Made by designating oneself" means meat produced—that is, brought about—by way of killing after having designated oneself as the victim.

Regarding the phrase "dependent karma," here the word *kamma* functions as the object (*kamma-sādhana*) and refers to the past tense; thus he says, "made depending upon oneself. This is [an example] of a karma that serves as a sign (*nimitta-kamma*).

“Designation” (*adhivacana*) is used here as in such expressions as “dependent on [the body], contact touches the action” (*paṭicca kammaṃ phusatī*). “Of the action that serves as the sign” (*nimittakammassa*) means of the action that is to be obtained by way of being a sign.

Because the action dependent [on it] exists here by way of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is “flesh dependent on action” (*maṃsaṃ paṭiccakammaṃ*), just as “intelligence” (*buddhi*) is [derived from] “one who has awakened” (*buddha*). One who possesses that [action] is “awakened” (*buddho*). The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Sīhasutta is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the Assājānīyasutta, etc. 13–14.
In the third [sutta], "deceits" (sāṭheyyāni) means deceptions (saṭhattāni). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Furthermore, those [qualities] of his, such as deceit and so forth—
They are specific modes of occurrence of a thought-moment accompanied by greed, which constitute the opposites of bodily and mental rectitude.
In this context, when someone wishes to stand in a certain place that is dangerous to people, the thought "I shall go ahead and stand in that very same dangerous place" does not arise;
because of the presence of a deceptive intention, he stands instead in the very place where he intended to stand.
He stands with his four feet immovable like a pillar driven into the ground; this is called "craftiness" (*sāṭheyya*), and this is the manifestation of that craftiness.
Likewise, when one wishes to turn back at some place and cause a caravan to fall, there is no thought:
"This place is dangerous for people; having gone ahead, I shall cause them to fall right there."
When one turns back and causes [the horse] to fall at the very place where one intended to make it fall, this is called "trickery" (kūṭa). When one desires to go sometimes to the left,
sometimes to the right, and sometimes by a straight path, and while there is no thought in the mind, "I shall act in such a way," regarding a place ahead that is dangerous to people—
[acting] at the very place and time where one intends to go as one pleases— this is called "straightness" (ujuga).
Sometimes he goes to the left, sometimes to the right, and sometimes he goes straight on.
Likewise, when he wishes to discharge excrement or urine, this place is well-swept, crowded with people, and pleasant.
He does not think, "It is not proper to do such a thing in this place; I shall go further ahead and do it in a concealed spot," but rather he does it right there.
This is called "crooked. However, when one wishes to turn back from a path at some place and ascend the opposite path,
and there is a place ahead that is dangerous to people, yet one does not think,
"I shall do so right there," but instead turns back from the path and ascends the opposite path precisely at the place where one intended to ascend it— this is [straight].
"He mounts"—this is what is called "crookedness. Thus, this was said with reference to these four kinds of action:
