"But as for those deceptions of his... [etc. ...he is one who reveals them. Regarding the fourth, there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Assājānīya-sutta* and others is concluded.
5–8. Commentary on the *Malasutta*, etc. 15–18. Regarding the fifth [verse]:

since any branch of learning (*pariyatti*) or craft (*sippa*) perishes for one who does not recite it or does not apply oneself to it, or because it does not remain constantly present before the mind, it is said: "The mantras have non-recitation as their defilement. Because...
However, for one living the household life, if they do not rise early and attend to the repair of what is worn out and so forth, the house will fall into ruin;
therefore it is said, "Houses have non-exertion as their defilement.
Likewise, whether for a householder or one gone forth, if through laziness one fails to attend to the body or to the maintenance of one's requisites, the body [will suffer].
He becomes ugly; therefore it is said, "Laziness is the stain of beauty.

Furthermore, while one is guarding cattle, if through negligence one sleeps or plays, those cattle may meet with ruin by leaping into a fordless river and so forth, or by the affliction of wild beasts, thieves, and the like, or by descending into others' rice fields and eating the crops; and he himself [incurs] punishment.
Or he incurs abuse; or else, when one who has gone forth does not guard the six sense doors and so on, the defilements descend through negligence and cause him to fall away from the Dispensation.
Therefore it is said: "Negligence is the stain of the guarded.
For that [negligence] is a stain because it serves as the basis for the stain that brings about his destruction.
“Misconduct” (duccarita) means transgression. For indeed, a husband even casts out a woman who is transgressive from the house;
even when she has gone to her parents, they cast her out, saying, “You have become like charcoal to the family; you are not even to be looked upon with the eyes.
Wandering about without a protector, she encounters great suffering. Therefore, her misconduct is called “dirt” (mala). “Giving” (dadato):...

For the donor: indeed, one who, at the time of plowing the field, thinks, "When this field is successful, I shall give rice-gruel tickets and other gifts," yet when the crop has ripened, gives rise to stinginess that obstructs the mind of generosity—such a person, because the mind of generosity does not take root due to stinginess, [fails to attain] the three kinds of success:
success as a human being, success as a divine being, and the success of Nibbāna.
He does not obtain it. Therefore it is said: "Miserliness is the stain of one who gives. This same principle applies to other such cases as well.
"Evil states" refers to unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*). These, moreover, are indeed a stain both in this world and in the next.
"Than that" means than the stain mentioned previously. "A greater stain" means an excessive stain. The sixth and subsequent verses have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the Māla-sutta and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the Pahārāda-sutta: 19.
In the ninth [sutta], "asuras" refers to those who, unlike the *devas*, do not rejoice, do not sport, and do not shine; thus they are called asuras. As for the term *surā*...
"Devas" refers to those who are their adversaries, namely the asuras such as Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others. Their abode is at the lower portion of Sineru.
When they enter and exit there, they create pavilions and other structures at the foot of Sineru and enjoy themselves playing.
That is their delight there. Having seen these qualities, he said: "The asuras, having seen them again and again..."
"Delighting in the great ocean.

Because worldly people [believe that] Jambudīpa, the Himavat, the oceans, lakes, and mountains established therein, and the rivers originating from them—among these, whatever is not within the range of human experience—they themselves become bewildered there and cause others to be bewildered as well; therefore...
In that regard, the passage beginning with “This, first of all, is Jambudīpa” was commenced for the purpose of dispelling delusion.
The intended meaning is that it measures ten thousand yojanas in both length and breadth. Therefore he said, “Therein,” and so forth.
It is submerged by water due to the exhaustion of the merit of the beings who enjoy it. A peak of beautiful appearance is *Sudassanakūṭa*, which is called “Hemakūṭa” in the world.

Root-fragrance is that of black sandalwood (*kālānusāri*) and so forth. Heartwood-fragrance is that of sandalwood (*candana*) and so forth. Sapwood-fragrance is that of *salala* and so forth. Bark-fragrance is that of cloves (*lavaṅga*) and so forth.
Outer-skin-fragrance is that of wood-apple (*kapittha*) and so forth. Juice-fragrance is that of *sajjula* and so forth. Leaf-fragrance is that of *tamāla*, *hiri-vera*, and so forth.
Flower-fragrance is that of *nāgakusuma* and so forth. Fruit-fragrance is that of nutmeg (*jātiphala*) and so forth. Fragrance-of-fragrances is [the fragrance] of all fragrances.
As for the fragrance: they say that all [the ponds] are fifty *yojanas* in width, and in length as well as in height, they are exactly two hundred *yojanas*.
"Charming stone slabs" means stone slabs for stairs that are delightful because they are made of jewels.
"Well-prepared" means they are perfectly prepared and well-constructed by the common karma of the beings who enjoy them. Fish, turtles, and so forth, [and] the water...

They make it turbid; because of the absence of that [turbidity], the waters are as stainless as crystal. That which is long from side to side and has a rising peak is called a "transverse mountain" (*tiracchānapabbata*).
Regarding the phrase "the former names and clans": here, "river," "stream," and so forth are the clan (*gotta*), while "Ganges," "Yamunā," and so forth are the name (*nāma*).
“Flowing” (*savamānā*) means streaming forth. “Fullness” (*pūratta*) means the state of being filled. Regarding *masāragalla*, they also call it “speckled crystal” (*cittaphalika*).
“Of great beings” (*mahataṃ bhūtānaṃ*) means of great creatures. *Timi*, *timiṅgala*, and *timitimiṅgala* are three species of fish.
Those capable of swallowing a *timi* are *timiṅgalas*. They say that those capable of swallowing both a *timi* and a *timiṅgala* are *timitimiṅgalas*.
“‘My disciples’ refers to noble persons such as stream-enterers and so forth. ‘He does not dwell together’ means he does not engage in communal life through such acts as the *uposatha* ceremony.
‘He ejects’ means he removes [them]. ‘The flavor of liberation’ is the flavor of being freed from the defilements (*kilesa*).
For all excellence in the Dispensation has as its sole purpose the liberation of the mind from the taints (*āsava*) by way of non-clinging.”

The "jewels" (ratana) are so called in the sense of producing delight (rati). For when the foundations of mindfulness and the other [factors] are cultivated, they produce no small measure of rapture and gladness even in the preliminary stage, let alone in the subsequent stage. Thus it has been said:
"From whatever [aspect] one comprehends The arising and passing away of the aggregates, One gains rapture and gladness; That is the deathless for one who knows."
But the rapture and joy born of the mundane jewels do not equal even a fraction of that [noble joy]. Moreover:
"That which is honored, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and enjoyed by beings who are no ordinary—this is called a 'jewel'."
And if something is called a "jewel" by virtue of being honored and so forth, then the status of being a jewel belongs truly only to the foundations of mindfulness and the like.

For such is the power of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) that disciples attain the knowledge of disciple-perfection, Paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of Pacceka-enlightenment, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas attain Perfect Enlightenment, because these [foundations of mindfulness] are the proximate cause. Indeed, it is the proximate cause—

The "decisive support" (upanissaya) for giving and so forth is the state of being a "jewel" (ratana) of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), in the sense that it generates delight and in the sense of being honored and so on.
Therefore it was said: "In this regard, these are the jewels, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)," and so forth.
Therein, it is a "foundation" (upaṭṭhāna) in the sense of establishing itself by entering into its object; mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus it is "foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna).
However, because the object (ārammaṇa) is fourfold by way of the body and so forth, it is said: "the four foundations of mindfulness" (cattāro satipaṭṭhānā).

For thus, their status as contemplation of the body and so forth is analyzed through the abandoning of the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, and through the grasping of the states of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
It is called *sammappadhāna* because by means of it one exerts oneself rightly, or because one exerts oneself rightly oneself, or because one exerts oneself in a praiseworthy or beautiful manner;
or, because it brings about the state of right exertion for a person, it is *sammappadhāna*.

This is a designation (*adhivacana*) for energy (*vīriya*). Furthermore, that [energy] functions by way of the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, and by way of the arising of unarisen wholesome states and the maintenance of arisen wholesome states.
And because they accomplish four functions by way of producing and establishing wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), it is said: "the four right efforts" (*cattāro sammappadhānā*).

It succeeds, thus it is *iddhi*; the meaning is that it is accomplished and brought to fruition. Or else, beings succeed through it—they become successful, prosperous, and reach excellence—thus it is *iddhi*.
Therefore, in the first sense, *iddhi* itself is the "foot" (*pāda*), hence *iddhipāda*, meaning a factor of success.
This is the meaning. In the second sense, it is called a *iddhipāda* because it is the basis, the foundation, and the means for the attainment of *iddhi*.
For by means of it, one reaches and attains *iddhi*, which consists of successive stages of distinction.
Since this *iddhipāda* is produced by making the four dominant factors (*adhipatidhamma*)—beginning with desire—the primary and foremost, it is therefore said that "there are four *iddhipādas*."

"The five faculties" refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). Among these, it is the faculty of faith because, having overcome lack of faith, it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) in the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*).

It is the faculty of energy because, having overcome laziness, it exercises its function in the characteristic of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness because, having overcome negligence, it exercises its function in the characteristic of establishment;
the faculty of concentration because, having overcome distraction, it exercises its function in the characteristic of non-distraction; and [the faculty of wisdom] because of ignorance...
The faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is so called because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of seeing by overcoming [the defilements].

These same factors should be understood as powers (*bala*) in the sense of being unshakable—since they cannot be overcome by lack of faith and so forth—and in the sense of stability among associated states.

"Seven factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*): they are factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or of one who is enlightened. For this collection of states (*dhammasāmaggī*)...

By means of this harmony of factors— consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity— which arises at the moment of the supramundane path and serves as the antidote to numerous calamities such as dullness and agitation,
their underlying tendencies, accumulation, devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism—
the noble disciple awakens, rises from the sleep of the defilements, and [realizes] the four noble truths.
It is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) because one penetrates [the truth] or realizes *nibbāna* itself.

The factors of that enlightenment—which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*)—are the "enlightenment factors" (*bojjhaṅga*), just like the "jhāna factors" (*jhānaṅga*) or "path factors" (*maggaṅga*).

Furthermore, the noble disciple is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) by virtue of awakening through that aforementioned harmony of states; the factors of that enlightenment are likewise the "enlightenment factors."
They are like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot. Therefore the ancients said: “They are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they are the factors (*aṅga*) for a person who is awakening.
The meaning of *bojjhaṅga* should also be understood in such ways as: “They are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they conduce to awakening (*bodhāya saṃvattanti*).

As for the noble eightfold path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*): it is so called because it is far removed (*āraka*) from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, and because it produces the state of a noble one (*ariyabhāva*).
It is "noble" (ariya) because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruits. It possesses eight factors, such as right view and the rest;

or rather, it consists of eight factors itself, thus it is "eight-factored" (aṭṭhaṅgika). It is called a "path" (magga) because it proceeds while destroying the defilements, or because it is sought after by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks Nibbāna.
In this way, the analysis of the meaning of these [factors], beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood.
"Sotāpanna" means one who has entered and reached the stream known as the Path;

the meaning is "one established in the fruit of stream-entry. "One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry" refers to one practicing for the sake of personally witnessing the fruit of stream-entry;
this is the stage of the first path, who is also called the "eighth person" (aṭṭhamaka). "Sakadāgāmī" means [one who returns] only once more to this...

One who has the nature of returning to the world by way of taking rebirth-linking is one established in the second fruit. An *anāgāmī* (non-returner) is one who has the nature of not returning to the sense-sphere world by way of taking rebirth-linking;

he is one established in the third fruit. Furthermore, the classification of noble persons such as the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*), the Dhamma-follower (*dhammānusārī*), the "single-seeded" (*ekabījī*), and so forth, is merely a sub-division of these very [two]. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Pahārāda Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta. 20.
Regarding the tenth [verse], "on that very day of the Uposatha" means on that day which was the Uposatha day. "For the purpose of performing the Uposatha."
To recite the Pātimokkha of exhortation. "When dawn has risen" means at the rising of the sun.
"Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus"—thus the Elder requested the Blessed One to recite the Pātimokkha.
At that time, it was because the training rule stating, "Bhikkhus, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day," had not yet been promulgated. But why [was this so]?
Did the Blessed One spend the night through three watches? From that time forth, wishing not to recite the *ovāda-pātimokkha*, he intended to make the matter public.

"He saw"—how did he see it? By means of his own knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*), while fully understanding the minds of the monks in that assembly, he perceived the mind of that immoral one. For when the mind is seen...
A person possessing those [defilements] is said to be "seen"; therefore it was said: "The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that person as immoral," and so forth.
For just as one who has attained the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) knows the minds of others occurring during the seven future days, so too does he know them in the past.
"Seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" means included within the Saṅgha.
"Seen by you" means: "You have been seen by the Blessed One as one who is not a regular member (*pakatatta*) within the community of monks.
And because you have been seen in this way, therefore there is no communal association for you with the monks, such as performing formal acts (*ekakamma*) together.
Since that association does not exist for you, therefore: "Arise, friend!"—in this manner the construction of the words should be understood here.

"Even for a third time that person remained silent. Although this was said many times, he remained silent either with the intention, "The elder will become weary himself and desist," or with the thought, "Now I shall know their conduct.
"Having taken him by the arm" means: "He has been seen by the Blessed One and by me exactly as he is; even up to three times [the Blessed One] said, 'Arise, friend!'"
"Since he has been told [this] and yet does not emerge, now is the time to expel him; let there be no obstruction to the Saṅgha’s Uposatha.
Having said this, he seized him by the arm. "Having expelled him outside the door-chamber" means having expelled him from the door-hall (*dvārasālā*).
Furthermore, "outside" indicates the place where he was expelled. Alternatively, *bahidvārakoṭṭhaka* means "outside the door-chamber."
"Having brought [him] out even from outside the gateway enclosure, and not merely from inside the gateway enclosure"—the meaning is that in both cases he was removed from the monastery.
"Having fitted the bolt and the upper bar" means having inserted the door-bolt and the upper cross-bar; the meaning is, "having firmly shut the door.
By the phrase "even to the point of seizing him by the arms," [the Buddha indicated]: "Ānanda, the assembly is impure."
Indeed, upon hearing those words, he ought to have departed immediately;
that this foolish man should wait even until being seized by the arm without having departed—this shows it is truly marvelous. And this should be understood as a marvel of censure.
Then the Blessed One thought: "Now a calamity has arisen within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; impure persons are attending the Uposatha."
“They come, yet the Tathāgatas do not perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly.
And when the Pātimokkha is not recited, the Uposatha of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is interrupted.
What if, from now on, I were to authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus alone? Having reflected thus, [he authorized] the bhikkhus alone.
He authorized the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Therefore it is said: “Then the Blessed One... ‘You should recite the Pātimokkha.
In that context, “I will not now” is connected with each negative particle (*na*) as follows: “I will not perform the Uposatha, nor will I recite the Pātimokkha.
For the Pātimokkha is of two kinds: the Pātimokkha of the formal injunction (*āṇā-pātimokkha*) and the Pātimokkha of the exhortation (*ovāda-pātimokkha*).
Among these, the phrase beginning with “Let the venerable ones hear me” (*suṇātu me, bhante*) and so forth is the *Āṇā-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha of Command).

That which is recited every half-month is recited by the disciples alone, not by the Buddhas. However, these three verses—“Patience is supreme…,” “The non-doing of all evil…,” and “Non-reproach and non-injury… this is the teaching of the Buddhas”—are called the *Ovāda-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha of Exhortation).
The Buddhas themselves recite this; the disciples do not. They recite it at the end of six years.
For during the lifetime of long-lived Buddhas, this is the only recitation of the Pātimokkha; however, for short-lived Buddhas, it occurs at the very first enlightenment.
After that, the other [recitation] takes place. Moreover, it is the monks themselves who recite it, not the Buddhas; therefore, our Blessed One [also acted accordingly].
Having recited this *ovāda-pātimokkha* for about twenty years, and having seen this obstacle, he did not recite it thereafter.
"Aṭṭhāna" means no cause. "Anavakāsa" is a synonym for that same term.
For just as a cause is called "ṭhāna" (a standing point) because the fruit stands there, depending upon it for its existence, so too is it called "avakāsa" (an occasion).
They fall into the grasping of mere activity.
What is the connection (*anusandhi*) for this statement: "Bhikkhus, there are these eight qualities of the great ocean"?

It is to show that what was described as the non-recitation of the *Pātimokkha* before an impure assembly is, in this Dhamma and Discipline, a marvelous and wonderful quality (*dhamma*), and that it is [to be understood] by others as well...
Desiring to analyze and demonstrate [the ocean] together with its seven wonderful and marvelous qualities,

the Teacher first showed eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean by way of a simile for those [seven], saying: "Bhikkhus, these eight [qualities] exist in the great ocean," and so forth.
The commentary on the Uposatha Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
3. The Chapter on Householders (Gahapativagga).
1–7. Commentary on the First Uggasutta, etc. 21–27.
Regarding the first and second [sections] of the third [sutta], there is nothing further to be said. In the third, where "Hatthago" should have been said, "Hatthako" is stated.
For he [passed] from the hand of the king’s men to the hand of the yakkha, and from the hand of the yakkha to the hand of the Blessed One.
Because he passed from the hand of the Blessed One back into the hands of the king’s men, he became known by the name Hatthaka Āḷavaka.
Therefore it is said: "The prince received the name Hatthaka because he was received from hand to hand from the hand of the yakkha Āḷavaka.
The fourth and subsequent verses have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the first Uggasutta is concluded.
8. Commentary on the second Balasutta:

In the eighth [sutta], the path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) functions by way of its activity through non-delusion regarding the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Showing that it is well-penetrated even by way of making insight (vipassanā) its object, he said: "together with the path-wisdom accompanied by insight.

He says "these two kinds of sensual pleasures" (kāmā), referring to both types of desire. For the fever (pariḷāha) that arises by way of defilement has the sense-desires as its basis and the sense-desires as its object;
thus, in the sense of being accompanied by fever, both are like a pit of glowing embers.
"They are said to be 'like embers. "Internal" (anto) is said in the sense of being base; it is "become void" (byantibhūta) because it is "voided" (byanta), meaning its end has departed.
Thus he said "become one whose end has departed," the meaning of which is "free from craving.
The commentary on the Second Strength Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Akkhaṇa Sutta.

29. Regarding the ninth [sutta]: since ghosts possessing great psychic power (mahiddhika-peta) enter into marriage alliances with gods and asuras, but not into wedlock, it should be understood that the host of asuras is included within the realm of ghosts (pettivisaya) itself.
Furthermore, ghost-asuras are simply ghosts; thus, they are [included] among them.
The inclusion of the *peta* (hungry ghosts) is established even without being explicitly stated.
The commentary on the *Akkhaṇa-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Anuruddha-mahāvitakka-sutta*.

30. In the tenth [verse], *appicchassa* means "of one who does not desire. Here, the word *appa-* has the sense of "absence," as in expressions such as *appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapā* ("free from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and heat").

One who is of few desires regarding requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*) is one who is devoid of longing for the requisites of robes and so forth. One who is of few desires regarding attainment (*adhigama-appiccha*) is one who is devoid of longing for the manifestation of attainments such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
One who is of few desires regarding learning (*pariyatti-appiccha*) is one who is devoid of longing for the manifestation of great erudition in the scriptures.

"Free from desire. "One who has few desires regarding the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)" means one who has few desires for the ascetic practices and is free from the desire to manifest the state of being an ascetic practitioner.

"By concealing his own virtues" means by hiding or covering up the qualities found within himself, such as the qualities of meditative absorption (jhāna) and so forth, as well as the quality of great learning and the quality of the ascetic practices.
"Is accomplished" means it is brought to completion or perfected. "Not for one of great desire."
For one possessed of great desire, success does not come about because even that which is in accordance with the Dhamma fails to be accomplished.
"Secluded" means secluded in various ways; thus he said, "secluded by way of seclusion of body, mind, and requisites.
By way of the basis for exertion means that, through application to meditation, solitude itself is intended as bodily seclusion, and not merely the absence of social company.
He shows this. "Kamma" means the practice of yoga.

"Saṅgaṇikā" is the gathering together or association with beings and defilements; one for whom that is a "pleasure-grove" (ārāma) in the sense of being something to be delighted in is a "saṅgaṇikārāma," meaning one who delights in such company.
Thus he said, "and by the company of crowds," and so forth. "Āraddhavīriyassa" means of one whose energy is exerted.
And that is because of the statement "this is the Dhamma" by way of inclining toward seclusion from the acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*). This same method applies to the others as well.
For here, what is intended is concentration that is dependent on turning away (*vivaṭṭanissita*), and wisdom likewise.

One who stands firm in the wisdom of having performed the task, knowing through the power of karma the various kinds of harm in the realms of existence, [seeks] the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma.

One aspires for it and exerts effort for its sake. Because pride and the other [defilements] cause the mental continuum of beings to proliferate—that is, to expand within saṃsāra—they are called "papañcas.
Thus it was said: "Because of being free from the papañcas of craving, pride, and views," and so forth. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Anuruddha-Mahāvitakka Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Householders is finished.
4. The Chapter on Giving (Dānavagga). 1–4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Giving, etc.
31–34. Regarding the first [offense] of the fourth [category]: *āsajja* means for the sake of meeting with the one to whom one gives, that is, on account of approaching them.
Regarding *bhayā*: it means on account of fear. One might ask: "Is not fear—like lust and other such factors arising from a desire for what has been obtained—a defiler of volition (*cetanā*)?
Why, then, is it included here? To show that this was not stated with reference to such things as the fear of public censure (*vohāra-bhaya*), [the author says:]...
"This one is a non-giver, a non-doer," and so forth, was said. "He gave to me" refers to that which is given after reflecting upon a benefit previously rendered.
"He will give to me" refers to that which is given with the hope for a return favor.
"Giving is good" means that this thing called giving is designated by the wise; thus, one gives while standing in virtuous conduct.

"Alaṅkāratthaṃ" means for the sake of adornment. For when one has given a gift and reflects upon it, joy, rapture, gladness, and so forth arise, while greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, and so forth are put far away.
Now, by way of nourishing favorable states and removing adverse states, giving serves as both an adornment and an accessory for the mind in its cultivation.
It is said that one gives "for the sake of adornment and for the sake of equipment. Therefore he says, "For giving makes the mind supple," and so forth.
Having received [a gift], the recipient becomes supple-minded, thinking, "He has shown me favor"; the giver likewise becomes supple-minded toward the recipient.
Hence it is said, "It makes the minds of both supple."
"Subduing the unsubdued": through giving, those who are unsubdued and disobedient become subdued and obedient, and they come under one's control.
"Non-giving is a defiler of the subdued": non-giving defiles the mind by producing distress even for those who were previously subdued and obedient.
"The givers rise up" because they are a source of respect and honor for others; "the recipients bow down."

For those who have been won over by giving and kind speech, the gift of adorning the mind alone is supreme, because it is unstained, perfectly pure, and a condition for the excellence of special qualities. The second and subsequent [sections] are of plain meaning.
The commentary on the first discourse on giving, etc., is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Dānūpapatti Sutta 35.
In the fifth [verse], "by reason of giving" (*dānapaccayā*) means by way of the cause of giving; the meaning is: because of having performed and accumulated merit consisting of giving.
"Rebirths" (*upapattiyo*) refers to the manifestations of birth among humans and devas. "Establishes" (*ṭhapeti*) means that, instead of being reborn only once, as follows...
It proceeds in that very same manner above; thus it establishes [the mind]. And since that itself is its resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), he says, "it is a synonym for that.

"Increases" means it develops it, not letting it diminish. "Liberated" (vimutta) means intent upon (adhimutta); the meaning is inclined, leaning toward, and tending toward [that state]. Or, "liberated" means released.
In the non-figurative sense, "higher" (uttara) refers to what is superior; even in the middle, there is the distinction between the inferior and the middling.
Regarding the phrase "because it is obtainable," it is said: "not further cultivated" means not cultivated for the sake of the higher paths and fruits.

A mind consisting of giving directed in such a way leads [to that result]. As for what is stated in the Pāḷi beginning with "And yet," that should be understood as being intended to show the absence of misconduct which acts as an obstacle to rebirth there, and not [as a denial] of the mind consisting of giving.
This should be understood as showing that it leads exclusively to merit. "Of one whose lust is eradicated" means one whose sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) has been eradicated;
for such a person might be reborn in the Brahma-world, but not one whose lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) has been eradicated.
And here, by the term "one free from lust," what is intended is freedom from lust regarding sense pleasures (*kāma*), by which rebirth in the Brahma-world may occur.
Therefore he said, "By giving alone," and so forth. If this is so, one might ask: what is the purpose of giving there? To this he replied, "But as for giving," and so forth.
"One whose mind is softened by giving" means one whose mind has become gentle through the acceptance of his own gift even from a person toward whom he harbors resentment or enmity.
The commentary on the *Dānūpapatti-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Puññakiriyavatthu Sutta 36.
In the sixth [verse], they produce the fruit of a venerable existence, or they purify their own continuum; thus they are "meritorious deeds" (*puññāni*).

Furthermore, because they are to be performed by means of causes and conditions, they are "actions" (*kiriyā*); therefore, they are "meritorious actions" (*puññakiriyā*). And it is precisely through these that there arise various benefits, such as being dear and agreeable to others.
They are called "bases for the performance of merit" because they serve as the foundation for such acts.

"Generosity" (*dāna*) refers to the volition of relinquishing one's own property to another, either by way of supporting someone whose roots of existence are not yet severed or by way of making an offering;
it is that by which one gives. "Consisting of generosity" (*dānamaya*) means simply generosity itself. The suffix *-maya* is used here merely to complete the meter.
The volition that occurs at three times—beginning from the procurement of the four requisites such as robes, or the ten objects of giving such as food, or the six sense-objects such as visible forms;
during the act of giving those things; and subsequently, at the time of recollection with a joyful mind—is called the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
For one who undertakes five, eight, or ten precepts by way of the perpetual virtue (*niccasīla*), the Uposatha virtue (*uposathasīla*), and so forth;
for one going to a monastery with the thought, "I shall go forth for the sake of fulfilling the precepts"; for one actually going forth;

for one reflecting, having brought his aspiration to its peak, "It is truly well and excellent that I have gone forth"; and for one fulfilling the *Pātimokkha* through faith—[the *saṅghādisesa* offense does not apply].

The volition that occurs when one reflects upon requisites such as robes with wisdom; when one restrains the eye-door and so forth regarding forms and other objects that have come into range through mindfulness;

and when one purifies one’s livelihood through energy—this is called the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*), because it "virtues" or "causes one to be virtuous."
For one who contemplates the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self by means of the path of insight described in the *Paṭisambhidā*, [and likewise] the ear...
the nose... the tongue... the body... visible forms... mental objects... eye-consciousness...
mind-consciousness... eye-contact... mind-contact... and feeling born of eye-contact... and so forth.
The volition of one who is practicing insight into mental-contact-born feeling … [and so on] … into aging-and-death as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and the jhāna-volition that occurs in regard to all thirty-eight objects, such as the earth-kasiṇa and others;
and that which occurs by way of attention to proficiency in blameless fields of action, fields of craft, and branches of knowledge, etc.

Volition (*cetanā*): all that one develops by means of this is "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*). According to the method already stated, it is a "basis for making merit consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
And herein, for one who performs each [of these] starting from the preliminary stage as appropriate, there is bodily action (*kāyakamma*). For the sake of that—
When one utters speech, it is verbal action (*vacīkamma*). When one thinks with the mind without moving either the limbs of the body or the members of speech, it is mental action (*manokamma*).

Furthermore, for one giving food and so forth—whether thinking, "I am giving gifts such as food," or having adverted to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*)—at the time of giving, it is a basis for the performance of merit consisting of giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*). For just as when one simply thinks, "I am giving gifts such as food..."
At the time of giving, it becomes a basis for meritorious action consisting of giving; thus, because one has recollected the perfection of giving with the thought,
"May this gift be a condition for perfect enlightenment," and because at the time of giving it proceeds precisely by way of the head of giving—
or alternatively, because one gives while standing at the head of right conduct, thinking, "This act of giving is my family lineage and ancestral tradition"— it is so called.

Giving that is performed out of a sense of duty and moral conduct constitutes the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya*). Giving while establishing the contemplation of impermanence and passing away constitutes the basis of meritorious action consisting in mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*).

For just as the volition of giving, even while proceeding by way of the relinquishment of the object to be given, becomes a basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue for one who gives while standing at the head of their practice, so it is after the stage of prior preparation.
And because volition proceeds in that manner.
The commentary on the *Puññakiriyavatthu-sutta* is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the *Sappurisadāna-sutta*, etc.

37–38. Regarding the phrase "In the seventh [case], he gives having discriminated," there are two kinds of discrimination here: discrimination regarding the recipient (*dakkhiṇeyya*) and discrimination regarding the offering (*dakkhiṇā*).

Among these, "discrimination regarding the recipient" refers to giving gifts after setting aside those outside this [Buddhist] tradition who have failed in virtue, as well as the ninety-five types of heretics, and instead giving to those who have gone forth within the Dispensation and are endowed with qualities such as virtue. Having set aside inferior and most inferior requisites...
Having investigated what is most excellent among the excellent, giving to them is called "the investigation of the recipient. Therefore, it was said:
"What is given to this one will be of great fruit," and so forth. In the eighth [sutta], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Sappurisadānasutta* and others is concluded.
9–10. Commentary on the *Abhisanda-sutta* and others. 39–40.

In the ninth [sutta], "streams of merit" (*puññābhisandā*) means rivers of merit. "Streams of the wholesome" (*kusalābhisandā*) means flows of the wholesome. "Nutriments of happiness" (*sukhassāhārā*) means conditions for happiness.

"Foremost" (*aggāni*) means they are known as foremost (*aggaññāni*) because they have been known from the beginning. "Ancient" (*rattaññāni*) means they have been known for a long time (*cirarattaṃ*). Of the noble ones (*ariyānaṃ*)...
They are called "lineages" (vaṃsa) because they are known as the lineages of the virtuous. They are called "ancient" (porāṇa) because they belong to the ancient primordial beings.
They are called "unmixed" (asaṃkiṇṇa) because they have not been mixed, scattered, or discarded by the virtuous in any way whatsoever.
And this principle applies to them just as it did in the past, so too now and in the future; thus he said: "Unmixed in the past, they are not being mixed [now]."
“They will not be suspicious. For that very reason, they are not censured; for wise recluses and brahmins never sanction unwholesome states such as violence.
“He gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings” means that, because he has laid aside the rod toward all living beings, he grants the absence of fear to the entire body of sentient beings.
“Harmless” (*avera*) means the absence of enmity. “Non-afflictive” (*abyābajjha*) means the absence of suffering. Thus it is here.
In brief, the commentary on the Pāḷi should be understood. In the tenth [sutta], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Abhisanda-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Dānavagga is finished.
5. Uposatha Chapter. 1–8.
Commentary on the Short Uposatha Sutta and others, 41–48.
Regarding the first and subsequent suttas of the fifth chapter, there is nothing further to be said. In the sixth [sutta], that which has five factors is "fivefold" (*pañcaṅga*).

"Five-limbed" (*pañcaṅgika*) means having five parts; [the text] refers to that which has five parts. A "large *daddarī*" is a specific type of lute, and since it too is "stretched," the qualification "covered with leather" (*cammapariyonaddhesu*) is applied.
Instruments with one surface include the *kumbhatūṇa*, the *daddarikā*, and so forth. Those with two surfaces include the *bherī*, the *mudiṅga*, and so forth.
That which is bound together after being covered with leather is "stretched and spread" (*ātatavitata*). That which is completely covered on all sides...
The *caturassambaṇa* and the *paṇava* and so forth; the inclusion of the *gomukhī* and others should also be understood as falling within this very category.

Regarding "flutes and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *saṅkha* (conch) and others. Regarding "drums and so forth" (*sammatādi*), this refers to the *sammatāḷa*, the *kaṃsatāḷa*, the *silātāḷa*, the *salākatāḷa*, and others.
Among these, the *sammatāḷa* is a drum made of ivory. The *kaṃsatāḷa* is made of bronze. The *silātāḷa* is a stone drum, and the one struck with an iron plate is the *ayopatta*.
A cymbal made of stone or wood. "Well-prepared" means thoroughly ready. "In measure" refers to the middle degree of tension, which is reckoned as neither too tight nor too loose.
"Skilled" means clever and proficient; and since that proficiency of his is captivating, he says "beautiful.

"To delight" means to arouse passion (*rāga*). "It is indeed pleasing" means it is simply agreeable. "One does not become weary of it" means one does not feel revulsion; because it is pleasant to the ear, it is truly to be cherished.
"She does not despise her husband" means that she does not desire anyone other than her husband even in her mind.
"Diligent" (*uṭṭhāhikā*) means endowed with the energy of exertion. "Unwearying" (*analasā*) means free from laziness.

"One who has won over her attendants" means one who has won over her attendants through such things as showing them respect, and by sending gifts such as beloved articles to be presented on festive occasions and the like. Here, "attendants" refers to...
The relatives of both the husband and oneself. "Accumulated" refers to wealth brought in by performing such tasks as farming and trade.
The seventh and eighth [sections] have their meaning obvious.
The commentary on the *Saṃkhittūposatha-sutta* and others is concluded.
9–10. Commentary on the First Discourse on This World, etc. 49–50.
Regarding the ninth [discourse], "for the conquest of this world" (*idhalokavijayāya*): it means for the purpose of conquering this world, for the purpose of overcoming it.
For whoever overcomes disadvantage pertaining to the present life by way of avoidance, and thereby accomplishes that very purpose, he is one who acts for the conquest of this world.
He is called "one who has set out" because he subdues adversaries and accomplishes his own welfare. Therefore it was said:

"This world is undertaken. (This bringing of praise should be understood as occurring through the bringing of praise itself, by means of fame and renown, and by causing sounds in this world to become pleasing to the mind and irresistible. "One whose work is well-arranged" means...
One who has well-ordered his work by carefully performing each respective task without letting the times for cooking gruel, eating meals, and so forth pass by;
"for the sake of conquering the next world" means for the purpose of winning and overcoming the next world.
For he who overcomes future misfortune by way of avoiding it, and thereby accomplishes that very purpose, is one acting for the sake of conquering the next world.
He is said to be "one who has entered upon the practice. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the first sutta beginning with "This world" is finished.
The commentary on the Uposatha Chapter is finished.
The First Fifty [Discourses] is concluded.
2. The Second Fifty [Discourses] (6) 1.
The Chapter on Gotamī.
1–3. Commentary on the *Gotamīsutta* and others (51–53).
In the first [verse] of the sixth [chapter], "Gotamī" is her clan name (*gotra*).

On the day of her naming ceremony, however, the brahmins who had received honors for her, seeing her perfection of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), said: "If this girl bears a daughter, she will become the wife of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin-rāja*)."
"She will become the chief queen. If she bears a son, he will become a wheel-turning monarch;
thus, in either case, her progeny will be great," they prophesied. Therefore, they gave her the name "Mahāpajāpatī.
For this reason, it is said: "She received this name because of the greatness of both her offspring of sons and her offspring of daughters."
“‘Fear has arisen from the staff of self; behold the people in their distress!
I shall proclaim the sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), just as it was stirred within me’—with these words he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
May those various acts of seduction, which strive through body and speech, become weary.”
"Having sent a message" is said because they sent a message, thinking, "We shall send a message. "To the Kuṇāla Lake" means to the shore of the Kuṇāla Lake.
"Having dispelled discontent" means having dispelled discontent by way of perceiving the faults of women and by revealing the corruption inherent in the outlets of sensual desire.
"Āpādikā" means those who raised [him]; the meaning is that they looked after him by growing his hands and feet while you were unable to perform the necessary tasks for them yourselves.
"Posikā" means she nourished you by bathing, feeding, and giving you drink two or three times a day.
Regarding "she gave you breast milk": it is said that Prince Nanda was only a few days old when the Bodhisatta...
When he was born, Mahāpajāpatī gave her own son to the nurses and, performing the nursing duties herself for the Bodhisatta, she suckled him with her own breast-milk.
With reference to this, the Elder spoke thus: "Daharo" means young;
"yuvā" means established in youth; "maṇḍanakajātiko" means one whose nature is to adorn. In that regard, someone might be young...
One does not become "young" merely by being very youthful. Nor does someone who, though young, is prone to vanity, or one who is overcome by sloth, misfortune, and so forth, truly qualify as such.
Here, however, the intended meaning is one who is both young and youthful, and moreover, naturally inclined toward adornment;
therefore, he spoke thus. And lotuses and the like are mentioned because they are recognized by the world as being naturally inclined toward adornment.
"Because women have gone forth"—this is an indication of the reason for the endurance of the True Dhamma for exactly five hundred years, rather than remaining beyond that.
It is stated by way of those whose taints are destroyed having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);

here, by the inclusion of those whose taints are destroyed who have attained the analytical knowledges, the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are also necessarily included, for there are no [arahants] devoid of absorption.

They say that every kind of excellence succeeds. Furthermore, it should be understood that what was stated regarding "a thousand years" and so forth, by way of the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), was spoken according to the opinion of the reciters of the Khandhaka.
It is also stated in the same manner in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.

In the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "It remained for a thousand years with those who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), for a thousand years with those possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), for a thousand years with those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*), for a thousand years with those practicing dry insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*), and for a thousand years with the Pātimokkha.
Here too, in the discussion on the disappearance of the Dispensation, [it says]: "Indeed, from the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas..."
For a thousand years they are able to produce the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*); beyond that, the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*);

when they are no longer able to produce even those, they produce the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*); and as time goes on, being unable to produce even those, they become dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
By this same method, [the paths of] non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) [are likewise affected].
"Stream-enterers," it is said.
However, in the *Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "At the time of the First Enlightenment, the monks attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Then, as time passed, they were no longer able to attain the analytical knowledges, but they became possessors of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). After that..."

Those unable to attain the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā) will reach the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā). As time passes now, those unable to reach the three types of higher knowledge will reach the mere destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya);
those unable to reach even that will reach the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); those unable to reach even that will reach the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala);
and those unable to reach even that will reach the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), as time goes on.
It is said: “They will not even be able to attain the fruit of stream-entry.
Since all of this is mutually contradictory, it should be understood that the teacher has presented there, in each respective instance, only the opinion of those particular reciters (*bhāṇaka*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of internal inconsistency within the teacher’s own work.

“Those very same” means those very five thousand years. He said, “The Dispensation has the scriptures (pariyatti) as its root,” because “without the scriptures, there is no penetration (paṭivedha),” and so forth.

For when the scriptures disappear, the practice (paṭipatti) disappears; when the practice disappears, the realization (adhigama) disappears. Why is that? Because these scriptures are for the sake of the practice.

Practice is the condition for realization. Thus, even from the standpoint of practice, the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) alone is the authority. There is nothing further to be said regarding the second and third [cases].
The commentary on the *Gotamīsutta* and others is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the *Dīghajāṇusutta* and others.
54–55. “In the fourth [case], one may enjoy wealth with one part” means that one may enjoy or consume wealth with one portion;
this is the meaning. “With two parts, one may engage in work” means that one may employ two portions for work such as farming, trade, and so forth.
“One may set aside” means that one should deposit and keep the fourth portion; the meaning is that one should store it away by placing it underground.
Regarding the phrase "it will be for times of distress": the affairs of families do not remain the same at all times; sometimes distress arises due to kings, fire, thieves, famine, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that when such distress has arisen, one should set aside one portion [of wealth] thinking, "This will be for times of distress.
Now, among these four portions, which portion should be taken and used for performing wholesome deeds (*kusala*)?
“‘One should enjoy wealth’ refers to the portion thus stated. Having taken from that, one should give alms to the bhikkhus as well as to the poor and the destitute;
one should also pay wages to weavers, barbers, and others. This is done by way of giving to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, and so forth;
by way of offerings to the *bali* for the deities dwelling therein; and by way of paying wages to barbers and others.”
And *viniyoga* is indeed the same as *upayoga*.

They go away (*apenti*), or they go by means of these; thus they are *apāyā*. Since they are *apāyā*, they are gates or doors, hence *apāyamukhāni*. The same method applies here to the phrase "doors of destruction" (*vināsadvārāni*). There is nothing further to be said regarding the fifth [factors].
The commentary on the *Dīghajāṇusutta* and others is concluded.
6–8. Commentary on the Bhayasutta, etc. (56–58).

Regarding the sixth [sutta], it is said that "womb" (*gabbha*) is used here by eliding the latter member of the compound; thus he says, "‘Womb’ means dwelling in the womb. The seventh and eighth [suttas] have their meanings obvious.
The commentary on the Bhayasutta, etc., is concluded.
6–10. Commentary on the *Puggala-sutta* and others. 59–60.
In the ninth [sutta], "to those giving gifts" means to those giving gifts with reference to a person worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).

It is called "resulting in acquisitions" (*upadhivipāka*) because by means of it acquisitions ripen, or because it ripens within acquisitions, or because its results are acquisitions. [This refers to] what is given to the Sangha.
"Of great fruit": a gift given to the Noble Saṅgha has a wide scope; the meaning is that it yields abundant fruit. There is nothing further to be said regarding the tenth [sutta].
The commentary on the *Puggala-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Gotamī-vagga* is finished.
(7) 2. Bhūmicālavagga 1–5.
Commentary on the *Icchāsutta* and others, 61–65.
The first [suttas] of the seventh chapter are easy to understand. Regarding the fifth: "he overcomes" (*abhibhavati*).

It is either mastery (*abhibhu*), the preliminary work (*parikamma*), or knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Since this has mastery as its sphere (*āyatana*), it is a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*); that is, the jhāna.
Or, since this has as its sphere the object termed the "thing to be mastered," it is a "sphere of mastery.

Alternatively, because it masters the object and because it is both "masterful" (*abhi*) and a "sphere" (*āyatana*)—insofar as it serves as the basis for the yogi’s specific excellences of happiness and constitutes the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*)—it is called a "sphere of mastery."
And even the jhāna associated with them is an *abhibhāyatana* (base of mastery). Therefore, he said: "Because they are the causes of mastery," and so forth.
"Those" refers to the jhānas designated as *abhibhāyatanas*. The phrase "for the sake of a person’s pre-eminence in knowledge" should be applied to both instances.
How? They master opposing states by way of being their antidotes, for the sake of a person’s pre-eminence in knowledge.
They overcome objects. For by the power of knowledge alone, the overcoming of opposing factors is like the overcoming of objects.
By way of preliminary work (*parikamma*), one perceives forms internally; not by way of absorption (*appanā*).
For an absorption whose object is a counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) cannot possibly have an internal domain as its object. However, that kasiṇa-sign obtained through internal preliminary work—
It is indeed impure; it is not pure as if obtained by means of external refinement.
"Limited" (*parittāni*) means they are just as they were received, merely the size of a small water-jar. Therefore he said, "unincreased.

"Precisely by way of being limited" means that even though there is mental attention (*ābhoga*) to their color, this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is described precisely by way of their limitation. This is their "limitedness."
This is the reason for its mastery. Whether the perception of beauty is present or absent, the development of the bases of mastery occurs only in one of sharp wisdom, not in another;
thus he said, "a person who has knowledge as his supreme quality.
Regarding the phrase "having mastered, he attains," here both the mastering and the attainment occur immediately after the achievement of access concentration.
Regarding the phrase "the production of absorption jhāna," it is said: "Right at the arising of the sign, one attains absorption here.

The expression "right at the arising of the sign" is a characteristic statement indicating the absence of a preparatory period (*parivāsa*) for absorption. For one who is called "one of quick direct knowledge" (*khippābhiñña*), even more so than that, the development of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) belongs to the highest grade of knowledge.
"Here" means in this sign. "Attains absorption" means he leads the development to absorption.
And here, some say: "When access concentration has arisen, the two or three rounds of impulsion that occur taking that as their object belong to the side of access concentration itself;

immediately after that, absorption occurs without the lapse of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or the practice of access, and one reaches absorption at the very moment the sign arises. This is merely their own opinion.

For it is not intended that there be immediate attainment (*appanā*) through a formal act of probation (*pārivāsika-kamma*), nor is reflective contemplation absolutely required in access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) as it is in the sublime and measureless meditations.

Therefore, one who reaches absorption after the conclusion of several life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) moments following the attainment of access concentration is said to "attain absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign. Regarding the phrase "simultaneously with the arising of the sign":
And this statement is intentional (*adhippāyika*), not of explicit meaning (*nītattha*). The intention should be understood in the manner already stated.
It is not [the case] within the attainment itself, because at that time such a mental application (*ābhoga*) is impossible;
rather, for one who has emerged from attainment, the mental application occurs by way of prior-stage cultivation, taking hold of the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of the jhāna.
It should be seen. However, in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "By this, his preliminary mental application (*pubbabhoga*) is explained.
As to why it is said, "even by the perception of jhāna," in the absence of such mental application within the attainment itself, he says: "Because of overcoming... there is [perception].
"Increased in measure" means "of vast measure"; it does not mean an increase by way of one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, and so forth.
"Made great" means that they have increased accordingly, because it is impossible for them not to increase here.
Therefore he said, "great. "Increased food" means food given after having been increased in the eating bowl; the meaning is, half of the food that should be eaten by a man at a single sitting.

"Perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) is the perception of form; one who possesses that is "possessed of the perception of form. One who is not possessed of the perception of form is "without the perception of form" (*arūpasaññī*). [This is stated] by way of the primary term "perception" (*saññā*).
He speaks of jhāna. Here, "non-attainment" refers precisely to the non-arising of the perception of form. "Arising only externally" means arising with respect to an external object alone.
In the Abhidhamma, however, regarding the four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), it is stated: "Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally—limited, beautiful or ugly;
immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Thus [it describes] the four bases of mastery.

Because it has been handed down in the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*, a challenge is raised: "Why is it that, whereas in the Suttanta it is said, 'One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited,' and so forth, here in all four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) it is stated only that one is 'not percipient of forms internally'?
To this, it is replied: "Because internal forms are not to be mastered."
Having stated the reason, it is said: "In that context as well as here, only external forms are to be mastered; therefore, they must necessarily be mentioned.
Thus, they are spoken of both there and here. However, the phrase 'perceiving forms internally' is merely an elegant stylistic device of the Teacher's teaching.
And herein, all [forms]—both those devoid of attention to color and those accompanied by it—are described as "limited, beautiful or ugly."

Likewise, regarding the phrase "immeasurable beautiful and ugly [forms]," there is indeed a method [of interpretation] according to which one "having overcome limited forms," and if at some time those are engaged with by way of color, then one has "overcome the beautiful and ugly. For the teaching of the Suttantas is an exposition by way of such methods.
However, because the Abhidhamma is a teaching that is free from such methods, [the objects] are listed separately, devoid of engagement with color.

They have been stated, and likewise combined. For there is a distinction in the overcoming (*abhibhavana*) in both cases; thus, because of the teaching by way of method (*pariyāyadesanā*), there is also a mode of overcoming for the liberations (*vimokkha*).
Therefore, the first liberation corresponds to the first and second bases of overcoming (*abhibhāyatana*) through the formula "perceiving forms internally," etc.;
the second liberation corresponds to the third and fourth bases of overcoming; and [the remaining ones correspond] to the bases of overcoming colors (*vaṇṇābhibhāyatana*).

And the third liberation is included because it proceeds by way of mastery. However, in the Abhidhamma, because of its teaching according to the definitive method (*nippariyāya*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are explained without omitting the liberations (*vimokkha*) in order to show the liberations and the bases of mastery without confusion.
Furthermore, all the functions of the liberations are stated in the teaching on the liberations as being the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). Thus, this [phrase] "internally... [is explained].

It is understood that a formal distinction has been made because the two *abhibhāyatana*s (bases of mastery) mentioned as "perceiving forms" (*rūpasaññī*) are not included among the *abhibhāyatana*s in the Abhidhamma,
and because such statements as "one possessing form sees forms" (*rūpī rūpāni passati*) are expressions common to the functions of all the liberations (*vimokkha*).
As for the phrase "because internal forms are not to be mastered," this [is not found] anywhere in the Abhidhamma.
Without stating "he sees internal forms," that which is stated everywhere as "he sees external forms" is the statement of the reason for it.

By this, he shows that whatever has another cause is stated by that specific cause; however, as for the statement in the Abhidhamma regarding the state of being "percipient of the formless internally"—which is caused by the elegance of the teaching—no other reason for it need be sought.
The fact that internal forms are not to be overcome is due to their lack of distinct manifestation, unlike external forms;

and the elegance of the teaching should be understood by way of the aforementioned analysis, because it is a discourse using available modes of expression according to the inclinations of those to be trained.
If it is argued that the bases of mastery over blue and so forth need not be mentioned, since they are already established by the phrase "beautiful and ugly" alone?
That is not so; for it is the very state of being blue and so forth, in those [objects] where one has performed the preliminary practice, that is the cause of mastery.
Indeed, it is neither the limitedness nor the immeasurableness of those pure or impure colors that is the cause of mastery, but rather the state of being blue and so forth itself.
And among these limited and other kasiṇa-forms, whichever of these bases of mastery corresponds to one's temperament...
In order to show how these succeed, the passage beginning with “But in these... was stated. “By way of including all” means by way of the commonality of blue color, blue appearance, and blue luster.

“By way of color” means by way of its intrinsic color (*sabhāvavaṇṇa*). “By way of appearance” means by way of being visible, that is, by way of being apprehended by the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) of eye-consciousness and the rest.
“By way of radiance” means by way of shining forth due to its possession of brilliance.
The commentary on the *Icchāsutta* and others is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Vimokkhasutta*. 66.

Regarding the sixth [question], "In what sense (*kenaṭṭhena*)": in what intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For an intrinsic nature is that which is to be known as it truly is by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), because it is to be sought after and understood.
“Meaning” (attha) is what is said; by changing the letter *t* to *ṭ*, that same word is spoken as “aṭṭha.
“In the sense of resolute confidence” (adhimuccanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of releasing (*muccana*) in an eminent or distinguished way (*adhika*).

By this, although all fine-material-sphere jhāna is liberated from its opposites by way of suppression, it is shown that through a particular distinction in cultivation, that jhāna is liberated from its opposites to a superior degree.

Having been liberated, it proceeds; thus, that particular excellence of development (bhāvanāvisesa) is illustrated. For indeed, even when joined with similar types [of persons], there is a distinction in the mode of proceeding due to the excellence of development.

Just as it is for one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta) compared to one liberated through faith (saddhāvimutta), so too is there [this distinction] by way of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states (paccanīkadhamma), by way of being fearless because of not being suppressed, and by way of being well-resolved in the sense of delighting [in the object].
[This is] liberation. Therefore he said, "And with respect to the object," and so forth.

But this meaning—namely, the sense of resolving (*adhimuccana*)—does not exist in the last liberation, which is cessation (*nirodha*). Only the sense of being liberated (*vimutta*) is found there; he himself will explain that later.

"Possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that by whatever form included within one's own continuity (*sasantati*) this person is endowed, that [form], by way of being the cause for the meditative absorption (*jhāna*),...
It possesses a distinguished form (*visiṭṭharūpa*), by which distinguished form it may be called "possessing form" (*rūpī*), because the word *rūpī* indicates the sense of excellence.
It should be understood that precisely this jhāna—attained by means of the form included within one's own continuity—is what establishes the state of possessing form in the ultimate sense here.
Therefore he said, "internally," and so forth. "Form-jhāna" (*rūpajjhāna*) is [formed] by the elision of the latter member of the compound; thus, "forms" (*rūpāni*).
In this context, the elision of the first member of the compound should be understood. Therefore it was said: "forms such as the blue kasiṇa.
Perception of form is *rūpasaññā*; one who possesses that is *rūpasaññī*. By way of the term "perception," he refers to the jhāna.
Its opposite is *arūpasaññī*. Hence he said: "internally not perceiving forms," and so forth.
By the statement, "In absorption there is no mental engagement (*ābhoga*) [thinking] 'beautiful'," it is shown that such a resolve (*adhimutti*) may arise by way of prior mental engagement.

For in this way, the objection regarding the attainment of being so described here would be untenable. This is because, in the case of the color-kasinas (*vaṇṇakasiṇa*) such as blue and so forth—which are perfectly purified—the sense of being well-resolved arises through the delight of those who have performed the necessary practice therein.
Therefore, the third liberation is described as such in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

However, because meditation proceeding by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest perceives beings as non-repulsive and proceeds by resolving upon them as beautiful (*subha*), the development of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) is called the "beautiful liberation" (*subhavimokkha*) in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. And this [third liberation] is both of these.
It should be understood that there is no contradiction because it has been stated by various methods.
"All" means without exception; for not even a single portion of the four immaterial aggregates remains there.
"Because they have been relinquished" means because they have been ceased within the time limit as defined. That which is called the "supreme liberation" belongs to the Noble Ones alone.
Because it is to be attained through meditative absorption, because it culminates in the noble fruits, and because it constitutes the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life.
The commentary on the *Vimokkha-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Anariya-vohāra-sutta*.
67. In the seventh [case], the mode of speech of ignoble and base persons is "ignoble speech. "One who speaks what was seen" means one who speaks thus:
"I have seen it. The same applies to the remaining cases. And here, the meaning should be understood by way of the volition that originates each respective [act].
Therefore he said: "By whichever volitions," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Anariyavohārasutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Parisāsutta*: 69.

Regarding the ninth [sutta], it is called a *samāgama* because one must assemble there, or because one assembles there; thus, it is a *parisā* (assembly). [It refers to the assembly] headed by Bimbisāra.
"Meeting" (*samāgama*) refers to the meeting with Bimbisāra. The same method applies to the other two cases as well.

The construction [of the phrase] "a retinue of kṣatriyas similar to the meeting with Bimbisāra" (*bimbisāra-pe-samāgamasadisaṃ khattiyaparisanti*) should be understood accordingly. The Teacher’s approach to the retinues of kṣatriyas and others is indeed found even in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
From the beginning, the Teacher’s speaking with them is "discourse" (*ālāpa*); their mutual exchange of speech is "dialogue" (*sallāpa*). It is connected with the Dhamma.

It is a discussion of the Dhamma consisting of questions and counter-questions. The term "shape" (saṇṭhāna) is used here because the word *vaṇṇa* (color/appearance) is employed as a synonym for shape, as in such expressions as “having manifested the great appearance of a king elephant” (*mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā*). The word “of them” (*tesaṃ*) refers to both preceding terms:
“Just as their characteristic marks and shape were known, so too the Teacher’s bodily shape was known only to them.”
Nor is it the case that the Blessed One has removed his jeweled earrings; such is the construction [of the phrase]. "With severed voices" means with voices split in two.
"With gurgling voices" means with hoarse voices. "Another language" means a language other than the speech of those beings. "Inquiry" means reflection. "For what purpose...
does he teach?"—surely this [question] is [intended to show that] when the Dhamma is taught after having made himself known, there is a special benefit for them.
Is this stated with the intention that "there is confidence"? It means that when the Dhamma is taught without making oneself known, confidence arises—not by making oneself known;
it is with reference to such cases that the Teacher acts in that way.

He states the purpose for this as "for the sake of impressioning (vāsanatthāya). "Even though heard in this way" means that even if the Dhamma is heard while the teacher remains unrecognized and the place of arrival remains unknown.
The very fact that his teaching is well-taught serves as a condition for one who hears it in the future.
The commentary on the *Parisā-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Bhūmicāla-sutta*.
70. "At the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena" means at the place made of bricks by way of being the abode of the yakkha named Udena, which was honored by the great multitude.
"A monastery built" means a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One. "It is called" refers to the former usage;
it is called "Udena Shrine. "In the case of Gotamaka and so forth" refers to such expressions as "Gotamaka Shrine," and so on.
“The same method” refers by extension to the fact that a monastery was built on the site of a cetiya. For instance, there was the Sattamba [Cetiya]:
seven princesses of King Kikī, having become filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), left their homes and practiced meditation there;
that place is called the “Sattamba Cetiya. And the Bahuputta [Cetiya] was a single banyan tree (nigrodha) with many branches.
Many people sought children from the deity dwelling there; because of that, the place became known as the "Bahuputtaka Cetiya" (The Shrine of Many Sons).
It was the abode of the yakkha named Sārandada, and it was also the abode of the yakkha named Cāpāla;
thus, all of these had previously been occupied by deities before the appearance of the Buddha.

They are designated by the conventional term "cetiyas," and even when monasteries (*vihāras*) have been built, they are still perceived in that same way. Regarding the word "delightful" (*rāmaṇeyyaka*):
here, the state of being delightful should be understood first of all in Vesālī due to its excellence of terrain and the ease with which alms-food is obtained.

As for the monasteries, however, it is because they are neither too far from the city nor too close to it, because of the excellence of the paths for coming and going, and because they are places where one can dwell without being crowded.
Its delightful nature is to be seen through its excellence of shade and water, and its suitability for seclusion.
"Developed" means brought to full growth by way of the completion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "Repeatedly performed" means set in motion again and again through the frequent practice of cultivation.
"Made like a harnessed chariot" means just as a harnessed thoroughbred chariot is [controlled] by a skillful charioteer.
That which has been resolved proceeds according to one’s wish; thus, it has been brought to the state of proceeding according to one’s wish.

"In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "Made like a site" means that by completely purifying all defilements, it has been made like a site where dangers have been thoroughly cleared away, because it serves as a foundation through its being the domain of psychic power (*iddhi*). It is "resolved" because its opposites have been distanced.

They are established through their well-cultivated state for the sake of fitness for their respective foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*). They are "heaped up on all sides" because they have been brought to the accumulation of development through every aspect.
Therefore he said, "well-increased. They are "thoroughly undertaken" because they have been properly practiced until reaching the pinnacle of the development of supernormal powers (*iddhi*).
"Indeterminately" means by the indeterminate expression "of anyone whatsoever. "Having determined" means having determined by showing the specific form as "of the Tathāgata.
"Life-span measure" refers to the maximum life-span. But what is meant here by "maximum life-span," and how is its measure delimited? It is said:
that which belongs to those various beings in their respective particular states of existence...

Just as specific qualities such as the color, shape, size, and other characteristics of the bodily parts [are determined] by way of the decisive support (upanissaya) of past established existence and aspiration,
so too, for beings in the womb, the sense-sphere gods, and the fine-material-sphere gods, there is generally a fixed limit within their respective destinies and classes;
this is the determination of the duration of the continuity of kamma-result (vipāka), which is supported by present conditions such as semen, blood, temperature, and food.
Thus, because the material and immaterial life-faculties (rūpārūpa-jīvitindriya) function by maintaining their own co-nascent material and immaterial phenomena—
which, though lasting for only a single moment— through the mode of establishing them; they are not merely guardians by acting as the cause for the momentary persistence of those phenomena,
but rather also serve as the cause for the non-interruption of the continuous succession [of moments] until the cutting off of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgupaccheda).
Therefore, because it is the cause of life, it is called "life" (*āyu*) by way of metaphorical designation; and because it defines the maximum limit, it is called "maximum life" (*paramāyu*).
Furthermore, that [maximum life] has a fixed limit for devas, denizens of hell, and those of Uttarakuru.
For those of Uttarakuru, however, the limit is exclusively and invariably fixed. As for the remaining humans, ghosts, and animals, there is an abundance of karma conducive to long-term existence.

At the time [of conception], there is an indefinite delimitation in terms of duration— whether long or short— due to the conditions of the semen and blood produced by a continuum conjoined with that karma,
as well as due to the conditions of the food and temperature produced by the regular or irregular revolutions of the moon and sun rooted therein.

And just as the determination of specific qualities such as color and shape within various destinies and classes was established through previous aspirations for existence, as proven by observation and tradition, so too...

Firstly, regarding the establishment of the grasp [of the lifespan]: thus, for beings born in various rebirths, having generally obtained the duration of their stay through seeing and hearsay, one should understand that the initial determination of the limit occurs by way of the aspiration for existence that proceeds from attachment to that ultimate limit.
For it is karma that, in those various rebirths, brings about the production of the specific color and other characteristics determined by each respective rebirth.
It is capable [of producing results], yet it is not capable of producing a result by exceeding the limit within births where the lifespan is thus fixed;
therefore it is said: "He would remain, completing whatever measure of human lifespan exists at that particular time."

But the Elder Mahāsīva said, “Keeping in mind that the karma which grants rebirth to Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence has the power to bring about an incalculable lifespan, and noting that it is recorded in the Canon that the life-force of Buddhas has the power to suppress dangers, [the Buddha] might have remained for this very Fortunate Aeon (bhaddakappa).
Thus he spoke. [The phrase] “overcome by decrepitude and so forth” means...
By this it is implied by the sense that just as there is no resistance to aging through the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), likewise there is no resistance to death through it.
