It should be understood that even when the Elder’s statement was uttered otherwise—as in, "Where was the arrow shot, and where did it fall?"—it was nonetheless validated by the words of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). Therefore he said: "But as for what is said... [etc. ...is determined."

"In a gross sign" means in the production of a coarse perception. This production of a coarse perception refers to the request for him to remain for an entire *kappa* with the words, "May the Blessed One stay for a *kappa*.

This is the manifestation, by way of an indirect statement—namely, through the passage beginning, "Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of psychic power"—of his own capacity to remain for a *kappa* by virtue of his cultivation of the four bases of psychic power.
"Obhāseti" means "to make manifest. For this is a manifest statement, namely, the direct revelation of one's own intention without resorting to figurative expression (*pariyāya*).
"With a mind obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhitacitto*) means having a mind overcome in such a way that it is impossible to discern what is beneficial or harmful.
That overcoming is like [the drowning of] a small amount of water by a great flood of water.
"It was as if he were being overwhelmed," thus it is said: "one whose mind is overwhelmed.
"Another" means someone other than the Elder, or even any ordinary person (puthujjana) other than the Noble Ones.

And the inclusion of the term "ordinary person" here is intended to show that just as one whose perversion has not been entirely abandoned and whose mind is obsessed by Māra is unable to discern what is beneficial or harmful, so too the Elder [was not able to do so] by the Blessed One...
This is for the purpose of showing that he did not perceive any manifestation of signs at all. Therefore he said, “Māra indeed,” and so forth. The four perversions (vipallāsā) are:
the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind regarding the foul as “beautiful”; and the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind regarding suffering as “pleasure.
These are the four perversions. By the word “therefore” (tena), even though the other eight...
The perversions have been abandoned; nevertheless, it is because of the state of those four aforementioned perversions not having been abandoned.
"Assa" refers to the Elder. "Crushes" means that by the mere act of contact, he is as if crushing [them]; otherwise, if they were crushed by him, the death of sentient beings would surely occur.
"Will he be able? He will not be able"—this is the intended meaning. Why will he not be able?
"Is it not true that he has entered the belly of the Chief Disciple? "It is true that he has entered, but it was for the purpose of displaying his own power, not with the intention of causing harm.
However, it is said here, 'What will he be able to do? because the crushing of the heart is what is emphasized.
Regarding the "appearance of signs," here [the phrase] "May the Blessed One remain for an eon" refers to the entire eon.

The sign (*nimitta*) consists in the production of a perception based on the capacity to remain for an eon through the power of one’s own cultivation of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), by means of an indirect statement such as, "Ānanda, whoever has cultivated the four bases of psychic power," etc., under the pretext of [answering] a question about stability. On the other hand,
the manifestation (*obhāsa*) is the direct disclosure of one’s own intention, having abandoned such an indirect method.
“Knowing indeed” means knowing indeed that he was possessed by Māra.

He said, “For the purpose of thinning out grief through the attribution of fault,” because grief for beings becomes slight rather than powerful when it arises from the cause of one’s own transgression.
But does the Elder only later know his conduct at the time his mind was possessed by Māra? No; he does not know it by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
But he knows it through the power of the Buddha.
Because Ānanda had come here for the purpose of his midday rest, [the Buddha said], "Go, Ānanda;
go, Ānanda, to whatever place you prefer for your midday rest. Therefore he said, "Now do as you deem fit. [The Buddha spoke thus] while directing him toward what is not beneficial.

He is called Māra because he kills by means of killing the virtues (guṇa), or because, by binding one to dispassion (virāga), he is as if killing those born here and there by making them signs for rebirth;
thus it is said, "he kills, therefore he is Māra. He is Pāpimā because of his extreme wickedness. He is Kaṇha because he is endowed with dark qualities (kaṇhadhamma).
He is Antaka because he brings about the end of virtues such as dispassion. He is called Namuci because he does not release beings from a course of conduct that brings them harm.
Namuci. He binds one who is heedless with his own snare of Māra; or, those who are heedless are his bonds, thus he is "the kinsman of the heedless" (*pamattabandhu*).

He says, "in the eighth week," referring to the seven days following the seventh week, but not because that eighth week has a specific, fixed function like the "seven-day sitting" (*pallaṅka-sattāha*) and so forth. For after the seventh week—
Knowing that the Blessed One had promised to teach the Dhamma at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree to Mahābrahmā and Sakka, the king of the gods, he stood there overcome with grief, thinking:
“Now he will lead beings beyond my domain by means of his teaching of the Dhamma;
alas, I shall now cause him to attain final Nibbāna by some stratagem, so that this desire of his may not be fulfilled.”
"It will undergo change, and my heart's desire will be fulfilled.
Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and, standing to one side, requested his final passing with the words, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now attain final nibbāna," and so forth.
With reference to this, it is said: "In the eighth week," and so on. Therein, "today" refers to the day of relinquishing the life-force.
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Although the Blessed One knew his intention to bind [him], he did not reveal it;
rather, rejecting the request, he manifested that it was the wrong time for his final *parinibbāna*. Therefore he said, "Not yet," and so forth.
"Skilled by way of the path" means skilled through proficiency in the penetration of the truths. Likewise, "disciplined" is also by way of the path alone.
They are disciplined by the complete eradication and removal of the defilements (*kilesa*). Likewise, they are "confident" (*visārada*):

through the very attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), they have attained confidence (*vesārajja*) in the Teacher’s dispensation; the meaning is that they have reached a state of confidence by the disappearance of evil states such as wrong views and doubt, which cause timidity.
It is by means of that hearing of the Dhamma (*suta*) that escape from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) becomes possible.
Regarding this, he said, "by way of the three Piṭakas," because here, according to the exalted exposition, it is intended as "the heard" (suta).
A collection of the three Piṭakas is *tepiṭaka*; or, the three Piṭakas themselves are *tipiṭaka*, and *tepiṭaka* is simply that same *tipiṭaka*. By way of that.

"That very thing" refers to that which is called "the heard" by virtue of its being something to be heard, namely the *tepiṭaka*. "The Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).
“They bear it” means they bear it by way of its being well-qualified and well-functioning, keeping it in their hearts without letting it perish—just like lion’s meat placed in a golden vessel.

Thus, having shown the state of being one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma by way of the Dhamma as study (*pariyatti*), the words beginning with “Alternatively” (*atha vā*) were spoken in order to show that same state also by way of the Dhamma as realization (*paṭivedha*). “Of the noble Dhamma” (*ariyadhammassa*)...
Of the dhamma of the path and its fruit, or of the ninefold supramundane dhamma. "Consistent with the dhamma" (anudhamma) means being a dhamma suitable for the attainment [of that goal].
By "conformable practice" (anucchavika-paṭipadā), he refers to that very same dhamma of insight (vipassanā), or else to the sixfold purification (visuddhi).
"Consistent with the dhamma" (anudhamma) means suitable for that aforementioned practice, characterized by effacement (abhisallekhita).
The qualities such as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*). "Those whose nature it is to practice" (*caraṇasīlā*) means those whose nature it is to undertake and maintain [the training].

Alternatively, *anudhammā* refers to that which has the quality of the subsequent path and its fruit; it is insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*). Those whose nature it is to practice this are *caraṇasīlā*.

"One's own teacher’s doctrine" (*attano ācariyavādaṃ*) means the doctrine of one's own teacher, the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). He is called a "teacher" (*ācariya*) because he trains the world, including the devas, in proper conduct.
The Blessed One, his teaching, and the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
"They will proclaim" means they will speak from the beginning; the sense is that they will cause others to learn according to the method they themselves have mastered.
"They will teach" means they will cause [others] to recite; the sense is that they will correctly awaken [others] to the Pāḷi. "They will describe" means...
"They will cause to understand" means they will cause to recollect; "they will establish" means they will set forth in various ways, that is, they will make manifest;
"they will reveal" means they will make open; "they will analyze" means they will make distinct;
"they will make plain" means they will make clear and evident that which was not clear and was deep; "by way of the Dhamma"—here the word *dhamma* [is used].

The "method of cause" (*kāraṇapariyāya*) refers to such passages as, "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); thus he says, "by means of speech that possesses a cause and possesses a reason.
"With its demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) means with its escape (*sanissaraṇa*).

Just as one's own doctrine is established after having refuted the doctrines of others, so too they will preach the Dhamma by accomplishing the matter as it has been realized through reasons and examples. Therefore he says, "leading to liberation" (*niyyānika*).
"Having done so, they will teach the Dhamma"—the meaning is that they will awaken others to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*navavidha-lokuttara-dhamma*).
Herein, by the six terms beginning with "they will proclaim" (*paññapessanti*), six subject-terms (*atthapada*) are shown; but by the first two terms, six phrasing-terms (*byañjanapada*) are shown.
To this extent, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas (*tepiṭaka-buddhavacana*) has been summarized according to the method of exposition.
This has been shown. For it is said in the *Nettippakaraṇa*: "The discourse consists of twelve terms; it includes both the phrasing and the meaning.
"Comprising the three trainings" means being included within the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

"The entire holy life of the Dispensation" refers to the supreme conduct that constitutes the Teacher's teaching in its entirety. "Fully accomplished" means properly increased. "By way of the flavor of jhāna" means...

"By means of the various meditative blisses attained by those respective bhikkhus. "Reached growth" means having come to complete full development through the attainment of a state that is sublime and exquisite.

It is "as if in full bloom" because, through the perfection of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), it has reached the pinnacle of the growth of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) by way of the accomplishment of the higher knowledges.
"By way of being established" means by way of finding a firm footing; that is, by way of attaining a foundation.
*Attha*: It is "beneficial to many" (*bāhujañña*) because it is for the welfare of many people by way of penetration. Therefore he said: “By way of the realization of the great multitude.
"Puthubhūta" means that which has become (*bhūta*) wide (*puthu*) or extensive (*puthula*), or that which has reached a state of multiplicity (*puthutta*).
Therefore he said: “All... [omission] ...reached. “Suṭṭhu pakāsitaṃ” means well-expounded; it has been proclaimed correctly and properly as being excellent in the beginning and so forth.
"Having established mindfulness well": "This burden of suffering called the 'personality' (*attabhāva*), consisting of the analysis of the body and so forth, has been carried by me for so long;

but from now on, it must no longer be carried. For the equipment of the Noble Path has been accumulated over a very long time in order to avoid carrying this [burden], and that Noble Path has now been penetrated.
Therefore, these bodies and so forth, from their true nature as impure and so forth..."
"Having thoroughly understood" means having made the fourfold right mindfulness well-established upon its object, distinguishing it as it truly is.

"Having delimited with knowledge" means that the welfare of oneself—which serves as the purpose for bearing this burden of suffering known as the personal existence—has already been fully accomplished at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
however, the welfare of others, which consists in the disciplining of those to be guided by a Buddha, remains to be accomplished.

"Thinking, 'This [teaching] will now reach completion in just three months, and I too shall attain final Nibbāna on the full moon of Visākha,' he thus delimited it with Buddha-knowledge and made a firm resolution through every aspect of his being.

'He relinquished the life-force' means he relinquished the volitional formation of life— the dhamma of fruition-attainment that sustains existence— thinking, 'I shall no longer enter into that attainment.'"
By that very act of relinquishing it, he relinquished the life-force (jīvitasaṅkhāra) which was being conditioned by him, thinking, "I will not cause it to proceed.
Therefore he said, "Therein," and so forth.
The earthquake was great both because of the vastness of its location and because of the vastness of the mode of its occurrence. Therein, by the vastness of its location...
In order to demonstrate the great magnitude of the earthquake, it is said: "At that time, indeed... [omitted] ...it shook.
However, that which shook was specifically the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*) consisting of the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), and not just any world-system whatsoever.

What is the reason that even when it shook during such events as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) and the Great Birth (*mahābhijāti*), it shook only to that extent? It is because of its status as the field of birth; for it was that very one which was first delimited.
This was due to what had been done [in the past], and his taking possession [of the field] should be understood as occurring by way of natural law (*dhammatā*).
For even for previous Buddhas, the birth-field (*jātikkhetta*) was exactly that much. Thus it is said: "The ten-thousandfold world system becomes silent and undisturbed...
the great ocean rolls back, and the ten-thousandfold world system quakes," and so forth. [It extends] to the limit of the water.
It is called "terrifying" (*bhiṃsana*) because it strikes fear into those who are not free from passion by means of its sixfold throbbing; thus he says "fear-inducing.
"Divine drum" (*devabherī*) is merely a synonym for the sound of the celestial drum (*devadundubhi*).
And here, no physical drum is intended by the term "drum," but rather the sound of a resonance occurring in the sky, which arises as a portent.

Therefore he said, “The god,” and so forth. “The god” means the cloud. For when it thunders, because of its thundering nature, a sound resembling dry thunder issues from the sky, which is then designated as the “drum of the gods. Thus he said, “The god thunders with dry thunder.
[The phrase] “released by the force of joy” means: “For such a long time this burden of suffering, known as this personal existence (attabhāva), has been carried;”
"Now, before long, I shall lay [the burden] down"—thus, with joy arisen, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) released by the force of his natural rapture.
And in order to show that this meaning was also established by him while uttering this *udāna*, the commentary states "For what reason? and so forth.

The word *tula* is explained as "that which weighs" (*tuliyati*); thus, to show that the term *tula* functions as a noun denoting the object of the action, the phrase beginning with "weighed" (*tulitam*) is stated.
[That which is weighed] is delimited because it possesses little power. For it is called "limited" (*paritta*) precisely because it is cut off on all sides.
Because it suppresses its opposites, and because of its long continuity and its vast fruit, it is not "weighed" and is not delimited. By whatever reasons this was previously [stated]...

In general, that which is sublime is called "incomparable" (*atula*). Since those causal factors exist in the immaterial realm (*arūpāvacara*) to a much greater degree than in the fine-material realm (*rūpāvacara*), the immaterial realm is called "incomparable," while the other is called "comparable" (*tula*).
Regarding "small result": among the three types of kamma, that which has slight ripening and is inferior is "comparable. Regarding "great result": that which has abundant ripening and is excellent—
That is "incomparable" (*atula*). However, that which is intermediate here should be divided into two parts—the inferior and the superior—and then included within both categories.

Alternatively, having determined the relative magnitude of the result according to the method explained in the commentary on the "Inferior Triad," the state of being comparable or incomparable should be understood by way of that.
He says "the cause of arising" (*sambhavahetubhūta*) because "arising" (*sambhava*) means that from which something comes into being.
“Delighting in his own internal states” means he delights in the phenomena of his own continuum through the cultivation of the object by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
Although it is accompanied by fruition, karma that yields only the fruition of the process-of-becoming (*pavatti*) is called “origination” in the sense of having fruition;

yet, since that does not constitute the formative force for existence such as sensual desire (*kāmabhava*), the term “existence-formative-force” (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) is used after stating “origination” in order to distinguish it from that. “He relinquished” means by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
He abandoned [them]. By saying "delighting within, concentrated," he stated the cause for both of these,

demonstrating the relinquishing of stolen goods— an act coexistent with the breaking of the defilements— and the defilement itself, which arises within oneself and remains enveloping one's person like a suit of armor.
In the first alternative, only the act of scrutinizing (*avasajjana*) was mentioned; here, showing the manner of that scrutiny, he says “Alternatively,” and so forth.
Therein, “scrutinizing” means examining [the matter] by way of such statements as, “Arising is danger, non-arising is security.

Having stated “The five aggregates,” etc., in order to show in detail the meaning briefly expressed by the phrase “weighing, scrutinizing,” and so on, [he speaks of] the formative process of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*).

He shows the mode of disparagement by way of its form. However, with the words "Thus," etc., he shows the meaning stated at the beginning of the commentary on the *udāna* verses by way of a conclusion.
He says, "By which occasion" or "in which occasion," because the word *yaṃ* is used in the instrumental or locative case as a nominative singular.
"Ukkhepakavātā" means winds that blow away [the water] from the place where it stands after cutting off the wind that supports the water.
When it says "sixty... thick," this is stated by taking only the height-measure of that wind;
however, in terms of length and breadth, it is equal to the measure of ten thousand world-systems, or even a hundred thousand million world-systems—the wind that supports the water.
It indeed cuts off [the flow]. "In space" means in the space previously established by the wind.
"Again the wind" means that when the lifting wind has ceased after having acted thus, the water-supporting wind again binds and seizes it.
Supporting the water so that it does not scatter, it seizes it by way of binding through the medium of a binding canopy. Then the water...
"It rises" means that from the point where it was bound and held fast, the water stirred up by that wind rises and goes upward.
"It indeed occurs" means that it occurs at intervals. "By way of its abundance" refers to the vastness of the great earth;
for the entire great earth then sinks down and rises up, and therefore no shaking is perceived.
“Of success” (ijjhanassa) means of the accomplishment of the desired goal, such as the attainment of sovereignty and so forth, which is to be experienced.
“Limited” (parittā) means merely acquired and not well-cultivated; and because such cultivation is not powerful, he says it is “weak.
For here, cultivation is spoken of by way of its characteristic of perception (saññā). “Immeasurable” (appamāṇā) means familiar and well-cultivated; for that is stable and more firm.
He said, "It is powerful," meaning it occurs. The statement, "The perception of earth is limited, the perception of water is immeasurable," is merely for the sake of the teaching;
however, the intended meaning here should be understood as follows: when the perception of water is well-developed, the shaking of the earth succeeds with ease.
Or else, he was either moving the divine king Sakka—who was negligent due to his celestial prosperity—toward spiritual urgency, or testing him.

He had indeed attained his own power of psychic success (*iddhibala*) to that extent. It is said that as soon as that venerable one attained Arahantship on the very day of his going forth, he thought:
"Is there any bhikkhu who, having attained Arahantship on the very day of his going forth, has previously caused the Vejayanta Palace to tremble?
Then, knowing that "there is no such person," he resolved, "I shall cause it to tremble," and by the power of his higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), [he set about doing so].
Standing on the summit of the Vejayanta Palace, he struck it with his foot but was unable to shake it.
Then the female dancers of Sakka said to him, "Son Saṅgharakkhita, you wish to shake the Vejayanta Palace with a head that reeks of putridity;
dear son, the palace is well-established, how could you possibly shake it?"
The novice thought, “These deities are playing with me, yet I have not found my teacher.
Where indeed is my teacher, the Elder Sāmuddikamahānāga? Having reflected thus, he knew, “He has fashioned a water-cave in the great ocean and is sitting there for his midday rest.
He went there, paid homage to the Elder, and stood before him. Then—
The Elder said to him, "Dear Saṅgharakkhita, you have entered the battle without even training," and asked, "My son, were you unable to shake Vejayanta?
"I did not succeed, venerable sir; I could not find my teacher.
Then the Elder said to him, "My son, if someone like you cannot shake it, who else will? Have you ever seen, my son, [a footprint] on the surface of water?"

“Father, know this by way of this simile: a piece of cow dung floating away, and a cake in a shell being cooked, which is limited by its edge,” he said. He replied, “It will suffice, Bhante; that much will do.
Having resolved, “Let there be water in the space occupied by the palace,” he set out toward the Vejayanta Palace. Seeing him, the daughters of the gods said, “Once—”
"Having been ashamed, he went away; yet the novice comes again, and he comes yet again," they said. Sakka, the king of the gods, said, "Do not speak with my son;
now that he has found a teacher, in an instant he will cause the palace to tremble.
The novice, too, struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, and the palace tilted in all four directions.
The deities cried out, “Give a foundation, dear one! Give a foundation for the palace, dear one!
The novice, having set the palace in its proper place, stood upon the roof of the palace and uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Today I have gone forth; today I have attained the destruction of the taints.”
Today I shake the palace; oh, how sublime is the Buddha!
“Today I have gone forth; today I have attained the destruction of the taints;
today I shake the palace; oh, how sublime is the Dhamma!”
“Today I have gone forth; today I have attained the destruction of the taints;
today I shake the palace—oh, the excellence of the Saṅgha!
“This is the natural law, monks, that when the Bodhisatta descends from the Tusita realm into his mother’s womb.”
Having said, "And this ten-thousandfold world system trembled, shook, and quaked," and likewise having said, "It is the natural law, monks,
that when the Bodhisatta issues from his mother’s womb, this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes,
and quakes," [he spoke] regarding the Great Being’s descent into the womb and his birth.

Since the earthquake is mentioned in the *Mahāpadāna* [Sutta] by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), it should be understood that in the other four instances as well, the earthquake occurs precisely by way of natural law; this is what is stated according to the sense.
Now, in order to show the distinction between these earthquakes according to their causes and the manner of their occurrence, the passage beginning with "Thus, among these... is given.
It has been said. "By the disturbance of the elements" means by the disturbance of the air-element known as the *ukkhepaka*-wind (the wind that causes tossing).

"By the power of success" (*iddhānubhāvena*) means by the power of knowledge-success (*ñāṇiddhi*) or by the power of success born of the ripening of karma; the meaning is "by its own nature. "By the splendor of merit" (*puññatejena*) means by the majesty of merit;

the meaning is "by the power of the merit of a Great Bodhisatta. "By the splendor of knowledge" (*ñāṇatejena*) means by the majesty of the penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) which is not shared with others.

"By way of giving a cry of 'Well done' (sādhukāra)" means: just as the great earth shook at the moment of full enlightenment when struck by the power of the penetrative knowledge (paṭivedhañāṇa) which is not shared by others, so too the great earth shook when struck by the power of the teaching-knowledge (desanāñāṇa) which is not shared by others;
and that [shaking] was, as it were, like the giving of a "well done" to it—thus it is said, "by way of giving a cry of 'Well done'."
To the Blessed One—whose physical body was adorned with the eighty minor marks and variegated by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;

whose Dhamma-body was enriched with the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue, purified in every aspect; who had reached the supreme pinnacle of greatness in merit, power, psychic potency, glory, and wisdom;
who was peerless, equal to the unequaled, without a rival, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One—to him, [the Blessed One] [regarding] his own person known as the self...

Although he was capable of remaining for an eon or the remainder of an eon, by means of a specific knowledge proceeding in the mode of revulsion toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), he did not regard even [the world] as a blade of grass;
thus, through the method of relinquishing the life-force (*āyu-saṅkhāra*), he relinquished it without attachment.
Struck by the power of that [act], the great earth shook at the relinquishing of the life-force. And yet, as if established in a nature of compassion, she [the earth] remained still.
It is said, "by way of compassion.
Because at the time of his final Nibbāna, the Blessed One entered twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments (samāpatti),
interspersed with the attainment of the fruition-attainments (phalasamāpatti), his [mind] in the preceding stage was exceedingly sharp and keen.
And he brought forth insight-knowledge. To him who had attained even greater and exceeding joy, thinking:
"For the sake of which I have for so very long accumulated this supreme, unsurpassed equipment of knowledge—unshared by any other—and for the sake of which I have attained the unsurpassed liberation;
indeed, today that ultimate goal, the fruit reaching its pinnacle, the element of Parinibbāna without residue, is being realized by me."
In the Blessed One, there arose a preeminent excellence of knowledge—a power more vast than the expansion of rapture (*pītivipphāra*) and other qualities—which was not shared by others.
With reference to the majesty of that excellence of knowledge, which was further augmented by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it was said:
"These two alms-offerings have equal fruit, equal result," and so forth. Therefore, [the earth] was struck down by the force of that majesty.
The great earth shook; at that moment, it was as if it had reached a state of weeping, and thus it is said, "the eighth [sign] was by way of weeping.
Now, expanding upon the meaning briefly stated, he says, "when descending into the mother’s womb," and so forth. This, then, is the meaning:
The meaning is stated by the passage beginning with “by way of giving a cry of ‘well done’,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “by way of the earth deity”:
it is said that, just like the ocean deity, there is a presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the great earth;
when such a cause exists, this great earth quakes, trembles, and shakes according to her mind. This is just as in the case of the wind and cloud deities.
The winds blow by the power of the mind; cold, heat, and the clouds of rain and thunder arise by the power of the minds of the deities who control them.

Thus, on the full moon of Visākha, in order to dispel the host of Māra that had appeared to create obstacles for the Lord of the World as he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the sake of his supreme enlightenment—
“This earth is insentient; it does not perceive pleasure or pain.
Yet even it has quaked seven times by the power of my gift.
Immediately upon these words, the great earth split open and overturned Māra along with his retinue. “This” refers to the giving of applause and so forth.
Even if it does not exist because it lacks consciousness, it can nevertheless be said that it occurs by way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*) according to the method already described.
For "the nature of things" means, in its actual sense, the state of being a phenomenon; it is the inherent power and essential character of either a meritorious phenomenon or a cognitive phenomenon.
All of this has already been investigated. And having established it thus—
“As he comprehends these phenomena, with their individual essences and specific characteristics,
the earth of the ten thousandfold world system trembles by the power of the Dhamma.
Thus the opening words are justified.
Furthermore, this great earth trembled on eight other occasions:

at the Great Renunciation, the approach to the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the taking up of rag-robe relics, the washing of those rag-robes, the *Kāḷaka-ārāma-sutta*, the *Gotamaka-sutta*, the *Vessantara-jātaka*, and the *Brahmajāla-sutta*.
Among these, it trembled through the power of his energy (*vīriya*) during the Great Renunciation and the approach to the seat of enlightenment.

Regarding the taking of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*), she trembled, overcome by the force of her wonder, thinking: "The Blessed One has performed a difficult feat, having gone forth and gone to the charnel ground to take rag-robes, after abandoning the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands.
She trembled due to the untimely shaking during the *Paṃsukūladhovana* and *Vessantara Jātaka*. [She also trembled] during the *Kāḷakārāma* and *Gotamaka Suttas*.
“I am a witness, O Blessed One,” he said, and the earth shook by way of his testimony.

Furthermore, it should be understood that when the sixty-two types of speculative views were being disentangled and cleared away as they were taught in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, the earth shook by way of his expression of approval (*sādhukāra*).
And it was not only on these occasions that the earth shook; rather, it also shook during the three assemblies of the Elder Mahinda.
On the day he arrived at this island, sat in the Jotivana, and taught the Dhamma, it quaked.
Furthermore, after sweeping the courtyard of the Piṇḍapātiya Thera’s cetiya in the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra and sitting right there, he experienced rapture directed toward the Buddha;
as he began this sutta, the earth quaked, reaching as far as the edge of the ocean at the conclusion of the discourse.
The eastern side of the Lohapāsāda was known as Ambalaṭṭhika; it was there that the Dīgha-bhāṇaka Theras sat down and began reciting the Brahmajāla Sutta.
Even at the conclusion of their recitation, the earth shook, having made water its boundary. If this is so, then [it is in accordance with the Buddha’s words]:
"Ānanda, these eight causes, these eight conditions, for the manifestation of a great earthquake."
Why are exactly eight causes stated? Because they constitute the fixed causes (*niyama-hetu*). For it is these eight causes alone that determine [the result], and no others.
Since those other factors may arise at any time, they are not counted because they lack such fixity. Indeed, this was said by the Elder Nāgasena in the *Milindapañha*:
"Monks, there are these eight causes and eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake. By Vessantara...
When the king was giving the great alms-giving, the great earth shook seven times;
and that, moreover, was not due to the eight causes, but was occasional and spontaneous, and therefore it was not counted among the eight causes.
“Great King, just as in the world only three kinds of clouds are reckoned—the rainy-season cloud, the winter cloud, and the autumn cloud—if...
When those have ceased, another cloud pours down rain; that cloud is not counted among the recognized clouds, but is designated as an "untimely cloud.

In the same way, Great King, when the great gift was being given by King Vessantara, the fact that the great earth shook seven times was an untimely occurrence, arising at an unexpected moment and free from the eight causes [of earthquakes].
It is not counted by eight reasons.

"Or again, Great King, just as five hundred rivers flow from the Himavat mountains, of those five hundred rivers, Great King, only ten rivers are counted in the reckoning of rivers. Namely: the Gaṅgā..."
The Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, Mahī, Sindhu, Sarassatī, Vetravatī, Vītansā, and Candabhāgā.
The remaining rivers were not included in the counting of the rivers. For what reason? Because those rivers do not have constant waters.
In the same way, Great King, when the great gift was being given by King Vessantara, as many times as the great earth...
It is trembling; it is not subject to time, it arises occasionally, and being free from the eight causes, it is not reckoned by those eight causes.
"Or again, Great King, as a king may have a hundred, two hundred, or three hundred ministers, yet only six persons among them are reckoned in the calculation of ministers.
Namely: the commander-in-chief, the chaplain, the treasurer,"
The treasurer, the umbrella-bearer, and the sword-bearer—these alone are counted in the reckoning of ministers. For what reason?
Because they are endowed with the qualities of a king. The remainder are not counted; yet all of them are nevertheless considered to be among the ranks of ministers.
In the same way, Great King, when King Vessantara was bestowing his great gift, as many times as the great earth...
“Trembling is not timely; it arises occasionally and is free from the eight causes. It is not reckoned among those things produced by the eight causes.
The commentary on the Bhūmicāla Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Cāpāla Vagga is finished.
(8) 3. Yamakavagga 1–10. Commentary on the *Saddhāsutta* and following, verses 71–80.

The first [verses] of the eighth [chapter] have their meaning already explained (*uttānattha*). In the tenth [verse], one who sinks into what is contemptible is a *kusīta*; this is due to the substitution of the letter *da*.
Having formed the word with the letter *ta*. That state by virtue of which a person is called "lazy" (*kusīta*) is what is expressed here by the word "laziness" (*kusita*).
For even without a word explicitly indicating an abstract state (*bhāva*), the meaning of the state is understood, as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭassa sukkaṃ*);
therefore, the meaning is "the bases for the state of laziness. Hence he said: "the causes of indolence."
"Meaning": he said "the distribution of robes and so forth" because such work is appropriate for a recluse (*samaṇa*). "Energy" refers to the energy of striving (*padhāna-vīriya*).
Since that can also be called "bodily" when performed by means of walking meditation (*caṅkama*), he said "both kinds.
"For the sake of attaining" means for the purpose of reaching [the goal]. "Sinking" refers to shrinking back from application to the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanānuyoga*). By months...

That which was heaped up and accumulated disperses after a month; that, I think, is what is meant. Because fruits that have been soaked for a month become especially heavy, it is said, "just as a soaked fruit," and so forth.
The intention is that he has emerged from his state of illness.
"Of those" refers to the bases for exertion. "By this very method" means by the same method stated regarding the bases for laziness.
“‘He exerts two kinds of energy’ and so forth. This is the first [basis for exertion].
The meaning should be understood from such passages as: “‘Now, indeed, I shall exert this energy,’ thus there is the first basis for exertion, which is the resolution through development”;
for the resolution that occurs first in whatever manner becomes the cause for the subsequent exertion of energy.
For it should be understood that the eight bases for initiative (*ārambhavatthu*) are the efforts accompanied by appropriate reflection,
or the reflections rooted therein.
The commentary on the *Saddhāsutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Yamaka-vagga is finished.

Thus ends [the portion from] the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
The Elucidation of the Unexpounded Meanings in the Commentary on the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta is completed.

The Chapter on Enlightenment (Sambodhivagga)
1–2. Commentary on the *Sambodhi-sutta* and others:
There is nothing further to be said regarding the first and second suttas of the Ninth Chapter.
3. Commentary on the *Meghiya-sutta*.
3. In the third [case], "Meghiya" is the name of that elder. "Was his attendant" means he was his personal servant.
For during the Blessed One’s first awakening, the attendants were not fixed;
at one time it was Nāgasamāla, at one time Nāgita, at one time Upavāṇa, at one time Sunakkhatta, at one time the novice Cunda, at one time Sāgata, and at one time Meghiya.
At that time too, the Elder Meghiya was his attendant. Therefore it is said: "Now at that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One’s attendant.
By "Kimikālā" is meant the river so named because of its abundance of black worms (*kālakimī*). "Jaṅghāvihāra" means...
"Wandering" means walking about for the purpose of dispelling the fatigue that has arisen in the shanks from sitting for a long time.
"Pleasant" (*pāsādika*) means it brings forth confidence (*pasāda*) to those who see it because the trees are not too dense and the leaves are glossy.

"Delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) means it delights the mind in the sense of generating joy and gladness for those who have entered within, due to its abundant shade and its charming ground. "Enough" (*alaṃ*) means sufficient.
“Yuttanto” also has the meaning of “one who is engaged. “One who desires striving” means one who desires striving through the practice of meditation (*bhāvanā*).
Since he is engaged in the work of striving and is thus called a “performer of the work of striving,” it is said, “of the performer of the work of striving.
“Āgaccheyyāhaṃ” means “I would come. It is said that formerly the Elder had visited that place five times in succession.
For hundreds of births, this park had been enjoyed by kings alone; therefore, as soon as he saw it, his mind inclined toward dwelling there.
"Until another monk comes"—meaning, until some other monk arrives in my presence.
The meaning is: "Let him come. There is also the reading "some monk is seen," and they read "let him come," as well as "let him be seen.

"There is nothing further to be done" means that because the sixteen tasks—such as full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth—have been performed by means of the four paths regarding the four truths, or because perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) has been attained, there is nothing other than that [to be done].
"There is nothing further to be done" means that the four tasks regarding the four truths have been accomplished;
this, however, is stated without considering the distinctions obtainable by way of the paths.

"There is an accumulation of what has been done" refers to the fact that because the noble path—consisting of the qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth—has not yet been realized within my own continuum, one must again [strive] for its sake.
There is an accumulation known as "increasing"; the meaning is that it is to be desired.

"Surrounded by a threefold troupe of dancers" means being encircled by three kinds of dancing women: great women, middle-aged women, and very young women—thus [surrounded] by dancing women of three types according to their roles as brides, maidens, and young girls.
"By unwholesome thoughts" refers to the aforementioned thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.
Others, however, say: "In that forest thicket, sensual thought arises through greed for the flowers, fruits, shoots, and so forth;
ill-will thought arises from hearing the harsh cries of birds and other creatures; and cruelty thought arises from the intention to harm them with clods of earth and the like.
Or, sensual thought arises there through a longing for it, thinking, 'May I dwell right here,' [directed toward] the forest-dwellers."

They say that when he sees various things here and there, thoughts of ill will arise through the mental misapprehension of those objects, and thoughts of cruelty arise with the intention of harming them.
Whether it be one way or another, the very occurrence of his wrong thoughts is the cause of wonder.
"It is indeed a wonder, sir!"—this is said to be a "wonder of censure. Just as the Venerable...
Seeing the Blessed One’s wrinkled limbs, Ānanda said, “It is wonderful, Bhante!
It is marvelous, Bhante! *Samparivāritā* means surrounded or interspersed. The plural number is seen used even for a single entity when it is heavy with respect to itself;
there is also a reading, “*anvāsatto*. But why did the Blessed One permit him to go there? [Because he thought: “Even though not permitted, this one would leave me...”
"He will surely go; perhaps it is because he desires to be an attendant that the Blessed One does not allow him to go, and this might lead to his ruin and suffering for a long time.
Having thus reported his own situation and sat down, the Blessed One, teaching him the Dhamma appropriate to him, said:
“Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind (cetovimutti) is not yet mature,” and so forth, he said. Therein, “not yet mature” means that which has not reached maturity.

“Liberation of mind” means the liberation of the mind from defilements. For in the earlier stage, there is liberation of mind by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and by way of suppression (vikkhambhana); in the later stage, it is by way of eradication (samuccheda).
And by way of subsiding. This liberation has already been explained in detail below;

therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there. In that context, when the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) has been matured and purified by the states conducive to the ripening of liberation, and when insight (*vipassanā*)—which is taking up the embryo of the Path—is reaching its own maturity, the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) is said to be "ripened."
When these are present, it is mature; in their absence, it is immature.

What, then, are the states that bring about the maturation of liberation? It should be understood that there are fifteen states by way of purifying the faculty of faith and the others. For this has been said:

"By avoiding persons lacking faith, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons endowed with faith, and by reflecting upon discourses that inspire confidence—in these three ways, the faculty of faith is purified."

“By avoiding persons who are indolent, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who have aroused energy, and by reviewing the right exertions—in these three ways the faculty of energy is purified.

By avoiding persons who are muddle-minded, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons whose mindfulness is established, and by reviewing the foundations of mindfulness—in these three ways the faculty of mindfulness is purified.”

“By avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who are concentrated, and by reviewing the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and liberations (vimokkha)—through these three modes, the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified.

By avoiding persons who lack wisdom, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons endowed with wisdom, and by reviewing the profound course of knowledge—through these three modes, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is purified.”

“Thus, for one who avoids these five persons, who associates with, frequents, and attends upon these five persons, and who reviews these five discourses, these five faculties are purified through these fifteen modes.
Furthermore, these five faculties are purified by another fifteen modes.

Moreover, there are fifteen other states that ripen for liberation: the five faculties beginning with faith, the perception of impermanence regarding the impermanent, the perception of suffering [regarding the impermanent], and so forth.
The five perceptions conducive to penetration—perception of suffering, perception of non-self, perception of relinquishment, perception of dispassion, and perception of cessation;
as well as friendship with the virtuous, restraint by virtue, effacement, arousal of energy, and penetrative wisdom.
Among these, the Teacher, skilled in taming those to be tamed, [taught] here friendship with the virtuous and the others in accordance with the disposition of the Elder Meghiya, who was to be tamed.

Demonstrating the qualities that ripen liberation, [the Blessed One] said, "Five things lead to ripening," and then, explaining them in detail, he said, "In this case, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has a good friend," and so forth.
Therein, "one with a good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) means one whose friend is good, auspicious, and beautiful; it refers to one who possesses qualities such as virtue and the like.
"One who provides for one's welfare and protects one from harm"—in this way, a friend is one who assists in every respect; such a person is indeed a "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*).
One who moves and proceeds together with those very virtuous persons mentioned above in all postures, and not without them, is a "virtuous companion" (*kalyāṇasahāya*).
It is by means of both mind and body that one inclines, leans, and tends toward virtuous persons alone.
"It proceeds" means it is "well-accompanied. Through these three phrases, one arouses respect for association with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*).

This quality called "virtuous friendship" is the first faultless state (*anavajjadhamma*) among these five states because it is stated first; for it is the beginning of the life of purity (*brahmacariya*), and because it is preeminent due to its great service to all wholesome qualities (*kusala-dhamma*).
It leads to the ripening of the liberation of mind by means of purifying faith and the other [faculties] that have not yet been purified.

And herein, regarding the great benefit and preeminence of a good friend, the Blessed One spoke twice to the Dhamma-keeper Ānanda— who had said, "Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life, namely, having a good friend"— saying, "Do not say so, Ānanda."
Having refuted [the contrary view], it should be understood through such introductory sutta passages as: "The whole of this holy life, Ānanda, is this: namely, good friendship, good companionship.
Furthermore, "again" (puna caparaṃ) means another category of Dhamma. Regarding the term "virtuous" (sīlavā): in what sense is it "virtue" (sīla)? It is in the sense of "steadfastness" (sīlana).

Virtue (*sīla*). What is this so-called "virtuous conduct" (*sīlana*)? It means composure; that is to say, the state of being undisturbed due to the well-disciplined nature of bodily action and so forth.
Alternatively, it means sustaining; that is to say, the state of being a support by way of providing a foundation for wholesome states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).

Therefore, it is called *sīla* because it makes one virtuous (*sīleti*) or because one is virtuous (*sīlati*). This, first of all, is the meaning of virtue according to the method of etymological definition (*saddalakkhaṇanaya*). Others...
However, they explain the meaning according to the method of etymology (nirutti) as: "the sense of head (siraṭṭha), the sense of coolness (sītalaṭṭha), the sense of virtue (sīlaṭṭha).
Thus, because he possesses virtue (sīla) that is either complete or preeminent, he is "virtuous" (sīlavā); the meaning is that he is "endowed with virtue" (sīlasampanna).
To show how he is virtuous and endowed with virtue, it is said: "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.

In this context, *pātimokkha* refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For it protects (*pāti*) and releases (*mokkheti*)—that is, liberates—one from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth;
thus it is called *pātimokkha*. Restraint (*saṃvaraṇaṃ*) is *saṃvara*; it is the non-transgression by means of body and speech. The *pātimokkha* itself as restraint is *pātimokkhasaṃvara*.
One who is restrained by that, with body and speech covered, is said to be "restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto*).
This is an exposition of his state of being established in that virtue (*sīla*). "Dwells" (*viharati*) is an exposition of his possession of a dwelling corresponding to that [virtue].

"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*) is an exposition of the qualities that assist both the restraint of the Pātimokkha mentioned below and the yoga of the higher distinctions.

"Seeing fear in even the slightest faults" (*aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī*) is an exposition of the quality of being subject to non-decline from the morality of the Pātimokkha. "Having undertaken" (*samādāya*)...
The phrase "of the training precepts" (*sikkhāpadānaṃ*) is an illustration of their undertaking in its entirety. "He trains" (*sikkhati*) is an illustration of being endowed with the training.
"In the training precepts" (*sikkhāpadesu*) is an illustration of the things that ought to be trained in.
According to another method: because of the powerful state of the defilements, because evil actions are easy to perform, and because meritorious actions...
He is a *pātī* because, due to his state of difficulty, he is prone to falling repeatedly into the states of misery (*apāya*); that is, the worldling (*puthujjana*).

Alternatively, because he is cast by the force of karma into existence and the other realms due to impermanence, and wanders about without stability like a potter’s wheel, he is one whose nature is to go;

thus he is a *pātī*. Or else, by way of death, he is one whose nature is to fall from one selfhood into another within various classes of beings; thus he is a *pātī*, namely, the continuum of sentient beings (*sattasantāna*).
Or rather, it is the mind itself. It is called the *pātimokkha* because it liberates (*mokkheti*) that [mind] from the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

For by the liberation of the mind, a being is said to be "liberated. Indeed, it is said: "By the purification of the mind, they are purified," and "The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging."
Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because by means of causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*), one falls into, goes toward, and wanders within *saṃsāra*.
For it is said: "Of beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, wandering and transmigrating...
Since liberation from that wandering being—from the threefold defilements beginning with craving—is achieved by this [code], it is the *Pātimokkha*.

Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because it causes one to fall (*pāteti*), to fall into ruin (*vinipāteti*), and to suffer (*dukkheti*). For it has been said: "The world is led by the mind; by the mind it is dragged along.

That which brings about the release (*mokkho*) of that which falls (*pātino*) is the *Pātimokkha*. Or else, it is called *pāti* because by means of it one falls into the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*) and the suffering of *saṃsāra*;
this refers to the defilement of craving (*taṇhā*) and so forth. For it has been said: "Craving gives birth to a person. Craving is his companion..."
And [the phrase] beginning with "a person" (*puriso*). From that, there is release (*mokkho*); thus it is *pātimokkha*.

Alternatively, it is *pāti* because one falls into it; namely, the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*). For it is said: "The world has arisen in the six; in the six it forms intimacy. From that which is reckoned as the six internal and external sense bases...
The *pātimokkha* is so called because it is liberation (*mokkha*) from transgression (*pāta*). Alternatively, that which possesses early downfall (*pāta-vinipāta*) is *pātī*, namely, *saṃsāra*;
liberation from that is the *pātimokkha*. Alternatively, the Blessed One, as the Lord of Dhamma due to his sovereignty over the entire world, is called *pati*;
that by which one is liberated is *mokkha*; and since it is prescribed by him—the liberation of the Lord—it is the *patimokkha*. Thus, it is the *patimokkha*.
Thus is the *pātimokkha*. Alternatively, because it is the root of all virtues, it is the "lord" (*pati*) in the sense of being supreme;
and since it is a liberation (*mokkha*) in the sense already explained, it is the *patimokkha*. The *pātimokkha* is simply the *patimokkha*. For it has been said: "‘Pātimokkha’:
this is the beginning, this is the mouth, this is the foremost," and so on in detail.

Alternatively, *pa-* is the syllable *pa*; *ati* is a particle in the sense of "absolute. Therefore, it is called *pātimokkha* because it absolutely releases (*mokkheti*) by means of various ways (*pakārehi*).

For this virtue (*sīla*), when combined with concentration and wisdom, absolutely releases or liberates (*moceti*) through the power of its own factors (*tadaṅga-vasena*), as well as through suppression (*vikkhambhana-vasena*) and eradication (*samuccheda-vasena*);
thus it is *pātimokkha*. Or, it is *patimokkha* because there is release (*mokkha*) for each individual (*pati pati*).
The meaning is that it is a "separate release" (paccēka-mokkho) from each respective fault of transgression. Thus, *patimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, *mokkha* means Nibbāna; it is called *paṭimokkha* because it is a counterpart (*paṭibimba*) to that Nibbāna.

For the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) is like the dawn preceding the rising of the sun; it is the precursor to the arising of Nibbāna, being its very image, since it extinguishes the defilements accordingly.
*Pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*. Alternatively, it is *patimokkha* because it leads toward liberation (*mokkha*), or it is *patimokkha* because it is directed toward liberation;
thus, *pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*. In this way, first, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* should be understood here.
It is called *saṃvara* because one restrains or covers [the mind] by means of it; *pātimokkha-saṃvara* is simply *pātimokkha* as restraint. As for its meaning:
Furthermore, because they are to be transgressed against here and there, [the precepts] are abstinences and volitions;
thus, one who is "endowed with" (*upeta*) and "possessed of" (*samannāgata*) that restraint of the Pātimokkha is "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed, well-endowed, approached, perfected, and possessed; therefore, he is called 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.'"
"He dwells" means he dwells by way of the dwelling in the postures; he moves and conducts himself.

"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" means that, by avoiding all improper conduct through the non-performance of wrong livelihood such as giving bamboo-shoots and so forth, and through the absence of physical immodesty and the like, there is bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression—thus, by the perfection of conduct befitting a bhikkhu as it has been described.

He is "perfect in conduct and resort" because he avoids the resort of prostitutes and the like, and because he possesses the practice of frequenting those places designated as suitable for approaching for the sake of alms-food and other necessities.
Furthermore, he is one who is respectful and deferential toward the Teacher, and respectful and deferential toward his fellow celibates.
Endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, well-clad and properly dressed, he was graceful in his forward and backward movements,
in looking ahead and looking aside, in bending and stretching his limbs; he was perfected in deportment, guarded in the doors of the senses,
moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, few in desires, contented, and secluded.
One who dwells unassociated with worldly society, acting with diligence and abounding in a sense of reverence toward the teacher, is called "perfected in conduct" (*ācārasampanna*).
As for the "range" (*gocara*), it is threefold: the range of support (*upanissaya-gocara*), the range of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the range of anchoring (*upanibandha-gocara*).

Among these, the "friend of virtue" (*kalyāṇamitta*)—endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of discourse and possessing the characteristics already described—is that which one relies upon so that what has not been heard...
One hears [the teaching], purifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one's view, and gladdens the mind;
and by training in accordance with that [teacher], one grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom—
this is called the "object of resort as decisive support" (*upanissaya-gocara*).
When a bhikkhu who has entered among the houses and set out upon the street walks with downcast eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead,

restrained, not looking at an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a foot-soldier, nor a woman, nor a man; not looking upward, nor looking downward, nor glancing about in the various directions— this is the protected range of activity.
The range for binding [the mind] (*upanibandha-gocara*), however, consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), wherein a bhikkhu binds his own mind.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, bhikkhus, is the bhikkhu’s own range, his ancestral domain?
That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness. Since the range of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-gocara*) has been explained previously, [the explanation] of the others...

Here, the sphere of activity (*gocara*) is to be understood by way of its basis. Thus, because he is endowed with both the aforementioned perfection of conduct (*ācāra-sampatti*) and this perfection of the sphere of activity, he is "perfect in conduct and sphere of activity" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanna*).
Regarding the phrase "seeing fear in even the slightest faults": because they are trifling, these faults are of minute measure; [he sees fear in them] due to negligence and unintentionally.
He is one whose nature is to see danger in faults, such as the occurrence of unwholesome thoughts regarding the training rules (sekhiya-dhammas) and so forth.

For that bhikkhu who perceives even a fault the size of an atom as being like Sineru, the king of mountains, rising six hundred and eighty thousand yojanas high; and he who perceives even the slightest minor offense of wrong speech as being like a pārājika offense—he too, regarding even minute matters...

"One who sees danger in the things to be avoided" means this. "Having undertaken, he trains in the rules of training" means that whatever is to be trained in among the rules of training, having undertaken all of it in every way, entirely and without exception, he trains in it;
the meaning is that he conducts himself and fulfills it.
"Conducive to self-effacement" (*abhisallekhikā*) means exceedingly conducive to the wearing away of the defilements (*kilesa*), being suitable for their attenuation and abandonment.

"Favorable to the opening of the mind" (*cetovivaraṇasappāyā*) means favorable to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), which are termed the "opening of the mind" by virtue of causing the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) that shroud the mind to recede;
or it means making manifest the opening of the very mind of serenity and insight.
Or, "suitable for the opening of the mind" means suitable for the expansion of the heart.

Now, in order to show by what means this discourse brings about disenchantment (*nibbidā*) and so forth—thereby being called "austerity-inducing" (*abhisallekhika*) and "suitable for the opening of the mind"—it is said:
"for the sake of absolute disenchantment," and so on. Therein, "for the sake of absolute disenchantment" (*ekantanibbidāya*) means exclusively.

For the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the suffering of saṃsāra. For fading away and cessation: for the purpose of the fading away of that very [suffering] and for the purpose of its cessation.
For tranquility: for the complete subsiding of all defilements. For direct knowledge: for the full realization of everything that is to be directly known.
For enlightenment: for the enlightenment of the four paths. For Nibbāna: for Nibbāna without residue. For among these, from the beginning...

Insight (vipassanā) is described by three terms, and Nibbāna by two. This shows that this entire higher human state (uttarimanussadhamma), beginning with serenity (samatha) and insight and ending with Nibbāna, is accomplished by one who attains the ten bases of discourse (dasakathāvatthu).
Now, explaining that discourse in detail, he says: "The discourse on fewness of desires" (appicchakathā), and so forth. Therein, "one of few desires" (appiccha) means:
"Niiccha" means talk on fewness of wishes (*appiccha-kathā*), or talk connected with the state of having few wishes.

In this context, there are four types of persons according to their desires: one who has excessive desire (*atriccha*), one who has evil desire (*pāpiccha*), one who has great desire (*mahiccha*), and one who has few wishes (*appiccha*).

Among these, "one who has excessive desire" refers to one who is not satisfied with the gains he has already received and desires further gain; it is with reference to such a person that it is said: [the following verse].
“From four he attained eight, and from eight, sixteen;
from sixteen, thirty-two—thus the wheel of insatiable desire rolled forward.
For the person overcome by craving, the wheel revolves upon the head.”
It is said: “By excessive desire, by excessive greed, and by the intoxication of excessive greed.
One who desires gain, honor, and fame, with the intention of being esteemed for qualities they do not actually possess, is one of evil desire.
Referring to such a person, it is said: “Here, someone being faithless wishes: ‘May people know me as faithful’; being immoral, he wishes: ‘May people know me as virtuous’...”
“‘May people know me as virtuous,’ thus he desires,” and so forth.
One who, with the intention of gaining esteem for his existing virtues, lacks moderation in receiving gifts and possesses great desire—referring to whom it was said:
“In this case, someone being faithful desires, ‘May people know me as faithful’; being virtuous, he desires, ‘May people know me as virtuous’...”
"He desires [to know] 'May he understand,'" and so forth. Indeed, because of his insatiability, even his own mother, once he is born, is unable to win over his heart. Therefore, this is said:
"A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire—these three cannot be satisfied even if they were given sustenance by means of a cart."
But having avoided these faults such as lack of fewness of wishes from afar, one who is moderate in receiving and possesses the intention to conceal his own virtues is "one of few wishes.

Being endowed with faith, he does not desire that people know him as "faithful" out of a wish to conceal the virtues existing within himself; likewise for being virtuous, learned, secluded, and energetic.
Being one whose mindfulness is established, concentrated, and wise, he does not desire that people should know him as "wise.

This [term] *appiccha* (one who desires little) is fourfold: one who desires little in terms of requisites, one who desires little in terms of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), one who desires little in terms of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), and one who desires little in terms of attainments (*adhigama*).
Among these, one who desires little regarding the four requisites, having observed the donor of the requisites, the gift to be given, and his own capacity, [proceeds accordingly].
For even if the gift to be given is abundant, if the donor wishes to give little, one takes only a small amount according to the donor's wish.
If the gift to be given is small, but the donor wishes to give much, one takes only a small amount according to the nature of the gift.
And if both the gift to be given is abundant and the donor wishes to give much, one takes only a measure appropriate to one's own strength, having understood that strength.
He takes it up. For such a bhikkhu produces unarisen gain, makes arisen gain stable, and gratifies the minds of donors.

One who does not wish to make known the presence within himself of the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is one who desires the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgappiccha). He who does not wish to make known his own state of being learned is—

One who desires little in regard to the scriptures (*pariyatti-appiccha*) is so called. However, one who, having become a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) or any other stage of attainment, does not even wish to let his fellow celibates know his status as a stream-enterer and so forth, is one who desires little in regard to realization (*adhigama-appiccha*).

Thus, regarding the state of desiring little belonging to these [two types] of those who desire little, by means of the method of demonstrating it together with its various aspects and manifold benefits...

The discourse on fewness of desires (*appiccha-kathā*) is that which proceeds by way of discerning the danger in conduct based on desire (*icchācāra*), which has its opposite and is divided into types such as excessive longing (*atricchā*).

Regarding the phrase "discourse on contentment" (*santuṭṭhi-kathā*): here, "contentment" (*santuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction with what one has obtained for oneself; thus it is "contentment" (*santuṭṭhi*). Now...
Or, having abandoned uneven desire for requisites, there is even contentment, which is *santuṭṭhi*. Or, contentment with what is available and peaceful is *santuṭṭhi*.
And this has been said:
"He is not bound to the past, nor does he long for the future;”
“Living on what is present, one is called ‘contented.

Contentment (*santuṭṭhi*) is satisfaction with the requisites according to the right way, by the method authorized by the Blessed One; in terms of meaning, it is contentment with whatever requisites are obtained.
That is twelvefold. How so? Regarding robes: contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment with whatever is suitable, and contentment with whatever is appropriate.
It is threefold. This applies likewise to almsfood and the other requisites.
Herein, this is the explanation of the classification: here a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether beautiful or ugly;
he makes do with that very one, does not long for another, and even if he receives one, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever robe is obtained.
Furthermore, if one is naturally weak or overcome by illness and old age, one may find it exhausting to wear heavy robes;
if such a person exchanges them with a fellow monk of similar status and remains content even while wearing light ones, this is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength.
Another person may be a recipient of excellent requisites, such as robes made of fine cloth like *paṭṭa*.
Even if one receives a certain expensive robe or many robes, and having given them to those elders who have long been ordained,
who are learned, saying, "This is suitable for them; let this be for the sick, the weak,
and those of little gain," one then wears a robe made from rags gathered by oneself from a rubbish heap, or having taken their old robes.
He is indeed content; this is his contentment with robes as they are appropriate.

Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he sustains himself with that alone, does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not accept it—this is his contentment with almsfood as it is obtained. Then, moreover...
He becomes afflicted; having eaten almsfood that is coarse, refined, naturally incompatible, or contrary to his illness, he falls into a severe sickness.

Yet, after giving to a fellow monk who is in the same condition and eating suitable food from that person's hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.

Another receives much excellent almsfood; thinking, "This almsfood is suitable for those who have long been gone forth," he gives it to them as if it were a robe, or eats the leftovers after they have eaten, or even when he goes for alms himself and eats mixed food, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with almsfood according to suitability.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu obtains a lodging—whether pleasing or unpleasing, even if it is merely a spread of grass—he is content with that alone.
If he later obtains something more beautiful, he does not take it; this is his contentment with whatever lodging is obtained.
Moreover, if he becomes ill or weak, or if [the lodging] is incompatible with his natural constitution...

If he receives a lodging that is incompatible with his illness, such that it is uncomfortable for him to dwell there, he gives it to a fellow monk of similar status and dwells in the suitable lodging belonging to that person; even while practicing the duty of a recluse, he remains content.
This is his contentment with a lodging according to his strength. Another, even when obtaining a beautiful lodging, does not accept it.
“Luxurious lodging is a ground for negligence”: because of his great merit, he may obtain many luxurious lodgings such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth;
yet, having given these away like robes and other requisites to those who have long been ordained and others, he remains content wherever he dwells.
This is his contentment with a lodging that is appropriate to his state.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicine, whether coarse or refined; he is content with that very thing and does not long for another.
Even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is contentment with what is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
Then again, one who needs oil receives molasses; he gives what he has received to a fellow bhikkhu of like standing.
Even when he prepares medicine with oil from his own hand and practices the duty of a recluse, he remains content;
this is his contentment according to his strength regarding the requisite of medicine. Another person of great merit receives abundant, high-quality medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses;
he gives these away like robes and other requisites to those who have been ordained for a long time and so forth, and accepts whatever is brought by them—be it even a mere scrap.

Even when preparing medicine, one remains contented. However, when someone has placed urine-soaked harītakī in one vessel and the four sweets (*catumadhura*) in another, and is told, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish," he thinks:
"If his illness is cured by either of these, this is called 'urine-soaked harītakī,' which was praised by the Buddha and others. [He considers it] as "medicine of putrid urine" (*pūtimuttabhesajja*).

Recalling the words, “Going forth depends on this; you should make an effort regarding it for as long as life lasts,” he rejects the four sweet foods and, preparing medicine with urine-soaked harītaka, remains supremely contented.
This is his appropriate contentment with the requisite of medicine.

Thus, all contentment, with its various divisions as described above, is called *santuṭṭhi* (contentment). Therefore it was said: "In terms of meaning, it is contentment with whatever conditions are available.

A discourse that proceeds by way of demonstrating the benefits of that contentment through the method of exposition beginning with "showing" (*sandassana*), and by way of demonstrating the danger of the conduct of desire—which consists of such things as immoderate longing (*atricchā*) and which is the opposite of that contentment—is called the "discourse on contentment" (*santuṭṭhikathā*).
The same method applies to the subsequent discourses as well; we shall state only the specific differences.
Regarding the "discourse on solitude," there are three kinds of solitude: solitude of body (*kāyaviveka*), solitude of mind (*cittaviveka*), and solitude from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).
Among these, one goes alone, one stands alone, one sits alone, one lies down alone, and one enters the village for alms alone.
One retreats, one advances, one resolves upon the walking meditation path, one wanders, and one dwells;
thus, in all postures and in all activities, having abandoned the company of crowds, dwelling in seclusion is called physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
The eight attainments (*samāpatti*), however, are called mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). Nibbāna is called seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*). For it has been said:
“Bodily seclusion belongs to those who have withdrawn from the body and delight in renunciation; mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and who have attained supreme clarity;
and seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons free from acquisitions who have reached the state beyond formations.
Thus, seclusion itself is *paviveka*; discourse connected with seclusion is *pavivekakathā*.

Regarding "talk on non-association": here there are five kinds of association—association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversing, association by sharing, and physical association. Among these, a certain bhikkhu here hears:
"In such and such a place, whether in a village or a town, there is a woman who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion."
Having heard that, he becomes despondent and disheartened; he is unable to maintain the holy life, and having renounced the training, he reverts to the lower state.
Thus, the intimacy with defilements arising from hearing about an unsuitable object is called "contact through hearing.
Furthermore, a monk does not merely hear of it, but personally sees a woman who is beautiful and lovely to behold.
[He sees] one who is inspiring and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion;
seeing him, he becomes dejected and despondent, unable to maintain the holy life, and having renounced the training, he reverts to the low life.

Thus, the intimacy arising from the sight of an unsuitable object is called "intimacy by sight. But as for [intimacy] after having seen [each other], it occurs by way of mutual conversation and discourse.

The arising of a defiled intimacy through mutual conversation and social contact is called "contact through conversation" (*samullapanasaṃsagga*). Laughter and the like are also included within this very category.

However, the arising of a defiled intimacy through the use of forest-gathered goods and so forth—whether one has given anything whatsoever belonging to oneself to a woman or not, or whether it was given by her—is called "contact through enjoyment" (*sambhogasaṃsagga*). [This occurs] by way of grasping a woman’s hand and so forth.
Familiarity with arisen defilements is what is called bodily contact.
And as for this [other type]: "He dwells in association with householders in an inappropriate association; he shares their sorrows and shares their joys;
he is happy when they are happy and sorrowful when they are sorrowful; and when there are duties or tasks to be performed, he personally becomes involved in them."

Thus it has been said: having abandoned all such unwholesome association with householders, as well as any association even with fellow practitioners of the holy life that serves as a cause for the arising of defilements—
one should cultivate a firm sense of spiritual urgency regarding the cycle of existence, a keen perception of fear toward conditioned phenomena,
a perception of repulsiveness toward the body, and a sense of shame and moral dread preceded by disgust for all unwholesome deeds in all one's actions.
“Mindfulness and clear comprehension” (*satisampajañña*) means having established everything [in the mind] so that there is a state of non-adherence everywhere, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf;

this is “non-association” (*asaṃsagga*) because it is the opposite of all forms of association. Discourse connected with that is “discourse on non-association. Regarding “discourse on the arousal of energy” (*vīriyārambhakathā*):
here, energy (*vīriya*) is the state of a hero (*vīra*), or it is action (*kamma*) in the sense that it is to be impelled or set in motion according to the proper method.
