Or it is energy; and that energy which is the undertaking for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states is "the arousal of energy.
This is twofold, being both physical and mental; it is threefold as the element of undertaking, the element of exertion, and the element of striving;
and it is fourfold by way of the right efforts. All of this is that which a bhikkhu...

It does not allow a defilement arisen while walking to reach the state of standing; it does not allow what has arisen while standing to reach sitting, nor what has arisen while sitting to reach lying down.

Right there and then, like one seizing a black snake by squeezing it with a staff, or like one striking an enemy in the neck with a sharp sword so that he cannot lift his head—so too [does mindfulness act].

If one restrains [the mind] by the power of energy without having given [it away], such exertion of energy should be understood as occurring through the influence of one who has already initiated energy;
discourse connected with that is "discourse on the initiation of energy.
Regarding the phrase "discourse on virtue" (*sīlakathā*) and so forth, virtue is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Of these, the mundane consists of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and the like.

The fourfold purified virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). The supramundane virtue consists of the virtue of the path (*maggasīla*) and the virtue of the fruit (*phalasīla*). Likewise for concentration (*samādhi*):
the eight attainments (*aṭṭha samāpatti*), together with access concentration (*upacāra*), which serve as the foundation for insight (*vipassanā*), are mundane concentration;

however, that which is associated with the path herein is called supramundane concentration. Likewise for wisdom (*paññā*): it is mundane when consisting of what is acquired through hearing (*sutamaya*), through reflection (*cintāmaya*), or associated with meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
And insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Specifically, however, it is the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) that should be understood here;
as well as the supramundane wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*) and the wisdom of the fruit (*phalapaññā*). Liberation (*vimutti*) is the liberation of the noble fruits and Nibbāna.

Others, moreover, explain the meaning here by way of the liberations consisting in substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*). The knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is also nineteenfold, being the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
Thus, discourse that proceeds by way of elucidating the manifold and diverse benefits of these qualities beginning with virtue (sīla) through the method of demonstration and so forth,
and by way of elucidating the dangers of their opposites such as immorality (dussīlya), or discourse associated therewith,
is called "discourse on virtue and the rest" (sīlādikathā).

And here, based on such statements as, “He himself is of few desires and speaks to others about being of few desires,” and “He is content with any kind of robe and speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe,” [the practice] should be carried out by one who is himself endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires,
and who acts for the sake of others with an inclination toward their welfare.

“Discourse of such a kind”: this should be understood as the discourse on fewness of wishes and so forth, which is spoken here specifically by way of its quality of being austere (*abhisallekhika*) and so on.
For it is the discourse of one who practices [the teaching] that is intended to accomplish the specific goal. Thus he will say:
“It is to be expected for a bhikkhu, Meghiya, who has a virtuous friend… that he will be one who gains without difficulty.”
"Of such a kind" means of this aforementioned sort. "One who gains at will" means one who gains according to his desire, one who gains according to his preference;
one who at all times obtains this discourse for hearing and investigating as he pleases. "One who gains without difficulty" means one who gains without hardship.
"One who gains without trouble" means one who gains in abundance.

“Āraddhavīriyo” means one who has exerted energy. “For the abandoning of unwholesome states” (akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya) means for the purpose of relinquishing unwholesome, evil states in the sense that they are produced by lack of skill.

“Of wholesome states” (kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ) refers to the states of the path and fruit together with insight, which are wholesome in the sense of being free from fault and in the sense of flowing away from what is blameworthy. “For the attainment” (upasampadāya) means...
"For the sake of accomplishment" means for the sake of producing [the path] within one's own continuum.

"Possessing fortitude" means endowed with the power of energy (*vīriya-thāma*) known as exertion (*ussoḷhi*). "Firm in effort" means possessing steadfast effort, one whose energy is not lax. "One who has not laid down the burden" means one who has not cast off the burden, one whose energy does not falter.
"Possessing wisdom" means possessing wisdom through insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). "Leading to arising and passing away" refers to the arising and... of the five aggregates.
"And we penetrate" [the path] that is "noble" (ariyā), meaning it stands far away from and remote from the defilements by way of suppression, and is thus faultless;

"penetrative" (nibbedhikā), meaning it partakes in penetration; and "leading rightly to the destruction of suffering" (sammā dukkhakkhayagāminī), meaning it proceeds rightly by way of cause and method toward the Noble Path, which has acquired the name "destruction of suffering" because it exhausts the suffering of the round of existence.
Furthermore, among these five qualities, virtue, energy, and wisdom are the internal factors for the yogi, while the other two are external factors.
Even there, the remaining fourfold [set] succeeds only through reliance upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*);
thus, showing the great assistance provided by the spiritual friend alone, the Teacher said: "For a bhikkhu who has a spiritual friend, Meghiya, this is to be expected," and so forth.
He increased his teaching. In this context, "to be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkha*) means that which must necessarily be desired;

it is something that will inevitably come to pass. The word *yaṃ* is a reference to the action. This is what is meant: regarding the statement "he will become virtuous," that which is the becoming virtuous—the possession of virtue—of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, [it follows] from that bhikkhu’s possession of virtue...
This is to be expected for him; the intention is that it will inevitably and certainly lead to his being bound to that state.
This same method applies to such passages as "he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
Thus, the Blessed One [spoke] so that one would not fail to adopt His own words, which are designated as the supreme spiritual friend in the world with its devas.

Having entered that forest grove, after demonstrating to the Venerable Meghiya— in whom such a transformation had occurred— the entirety of the excellence of the Dispensation through means such as the influence of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*),
[the Buddha] now taught the method of meditation (*bhāvanānaya*) for one who has developed a sense of urgency regarding that very place,

and for whom the meditation subject had previously failed to succeed because he was afflicted by sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and the like, since those thoughts were the direct opposites of that practice.

Having thus explained [the preliminary qualities], he then spoke the passage beginning with, “But, Meghiya, that bhikkhu, having established himself in these five things, should further develop four things,” while pointing out the meditation subject for arahantship.
Therein, “by him” means by one who, through reliance on a spiritual friend, is endowed with the virtues of virtue and so forth as previously described. For this very reason, it was said:

“By being established in these five things”: for one who has begun and possesses nascent insight (*vipassanā*), if perils such as lust should arise, then for the purpose of purifying them, four further things must be developed, produced, and increased beyond those [five].
“Foulnesses” (*asubha*) refers to the development of foulness in any of the eleven foulness meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as appropriate.
“For the abandoning of lust” means for the purpose of abandoning sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). This meaning should be clarified by the simile of the cock and the rice-water.
With reference to such a method of development, it is said: “The foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust.
“Loving-kindness” refers to the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*). “For the abandoning of ill will” refers, in the same manner already described, to anger that has arisen.
"For the purpose of abandoning": this refers to the sixteen bases of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
"For the purpose of cutting off discursive thought (*vitakka*)," means for the purpose of severing discursive thoughts that have arisen, according to the method already stated.
"For the purpose of uprooting the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" means for the purpose of completely eradicating the ninefold conceit that arises as "I am."

“Perceiving impermanence”: they perceive impermanence by way of the contemplation of impermanence that occurs thus: “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” because of their non-existence after having been, because of their possession of arising and passing away, because of their fragility, because of their temporariness, and because of their opposition to permanence. “The perception of non-self becomes established”:

[they perceive it] because of the lack of essence, because of the absence of mastery, because of being other, because of being empty, because of being vain, and because of being void—thus, “all phenomena...”
The perception of non-self—defined as the contemplation of non-self that occurs in the form "this is non-self"—becomes established in the mind and becomes firmly rooted.
For when the characteristic of impermanence is seen, the characteristic of non-self is indeed seen.
Indeed, when one of the three characteristics is seen, the other two are also seen. Therefore it was said: "O Meghiya, for one who perceives impermanence..."
“The perception of non-self becomes established. When the characteristic of non-self is well-seen, the conceit that arises as “I am” is easily abandoned;
thus it is said: “One who perceives non-self reaches the eradication of the conceit ‘I am’.
“Nibbāna in this very life” means that one reaches the unconditioned final Nibbāna in this very visible state, in this very selfhood. This is the summary here.
In detail, however, the method for the development of the foul (asubha) and so forth should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The commentary on the Meghiya Sutta is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Nandaka Sutta and others.
4–5. In the fourth [case], "waiting" means looking on; the meaning is that the Buddha did not enter abruptly, but remained until that conversation was concluded.

Therefore he said: "He waited for this conclusion of the conversation. Regarding the phrase "of the knowledge of insight into the discernment of formations," it is called "higher wisdom-insight" (*adhipaññā-vipassanā*) because it is the investigation of all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth. Thus he said: "of the knowledge of insight into the discernment of formations."
*Mānasa* refers to lust, mind, and even Arahantship. In the passage, “The snare that roams the sky, which wanders as *mānasa*,” it means lust.
In the passage, “Mind (*citta*), intellect (*mano*), *mānasa*,” it means mind.

In the passage, “A trainee who has not attained *mānasa* might die, O learned one,” it means Arahantship. Here too, it is Arahantship alone that is intended. Therefore he said, “who have not attained *mānasa*.”
“Those who have not attained Arahantship. Because their minds (*mānasa*) have not attained Arahantship, they are called “those whose minds have not attained” (*appattamānasā*).
Now, referring specifically to the word *mānasa* as a synonym for consciousness (*citta*), he says, “or Arahantship,” and so forth. The fifth [section] is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Nandaka-sutta and others is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Sevanāsutta*.
In the sixth [sutta], "requisites for life" (*jīvitasambhārā*) refers to the requisites or conditions for the maintenance of life.

"To be procured" (*samudānetabbā*) means they must be properly brought forth and obtained through blameless conduct such as seeking alms (*uñchācariyā*) in accordance with the right method. Once those have been procured...
He said, "They must be collected," meaning that they are called "collected" because they have been gathered together. "They arise with difficulty" means they do not arise easily;
by this, he shows their state of being unsuitable as objects (*gocara-asappāya*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "during a portion of the night or a portion of the day," he said, "in a section of the night or a section of the day," using the accusative case in the sense of the locative. One should set out only at night.
Because the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*) is not accomplished there. Even by reflecting thus: “The purpose for which I went forth is not being fulfilled here;
rather, robes and other requisites are being acquired, but I did not go forth for that sake—what is the use of my staying here?
Therefore it was said: “Having understood the failure to reach the full perfection of the development of the goal of recluseship.”

In the subsequent section, having understood that the joy of volitional formation (*saṅkhāpīti*) is the means by which the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) is accomplished, it is said: "That person should depart without asking leave;
he should not be followed. Thus, the phrase "that person" is connected with the words "should not be followed.
For whatever has a connection with something else, that relationship holds even when they are far apart. Therefore, "that person" refers to the aforementioned individual.
The meaning is that one should depart without asking permission of that person after changing the nominative case into the accusative.
For the change of grammatical case occurs according to the sense. And "one should depart after asking permission" is an exhortation to recognize what has been done and to be grateful for it.
"Of such a kind" refers to one depending upon whom a bhikkhu may expect only growth in virtue and in the requisite conditions.

The phrase "even if" (*sacepi*) and so forth shows that even if such a danger exists, one should not abandon [the person] if they can be restrained by means of disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakamma*) and the like.
The commentary on the *Sevanā-sutta* is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the *Sutavā-sutta* and others.
7–10. In the seventh [case], the statement beginning with “a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally killing a living being” is merely a formal teaching (*desanāsīsaka*).

However, stream-enterers and others are likewise incapable; this was stated in this way for the purpose of censuring ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and praising those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
An ordinary worldling is to be reproached because he commits such acts as matricide, whereas one whose taints are destroyed is to be praised even for such acts as killing an ant or a termite.
"He does not do so" means: "One who makes a store for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.

Just as one who has become a householder enjoys material sensual pleasures after making a store, so too [the monk] is now incapable of enjoying sesame, rice, ghee, butter, and so forth after having made a store.
However, those who enjoy material sensual pleasures by hoarding them depend upon that [store].

He said, "Having stored up both sensual objects as bases (*vatthukāma*) and sensual defilements (*kilesakāma*), they consume them," because even those with taints destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are seen to have sesame, rice, and so forth in their dwelling places. But do they not store these for their own sake? No;

they do not store them for their own benefit, but rather for the sake of those who have gone forth [into homelessness] who are in need or otherwise uncomfortable. What about the case of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)? For him too, there are five...
All sensual qualities have been abandoned; however, he enjoys what has been obtained in accordance with the Dhamma after having reflected upon it.
This was said with reference to unwholesome sensual qualities, not with reference to those associated with beds, chairs, rugs, coverlets, and so forth.
"Just as formerly when he was a householder" means that he is incapable of enjoying things in the same manner as he did when he was a layman living in a household. In the midst of the home...
For stream-enterers and others remain in the guise of householders for as long as they live.

However, one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), having attained arahantship, passes away in final nibbāna or goes forth into homelessness while still in human form; he does not remain even for a moment among the sense-sphere deities such as those of the Four Great Kings.
Why? Because of the absence of secluded places there. But while remaining in the state of existence as a terrestrial deity, [he may pass away].
Even after attaining arahantship, he remains [in that state] because of the possibility of dwelling in seclusion. The eighth and subsequent suttas have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the Sutasoma-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Sambodhi-vagga is finished.
2. The Chapter on the Lion’s Roar (Sīhanādavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar (Sīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā) 11.
In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], "avāpuraṇaṃ" means that by means of this they open or uncover the door. It carries away dust.
By this [word], a dust-remover (*rajo-haraṇa*) is meant. "With a basket in hand" means with a vessel made of bamboo; some also say "with a vessel made of leather.
"One whose horns are cut off" means one for whom the horns have been severed; he is both a bull and one whose horns are cut off, thus "a bull with cut-off horns.
This is a descriptive compound (*visesana-paro samāso*). The phrase beginning with "or with a snake's carcass" is intended to show carcasses that are exceedingly loathsome and repulsive.
It is said: "With one fastened around the neck" means having been brought by some enemy and bound around the neck;

the meaning is "having been hung. "Afflicted" (*aṭṭo*) means sick, oppressed by the pressure of a foul odor. "Acceptance of the transgression" (*accayassa paṭiggaṇhanaṃ*) or "endurance" (*adhivāsanaṃ*):
for in this way, when the reason is confessed, that [transgression] is said to have departed from him. Therefore he said: "May he accept it" means "may he forgive it."
The rest here is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Saupādisesa Sutta.
12. In the second [verse], the term "the brevity of existence" refers to its short duration; thus he said, "even for as long as a finger-snap.
The commentary on the *Saupādisesa Sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Koṭṭhika Sutta*.

13. In the third [case], "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the manifest personal existence (*attabhāva*). The fruit to be experienced therein is "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*). Therefore, he said: "in this very personal existence.

Because it has the four or five aggregates as its fruit, karma leading to the realm of non-perception (*asaññābhava*) is "to be experienced much" (*bahuvedanīya*). Because it has a single aggregate as its fruit, karma leading to the realm of non-perception is...

It is said, “not to be experienced much” (*appavedanīya*). However, some say: “Formless-sphere karma is ‘to be experienced much’ (*bahuvedanīya*) because its fruit is to be experienced over a long period;
the other is ‘not to be experienced much. Alternatively, form- and formless-sphere karma is ‘to be experienced much,’ while limited (*paritta*) karma is ‘not to be experienced much.
“To be experienced” (*vedanīya*) means that which is capable of producing a result when there is a convergence of other conditions.

It is not only that which has already begun its ripening. "Not to be experienced" (*avedanīya*) refers to that which is incapable of ripening due to a deficiency in conditions, such as the various types of *ahosi-kamma* (ineffective karma) and so forth.
The commentary on the *Koṭṭhika-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Samiddhi-sutta*.
14. Regarding "Samiddhi" in the fourth [case]: it is said that the elder’s physical form (*attabhāva*) was perfected, handsome, and pleasing;

therefore, he was designated simply as "Samiddhi. Thus he said, "Because of the perfection of his physical form," and so forth. In the phrase "in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), etc.," the word "etc.
includes the realm of sound (*saddadhātu*) and the others.
The commentary on the *Samiddhi-sutta* is finished.
5–9. Commentary on the *Gaṇḍa-sutta* and following, 15–19.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "born from mother and father" (*mātāpettikasambhava*) means: produced from both the mother and the father; that which arises from the mother and father.
Of that which is produced from semen and blood. "Subject to being rubbed" means having a nature that must be rubbed. "Subject to being massaged" means having a nature that must be massaged.
And here, growth is spoken of by the terms "accumulation of rice and gruel" and "being rubbed," while decline is spoken of by the terms "impermanence, breaking up, and destruction.
Alternatively, the former terms refer to the arising [of the body], and the latter terms refer to its passing away.
Thus have been shown the growth, decline, production, and dissolution of this body composed of the four great elements. The remainder is easily understood.
The sixth and subsequent sections have their meanings explained in plain terms.
The commentary on the Gaṇḍa-sutta and the following discourses is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Velāma Sutta 20.
Regarding the tenth [case], "sakuṇḍaka-bhatta" means rice with broken grains (*sakuṇḍaka*).
Rice that has been cooked together with small broken grains is likewise called "with broken grains" (*uttaṇḍula*). "Biḷaṅga" refers to sour gruel (*āranāḷa*), because it is produced from *biḷaṅga*.
That which is born from *kañji* (rice-gruel) is itself called *kañji*; that which has this as its second [ingredient] is *biḷaṅgadutiya*. It is thus stated as "having *kañji* as the second.

"Without honoring" means without honoring either the gift to be given (*deyyadhamma*) or the person. Not honoring the gift to be given is a lack of proper preparation; not honoring the person is a lack of respect.
For one who does not honor the gift to be given [offers] that which is possessed of faults such as being overcooked rice, etc.

He gives food, but does not prepare it properly. Without honoring the person, he has them sit anywhere or on any seat without having swept the place where they sit, and he gives it by sending whichever child happens to be there.
"Without showing respect" means not making it an object of esteem; the meaning is "not worshipping. For one who worships places the object of worship in the mind, and not [otherwise].
He treats it with contempt. "Cittīkaraṇa" (making a mental mark) refers to the act of honoring the practice by regarding it as wonderful;
its opposite, "acittīkaraṇa," is the act of not honoring it. "Apaviddha" means cast aside like something to be discarded, such as leftover food and the like.
For one who, desiring to discard [the body], has smeared rice and other foods upon the body of a sick person and [thrown it] into an anthill...
He gives as if throwing away a disease; this is called giving what is cast aside.

"One who holds the view of non-return" means one who possesses the view of being the owner of one's actions (*kammassakata*), thinking, "Surely the fruit of this gift will come back to me"—such a person is one who holds the view of return. But this person is not like that;
thus he is one who holds the view of non-return, meaning he does not give with the expectation of a result.
Therefore he said: "He does not give having faith in both the action and the fruit.

Regarding the term *velāmo*: here the word *mā* is a term of negation. It is called *velāmo* because in this [person] there is no *velā*, that is, no limit or boundary, for qualities such as birth, lineage, beauty, wealth, and so forth.
Alternatively, it is so called because the *velā*, the limit or boundary, of the aforementioned qualities reaches its end (*amati*) or comes to a conclusion (*osāna*) in him.

In this context, *velāma* means that which wanders (*amati*), goes, or transgresses its time (*vela*) or boundary (*mariyāda*); thus it is called *velāma*. Therefore he said: “of such birth, clan... and so named.
It is given, thus it is a *dāna* (gift), meaning the object of giving. That which is brought forward (*aggīyati*) or relinquished (*nissajjīyati*) therein is the *dānagga* (the pinnacle of giving).
Alternatively, that wherein they receive the gift is the *dānagga*; likewise, the *bhattagga* (the pinnacle of the meal) refers to the place where the distribution of food occurs.
*Dukūlasandānāni* means those for which there are *dukūla* cloths serving as straps attached to silver vessels and so forth;
thus they are called *dukūlasandānāni*. *Kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni* means silver milking vessels. Therefore he said, "silver receptacles for milk.
*Rajatamayakhīrapaṭicchakāni* means those for which there are silver receptacles—vessels for receiving milk—thus they are called *rajatamayakhīrapaṭicchakāni*.
"Sodheyya" means one should purify by making it yield great fruit; for it is through the attainment of the state of great fruit that a gift (dakkhiṇā) is said to be purified.
By the phrase "come by way of the Path, not turning back, a refuge," he illustrates the supramundane going for refuge.
By the words "others," etc., the mundane going for refuge is stated. "Refuge" (saraṇaṃ) refers to the merit consisting in the sacrifice of one's life for the Three Jewels.
It bestows all forms of success; therefore, the intention is that it is even more fruitful.
And this—even if someone were to deprive one of life with a sharp blade, saying, "If you do not abandon the refuge as it was taken, I shall kill you"—nevertheless, [one thinks]:
"I will neither say 'it is not the Buddha' regarding the Buddha, nor 'it is not the Dhamma' regarding the Dhamma, nor 'it is not the Saṅgha' regarding the Saṅgha..."

This is stated with reference to that which is grasped by making it firmer through the thought, “I say there is no Saṅgha. By the phrase “attained by means of the path,” he speaks with reference to supramundane virtue (lokuttara-sīla).
However, by the words “others,” etc., mundane virtue (lokiya-sīla) is described.

Its great fruitfulness and great benefit should be understood from its being the foundation for all mundane and supramundane qualities, due to its granting life to all beings and its abstention from taking life.
"Upasiṅghanamattaṃ" means merely sniffing. "Gaddohanamattaṃ" is a variant reading meaning the time required for milking a cow (*godohana-mattaṃ*).
To show that this does not refer to the entire duration of the milking process, the meaning is stated as "merely the time for a cow to suckle once.
"Añchanamattaṃ" means merely pulling [the udder]. It refers even to the brief moment of milking a single drop of milk after having grasped the cow's udder.
They say it is "the duration of milking a cow. For even for such a short time as that,

whoever is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness that radiates benefit toward all beings— whether defined by the limits of one's own dwelling, room, courtyard, or monastery, or throughout the infinite world-systems—
this yields a much greater fruit than the aforementioned forms of giving and so forth.
The commentary on the Velāma Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Sīhanāda Vagga is finished.
3. The Sattāvāsa Vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Tiṭṭhānasutta* 21.
In the first [verse] of the third [sutta], "without 'mine'" (*amamā*) means they are devoid of possessiveness even toward clothing, ornaments, drinks, food, and so forth.
"Without property" (*apariggahā*) means they are without the property of women; for it is said that they have no possessiveness toward them, thinking, "This is my wife."
Upon seeing his mother or sister, no sensual desire arises.
By the power of virtue established through natural law (*dhammatā*), as soon as he sees his sons, milk flows from the mother’s breasts;
by that sign, the recognition of "mother" arises in the son toward the mother, and the recognition of "son" arises in the mother toward the son—so say some.
Furthermore, this other distinction, established through the power of the merit of those from Uttarakuru, should also be understood.

It is said that there, in various locations, trees with thickly clustered and densely covered branches and twigs—resembling gabled houses and delightful to behold—fulfill the function of dwellings for those people;
therein they live happily, and other things as well are found there.

The trees stand always well-grown, their tips in full bloom. The bodies of water also remain at all times covered with blossoming lotuses, blue lilies, white lilies, fragrant water-lilies, and other flowers, wafting a supreme fragrance in every direction.
Their bodies, moreover, are free from defects such as being too tall;
they are endowed with perfect height and girth, and because they are not overcome by old age, they remain free from wrinkles, grey hair, and other such flaws for the duration of their lifespan.
It remains with its speed, strength, power, and splendor entirely undiminished.
Because they subsist on the fruits of non-action, they have no suffering arising from the search for food through such means as agriculture or commerce;

consequently, they have no possession of male or female slaves, laborers, and so forth, nor do they face the perils of cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, creeping reptiles, or thorns. Just as...

Just as in the last month of summer at dawn the temperature is perfectly balanced between cold and heat, even so at all times there the temperature remains perfectly balanced between cold and heat, and no harm or affliction arises for them.
They consume rice that ripens without being cultivated—free from husks and powder, pure, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains. As they eat that, [no excrement is produced].
No disease such as leprosy, boils, ringworm, consumption, cough, asthma, epilepsy,
or old age arises among them; nor do they become hunchbacked, dwarfish, one-eyed, withered, lame, crippled in their limbs, deformed, or deficient in their faculties.
The women there are neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;

they possess forms endowed with supreme beauty. For indeed, they have long fingers, copper-colored nails, pendulous breasts, slender waists, faces like the full moon, large eyes, soft limbs, thighs joined together, white teeth, deep navels, and slender shanks.
With long, dark, wavy hair; with broad and beautiful hips; neither too hairy nor hairless; fortunate;
pleasant to touch according to the season; soft; gentle; easy to converse with; adorned with various ornaments, they wander about.
They always appear as if sixteen years of age, and the men appear as if twenty-five years of age. They do not feel lust for their children or wives. This is the natural law therein.
There, men and women dwell for exactly seven days in the delight of sensual pleasure. Thereafter, as if free from passion, they depart each to their own place;
there is no suffering there such as exists here, rooted in the descent into the womb, the maintenance of the fetus, or the act of birth.
Like a golden statue emerging from a red cloth, the children emerge from the mother’s womb unsullied.
In this way, they emerge easily, as if with mucus and so forth; this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in that regard.
But having given birth to a son or a daughter, the mother places them in a place suitable for wandering and departs as she pleases, regardless of them.
As for those men or women who see them lying there, they [take them] for themselves...
They stretch out their fingers. By the power of their karma, milk flows forth from them, and by that the children are sustained.
Growing in this way, after only a few days they have gained strength; then the girls approach women, and the boys approach men.
Furthermore, their clothing and ornaments are produced right there from the wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha), variegated with various colors and hues.
Indeed, there hang here and there upon the *kappa*-trees garments that are delicate and pleasant to the touch.

From the *kappa*-tree come golden ornaments— head-ornaments, neck-ornaments, hand-ornaments, waist-ornaments, and foot-ornaments— interlaced with various colored gems blazing with networks of diverse rays, and variegated with many kinds of floral designs, vine-patterns, and wall-mosaics.
Likewise, musical instruments such as lutes, drums, small drums, clappers, conchs, flutes, cymbals, lutes with resonators, and harps hang down here and there.
There, many fruit trees bear fruits the size of jars that have a sweet taste;
by consuming these, those beings are not afflicted by hunger or thirst even for seven days.
There, too, rivers flow with very pure water, well-established, delightful, free from mud, with beds of sand;
they are neither too cold nor too hot, covered with fragrant water-born flowers, and always wafting sweet scents as they flow.
There are no thorny or harsh shrubs and creepers there; instead, they are entirely without thorns and abound with flowers and fruits.
Sandalwood and agarwood trees exude their resin of their own accord.

When those wishing to bathe place their clothes and ornaments together at a river landing, descend into the river, bathe, and emerge, they take whichever clothes and ornaments are nearest to them as they come out;
it does not occur to them, "This is mine, this is another's. It is for this very reason...
Among them, there is neither quarrel nor dispute. Their play for sensual delight lasts only seven days, after which they wander about as if free from passion.
Wherever they wish to sleep under a tree, right there a bed is found.
When they see deceased beings, they do not weep or grieve; rather, having adorned them, they set them down, and immediately—
Furthermore, such birds do not approach them and carry the dead to another island; therefore, there is neither a cemetery nor an impure place there.
Nor do the dead from that place fall into hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).
They say that by the power of the five precepts established through the nature of things (*dhammatā*), they are reborn in the world of the gods. [This lasts] for exactly a thousand years.
And their life-span is not fixed for all time; all of this is established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā*), just like their five precepts.
The commentary on the *Tiṭṭhāna-sutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Taṇhāmūlaka-sutta*.
23. In the third [verse], *esanatāṇhā* is craving that occurs by way of the seeking after enjoyments. *Esitatāṇhā* is the craving that arises regarding enjoyments already sought.
It is called *pariyesanā* because one seeks by means of agitation (*paritassanā*);

thus, it is a mental state occurring as such, consisting of both the underlying disposition and the actual application. Therefore he said: "When there is craving, there is [seeking]. *Rūpādi-ārammaṇa-paṭilābho* means the acquisition of objects such as visible forms.
Acquisition is the obtaining [of things] by way of searching for material forms and other objects that have a physical basis.

However, even that which is obtained without being sought after is, in fact, merely what has been obtained through searching, because it is obtained precisely due to the performance of such karma in the past.
Therefore he said: "For that exists when there is searching."
"Sukhavinicchaya" means that which specifically determines pleasure; thus it is "the determination of pleasure.

Knowledge of the occurrence [of pleasure] precisely as it is—by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), its origin (*samudaya*), its passing away (*atthaṅgama*), its danger (*ādīnava*), and the escape from it (*nissaraṇa*)—is indeed the "determination of pleasure.
"Jaññā" means one should know. One should know the various unreal modes regarding objects, such as "beauty is pleasure," and so forth.

The analytical determination (*vinicchaya*) is that it accumulates and imposes by way of its downward inclination; craving (*taṇhā*) is the contemplation of gratification. The nature of the analytical determination for views (*diṭṭhi*) should also be understood in exactly the same way.
However, the construction here is that only thought (*vitakka*) is mentioned in this sutta.
"In this sutta" refers to the *Sakkapañha Sutta*, for therein it says: "Desire, O Lord of the Devas, has thought as its source."
"Arrived. "Here" means in this sutta. "Deciding by means of thought alone":

by this he states the instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*) of the word *vinicchaya* as "that by which one decides is a decision (*vinicchaya*). "To such an extent," etc., is a demonstration of the manner of deciding.

"Desire" (*chanda*) is so called in the sense of wishing; "lust" (*rāga*) is so called in the sense of coloring—thus, "desire-and-lust" (*chandarāga*). This [lust], due to its lack of repeated cultivation...
“Proceeding as something dull,” it is said here with this intended meaning; thus he says, “a designation for weak lust.
“Clinging” (*ajjhosāna*) means adherence by way of craving and views. For the grasping of craving, thinking “this is mine,” is for the most part dependent upon the grasping of a self.
Therefore he says, “I” and “mine. And “strong conviction” refers to the attainment of stability in those graspings.

"Appropriation by way of craving and views" refers to the state of having appropriated—by means of a powerful conviction of "I" and "mine"—the object of the grasping for self and what belongs to self as if it were not shared with others; it is the arising of a thought-moment accompanied by greed that functions in such a manner.
It is [the cause] by virtue of which an object appropriated by oneself becomes something not shared with others by others.
A person is "one who does not endure"; that phenomenon is non-endurance (*asahanatā*). Thus they explain the meaning of the word according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*).

According to the characteristic of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*), however, by virtue of which phenomenon a person is "miserly" (*maccharo*) due to being joined with miserliness, the state or the action of that is "miserliness" (*macchariya*);
it is the phenomenon of miserliness. Because of the powerful nature of miserliness, [it is spoken of] with care...
"Guarding is protection," he said; "the thorough guarding of the doors...
It is called a *karaṇa* because it produces its own fruit; that is, any cause whatsoever. An *adhikaraṇa* is an additional cause—that is, a specific cause.
And this specific cause is for the occurrence of misfortune regarding wealth, such as the taking up of weapons for its protection, and so forth; thus it was stated.
“Concerning protection,” and so forth. “For the purpose of harming others” means for the purpose of afflicting others by means of killing and the like.
It is called *ādāna* because one takes up (*ādiyati*) it; the taking up of a staff is *daṇḍādāna*, which is the arising of a thought to harass another after having taken up a staff.
The same method applies to the taking up of a weapon (*satthādāna*). A quarrel to be performed with the body by way of seizing the hands and so forth is a “bodily quarrel” (*kāyakalaha*).
A quarrel by means of speech is a *vācā-kalaha* (verbal quarrel), such as that which is to be performed through the striking of breasts and so forth.

It is called a *viggaha* because one takes up what is deformed (*virūpa*) by way of conflict (*virujjhanavasena*). It is called a *vivāda* because one speaks what is contradictory (*viruddha*) by means of it. It is called *tuvaṃtuvaṃ* because it is accompanied by disrespectful speech such as "you, you.
All those mental states (*cittuppāda*) occurring in that manner should be understood as being associated with faults. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Many evil, unwholesome states arise.
The commentary on the Taṇhāmūlaka Sutta is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Sattāvāsa Sutta and others.
24–25. "Beings dwell in these" is the derivation of *sattāvāsā* (abodes of beings); they are classes of beings distinguished by such factors as having diverse perceptions (*nānattasaññī*).

Because those various abodes of beings deserve to be described as the support for the beings included therein—precisely because of that inclusion—just as the behavior of a whole belongs to its parts, as in the expression "a branch on a tree. Therefore...
“It means ‘abodes of beings,’ that is, dwelling places,” it is said. Even the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) are indeed abodes of beings, because of the statement:
“Monks, that abode of beings is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes.
If this is so, why are they not included here? To that, he states the reason:
“Because they do not exist at all times,” and so forth. It should be understood, however, that those who have reached the Vehapphala [heaven] belong only to the fourth abode of beings.
The fifth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sattāvāsa-sutta* and others is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Sīlāyūpa Sutta 26.
In the sixth [verse], a hand (*hattha*) of a man of medium stature is twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
this is called a *kukkū*, and "kakkū" is also a name for it. Eight *kukkūs* above the rim (*nemi*) means that eight hands rise up from the top of the pit and stand there.
[They] would be so. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Silāyūpa Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Paṭhama-vera Sutta*.
27. *Sattame yato*: "In which time" (*yasmiṃ kāle*). For here the word *to* has the same scope as the word *dā*;

thus it means "when" (*yadā*). *Bhayāni verāni*: "Fears and enmities. "Fear" (*bhaya*) is that by which one fears; [the term refers to] volition and so forth, which receive the name "fear" because they are associated with fear, or "fear" because they are objects to be feared, and the name "enmity" (*vera*) because they give rise to enmity. For those [volitions] in whom killing and so forth proceed—
Furthermore, those things which are pursued for their own sake bring enmity to both parties; for that very reason, they should be feared as "producers of enmity.
The "stream-entry" (*sotāpatti*) consists of the initial arrival at the noble path (*ariyamagga*), its practice, and its attainment.

The factors conducive to that [attainment] for one established therein are the "factors of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiyaṅgāni*). Indeed, the factor of stream-entry is twofold: that which exists for the sake of stream-entry...
And "factor" (*aṅga*) means cause; that which, prior to the attainment of the stream-entry path, conduces to the attainment of stream-entry, is stated as:
"association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, it is a factor for one who has attained the qualities and stands having reached stream-entry, as in the case of a stream-enterer...

“Factor” (*aṅga*) is also said [to mean] “one who is characterized (*aṅgīyati*) or known by means of this,” making it a designation for the confirmed confidence in the Buddha and the other qualities. This is what is intended here.
In such expressions as “one whose hell is exhausted” (*khīṇaniraya*), hell is said to be “exhausted” because it will not arise there in the future; thus, “I am one whose hell is exhausted.”

This method applies everywhere. "Stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) means one who has entered the stream of the Path. "One whose nature is not subject to falling away" (*avinipātadhamma*) means one whose nature is not that of the states of ruin.
"Destined" (*niyata*) means destined by the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), which is designated as the first Path. "Having full enlightenment as one's final goal" (*sambodhiparāyaṇa*):
"Full enlightenment is my supreme destination (*para-ayana*)," thus I am "one having full enlightenment as my final goal"; the meaning is one who will certainly awaken to full enlightenment.
“On account of killing living beings” means by reason of performing the kamma of killing living beings. “Fear and enmity” are one in meaning. Enmity (*vera*) is called opposition;
that very thing is called “fear” because it is to be feared. Furthermore, this is twofold: external and internal.
For instance, the father of one person might have been killed by another. That person thinks: “It seems that by him...”
"My father was killed; I too shall kill him," he says, and wanders about carrying a sharpened weapon.

That volition of enmity which has arisen within him is called "external enmity" (bāhiraṃ veraṃ), because it exists externally to the person who committed the act of enmity, which is the root of that enmity.
As for the other [person], thinking, "It seems he wanders about with the intent to kill me..."
The volition that arises, "I myself shall kill him first," is called internal enmity.

Both of these, for their part, pertain only to the present life (diṭṭhadhammika). However, when a warder of hell sees one who has arisen in hell and, thinking "I will strike him," takes up a flaming club, the volition that arises in that warder of hell is his pertaining to the future life (samparāyika).

External enmity. Furthermore, when the volition arises in him, “He comes thinking, ‘I shall strike this faultless person,’ and I myself shall strike him first,” this is his internal enmity pertaining to the future.
As for that external enmity, it is called “personal enmity” (*puggalavaira*) in the commentaries. In terms of meaning, it is suffering and mental distress.
It is exactly the same. And as it is here, so too in the remaining cases, the manifestation of enmity should be understood by way of such expressions as:

"My property was stolen by him," "He has committed adultery with my wife," "Having told a lie, his purpose failed," or "Intoxicated by liquor and pride, he did this and that. Etc. according to this method.
"With confident faith" means with the unshakable faith that has been attained. "Beloved by the Noble Ones" refers to the five precepts.
For these are dear and beloved to the Noble Ones; even when the Noble Ones have passed into another existence, they do not abandon them;
therefore, they are called "beloved by the Noble Ones. Whatever else might need to be said here, all of it is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.
It should be understood that this was stated in the exposition of the recollections (*anussati-niddesa*).
The commentary on the First Discourse on Enmity is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Grounds for Resentment (*Āghātavatthu-sutta*).
29. In the ninth [section], it is called "basis" (*vatthu*) because the fruit arises there due to its being the cause; thus he says, "grounds for resentment" (*āghātavatthūni*).
This anger, which arises with respect to a certain basis, does not arise there only once, but rather arises again and again;
hence it is said that it "binds. Alternatively, it refers to that which arises by way of specific conditions.
Ill-will (āghāta), being bound as it were to its own object, does not depart; rather, it arises again and again. With reference to this, it is said: "he binds ill-will.
Furthermore, its production by way of conditions is simply its arising; thus it is said: "he produces [it].
The commentary on the *Āghātavatthu-sutta* is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Removal of Malice (Āghātapaṭivinayasutta) 30.
Regarding the tenth [discourse], the phrase “Where could that be found?”—here, *taṃ* (*that*) refers back to the action.
The meaning should be understood through the elision of words; thus he said, “May that practice of harmful conduct not be,” and so forth. For what reason is it to be obtained?

Because it is purposeless. For beings are the owners of their own karma; they become miserable or happy according to their own deeds, so my acting for their harm is entirely futile. This is the intended meaning:
"How could such a cause for anger be found here in this person? From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), how could there be anything to be angry at or anyone who is angry?
And because of their non-existence. For this fivefold aggregate, which is called a "being," is merely a conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*);
those formations are momentary. What, then, could be angry with whom? This is the meaning. What indeed could be gains other than the arising of misfortune?
The commentary on the *Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Anupubbanirodha Sutta* 31.

Regarding the eleventh [sutta], "successive cessations" (*anupubbanirodha*) means cessations that should be brought about by way of succession, that is, by way of gradual order. Therefore, it is said: "cessations in successive sequence.
The commentary on the *Anupubbanirodha Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Abodes of Beings is finished.
4. The Great Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Successive Abidings.

32. Regarding the first [section] of the fourth [sutta]: "They are to be dwelt in successively" means they are *anupubbavihārā*. "In succession" (*anupaṭipāṭiyā*) means by way of gradual order. "States to be attained" (*samāpajjitabbavihārā*) means states to be dwelt in after having attained them and having become possessed of them.
The commentary on the *Anupubbavihāra Sutta* is finished.
2–3. Commentary on the *Anupubbavihārasamāpatti Sutta*, etc.
33–34. In the second [verse], "hunger" (*chāta*) refers to craving and views, because one must fall into sensual pleasures and because one conducts oneself under their influence;

they are "without hunger" (*nicchātā*) because there is no hunger toward them due to being inclined toward those [states]. Therefore he said, "of the hunger of craving and views," and so forth. In the third [verse], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Anupubbavihārasamāpatti-sutta* and others is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Cow Simile Sutta 35.

In the fourth [simile], "one who frequents the mountains" means one who by nature frequently roams the mountains. "One who does not know the field" means one who does not know the proper range (agocara).
He is called a fool because he lacks proficiency in purifying those who have fallen away from concentration. Regarding the attainment of mastery in bringing the jhāna to a state of skillfulness...

One is "unskilled" (*abyatta*) due to the absence [of practice]. One is "unacquainted with the field" (*akhettaññū*) through the lack of realization of the state of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for higher knowledge.

One is "unskilled" (*akusala*) in every respect because of the absence of proficiency in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Or, one is "foolish" (*bāla*) due to a lack of cultivation of the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*);

"unskilled" due to a lack of development (*abhāvanā*); "unacquainted with the field" due to a lack of frequent practice (*abahalīkāra*); and "unskilled" due to a lack of right resolve (*anadhiṭṭhāna*)—thus it should be construed.

"Fallen from both" means fallen from both meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). For he, due to a lack of proficiency and because they were not well-established—having fallen away from the two absorptions despite his enthusiasm, owing to their destruction and incapacity—is one who has lost them.
The commentary on the "Simile of the Cow" Sutta is finished.

5. Commentary on the Jhāna Sutta 36. In the fifth [sutta], by the phrase "as impermanent" (*aniccatā*), he states their impermanence through the negation of permanence. Precisely for that reason, it is illuminated that they are impermanent because they possess arising and passing away, because they are subject to change, and because they are merely temporary. For whatever is not permanent— [The text continues: ...that is impermanent. And what is impermanent is suffering; and what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, that is not fit to be regarded as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Thus it was said. And why was it said? Because it is seen thus as it really is with proper wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Therefore it was said: ‘Bhikkhus, form is impermanent... etc. Herein, “form” is the four great elements and the form derived from them. “Feeling” is the three feelings or the fivefold division of feeling. “Perception” is the grasping of the sign of the blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, and so forth. “Formations” are the six classes of volition. “Consciousness” is the six classes of consciousness. “Impermanent” means that which does not last, which is transitory, which is subject to cessation. “Suffering” means that which oppresses, which is painful, which is the basis for pain, and which is contrary to desire. “Not-self” means that which has no self, no essence, no owner, no master, and no controller. “To be regarded as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’” means to be viewed, considered, and reflected upon in this way. “Thus it was said” means it was spoken by the Blessed One. “And why was it said? is asked to show the reason for its being said. “Because it is seen thus as it really is with proper wisdom” means because it is seen with the eye of wisdom, with the knowledge of insight, according to reality. “Therefore it was said” means for that reason it was stated. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent... etc. is a summary of the meaning already explained. “Herein, form is the four great elements and the form derived from them”: the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and air; the form derived from them is the twenty-four kinds of derived form, such as the eye-faculty and so forth. “Feeling is the three feelings or the fivefold division of feeling”: the three feelings are pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; the fivefold division is the division into bodily pleasure, bodily pain, mental joy, mental grief, and equanimity. “Perception is the grasping of the sign of the blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, and so forth”: this is the perceiving of the characteristic marks of objects. “Formations are the six classes of volition”: these are the volitions regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. “Consciousness is the six classes of consciousness”: these are the consciousnesses associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. “Impermanent” means that which does not last, which is transitory, which is subject to cessation: it is called impermanent because it is devoid of permanence, because it is momentary, and because it ceases. “Suffering” means that which oppresses, which is painful, which is the basis for pain, and which is contrary to desire: it is called suffering because it afflicts, because it is the nature of pain, because it is the cause of pain, and because it is incompatible with the wish for happiness. “Not-self” means that which has no self, no essence, no owner, no master, and no controller: it is called not-self because it lacks a permanent soul, because it is empty of intrinsic nature, because there is no one who owns it, because there is no sovereign over it, and because there is no agent within it. “To be regarded as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’” means to be viewed, considered, and reflected upon in this way. “Thus it was said” means it was spoken by the Blessed One. “And why was it said? is asked to show the reason for its being said. “Because it is seen thus as it really is with proper wisdom” means because it is seen with the eye of wisdom, with the knowledge of insight, according to reality. “Therefore it was said” means for that reason it was stated. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent... etc. is a summary of the meaning already explained. This concludes the commentary on the first sutta. [The text continues with the second, third, fourth, and fifth suttas. In the second sutta, the Blessed One spoke thus: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I shall make known to you the coming and going of beings, their passing away and rebirth, but I shall not make known to you the Noble Truth of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering,’ that would be impossible. But if one should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering,’ that is possible. What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one desires is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, letting it go, and not relying on it. What is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. In the third sutta, the Blessed One spoke thus: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of Suffering, but I shall not make known to you the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering,’ that would be impossible. But if one should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering,’ that is possible. What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence... [as above]... What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving... [as above]... What is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path... [as above]. In the fourth sutta, the Blessed One spoke thus: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, but I shall not make known to you the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering,’ that would be impossible. But if one should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering... the Noble Truth of Suffering,’ that is possible. What is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path... [as above]... What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering... [as above]... What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence... [as above]. In the fifth sutta, the Blessed One spoke thus: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, but I shall not make known to you the Noble Truth of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering,’ that would be impossible. But if one should say: ‘I shall make known to you the Noble Truth of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering,’ that is possible. What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering... [as above]... What is
It is transformed in two ways—by aging and by death delimited by arising and passing away—and it exists for only a momentary duration.
"As suffering" means not as pleasure. By this, he states their state of suffering through the negation of pleasure.

And for that very reason, they are shown to be suffering because of constant oppression and because they are the basis of suffering. For, due to their possession of arising and passing away, they are constantly oppressed.

It is [viewed] as suffering because it is the very basis for suffering due to its state of uninterrupted pain; as a disease because it is the root of disease due to its dependence on conditions for maintenance;
as an abscess because it is joined with the sting of suffering, drips with the filth of defilements, and swells, ripens, and bursts through arising, aging, and dissolution;
as an arrow because it produces oppression, pierces within, and is difficult to extract; and as a failure because it brings about non-prosperity.

It is suffering because it is the basis for suffering and because it is itself suffering. It is an affliction because it gives rise to a state of lack of mastery and because it is the locus of disease.
It is the other because it does not function under one's own control and is not subject to one's will. It is disintegrating because it is liable to be broken down by sickness, aging, and death.

It is empty because it is devoid of a master, an inhabitant, a doer, an experiencer, and a controller. It is non-self in the sense of the negation of a self. Thus, even phenomena such as form and so forth are [to be understood] in this way: "There is no self here."
"Anattā": thus, because they themselves are not a self, they are "anattā. By this, it is shown that they are "anattā" due to their lack of agency, lack of effort, and emptiness.
To show that the three characteristics themselves have been grasped by dividing them into eleven terms for the sake of easy understanding, it was said:
"Because [they are seen] as impermanent," and so forth. "Within the attainment" means, due to their co-nascence with the attainments, within the attainments.
“He withdraws the mind within” means that by suppressing the defilements such as desire and lust bound up with it, he withdraws the insight-mind.
Therefore he said, “he releases and removes it. “By way of hearing” means by way of hearing [the words] beginning with “the stilling of all formations.
“By way of praise” means by way of extolling it in that same manner, that is, by way of proclaiming its qualities. “By way of the scriptures” means...
By means of mastering that Dhamma. "By way of its description" means by way of describing its meaning.
One directs the path-consciousness precisely by making it an object; the phrase "this is peaceful," etc., however, shows the meaning as determined by the exclusion [of other states].
Just as insight directs the mind toward the unconditioned element by saying, "This is peaceful, this is sublime," and so forth.

Thus, while realizing Nibbāna by way of the breakthrough of realization through the path, and penetrating all the specific qualities obtainable therein without confusion, he directs his mind toward it. Therefore, he said: "But in this manner," and so forth.
"Established therein" means that the yogi, who is one whose insight is not sluggish, is established therein upon that object consisting of the three characteristics such as impermanence.
Established in insight (*vipassanā*). "In all" means in all instances of the serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) produced for the attainment of each respective path.

"Being unable [to progress], he becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmī*)" means that, having abandoned desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) for the serenity and insight that lead to the lower paths, yet being unable to exhaust his attachment (*nikanti*) toward those leading to the highest path, he settles precisely at the stage of non-returning.
"Because of having completely transcended" means because of having transcended form in every way—both by way of serenity (*samatha*) and by way of insight (*vipassanā*).

Therefore he said, "For this," and so forth. "By this" refers to the yogi. "Having transcended that" refers to one who, having first correctly contemplated the phenomena included within the fivefold and singlefold existences and having relinquished them, subsequently enters the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) and [contemplates] the formless phenomena.
It was said with reference to that [formless attainment]. Therefore he said: "Now he comprehends the formless.
The commentary on the Jhāna Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta.
37. "Attainment of opportunity" (*okāsādhigama*) means that by means of this, one attains an occasion or scope;
or, it is an "opportunity" because it serves as the occasion for the attainment of the bliss of the paths and fruits. Its attainment is "attainment of opportunity.
And herein, according to the *Dīgha Nikāya* alone, in the teaching of the Suttantas, there are three attainments of opportunity: the first jhāna, the fourth jhāna, and the path of arahantship.
It has arrived. In that context, because the first jhāna remains having suppressed the five hindrances and taken its own place, it is called "the first attainment of an opportunity.

Furthermore, because the fourth jhāna remains having suppressed pleasure and pain and taken its own place, it is the second attainment of an opportunity. The path of arahantship [remains] having suppressed all defilements...
"Standing having taken its own place" is called "the third attainment of a place.

However, here the term "attainment of a place" is used with reference to the three formless jhānas that will be explained below. And the reason for including only those [three] he himself will state later.
"For the purpose of bringing about the purification of beings" means [purification] from the stains of greed and so forth, and from the secondary defilements such as covetousness and improper greed.
It is for the purpose of bringing about purification and transcendence for beings with defiled minds. For here, "transcendence" (*samatikkama*) is said to mean non-arising in the future.

"For the purpose of reaching the goal" means for the subsiding—that is, the cessation—of these two: bodily pain and mental grief. Nibbāna is so called because it moves (*kamati*) with certainty (*ñāyati*).
It is called a *ñāya* because by means of it one knows or penetrates; it is the noble path in the sense of being the state of total eradication. Thus he says, "of the path together with insight.

"For the purpose of making manifest" means for the sake of personal realization (*attapaccakkhatāya*). For making manifest without depending on another is what is termed "realization" (*sacchikiriyā*).
"Unadulterated" means not obstructed and not impaired by bile, phlegm, and so forth.
Concentration accompanied by lust is called "inclined" because it proceeds by way of being directed toward the object;

that accompanied by hatred is "withdrawn" because it proceeds by way of turning away. Since [concentration] is described as "neither inclined nor withdrawn" by way of the negation of both, he says "by way of lust," and so forth.
It is not "with effort, restrained, and checked" because these refer to mundane jhāna-consciousnesses.

It does not stand having suppressed and restrained [the defilements] by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), with effort and application as if [struggling against them].
Rather, it has arisen when the very roots of the defilements have been cut. This was said with reference to the fruition-concentration (*phalasamādhi*) that has become such.
Therefore he said: "Not with effort... [etc. ...arisen when the roots are cut."
The commentary on the Ānanda-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Lokāyatika-sutta: 38.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "proponents of Lokāyata": that by which the world does not strive (*yatati*) nor grow (*viruhati*) toward future welfare is *lokāyata*.
The weapon of cavil (*vitaṇḍasattha*). For, relying on that treatise, beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds;
thus they are called "proponents of Lokāyata" (*lokāyatavādaka*).
One who possesses a bow that is firm and strong is a "strong-bowed one" (*daḷhadhanvā*); he alone is called "one of firm nature" (*daḷhadhammā*). For the purpose of destroying adversaries...
One who takes up the bow is a *dhanuggaha* (archer). One who shoots or hurls arrows (*issu-sara*) is an *issāsa* (marksman).
"Strength of two thousand" means capable of carrying a load of iron and so forth weighing two thousand [units]; thus he said, "What is called 'strength of two thousand,'" and so on.
"In the staff" means in the staff of the bow. "As far as the measure of the arrow" means for as long as the length of the arrow's measure extends.

As soon as the bow-staff is raised and the bow-strings are fixed, if that burden is released from the ground, it should be understood that this is what is called a "bow of two-thousand-fold strength. One who has mastered the craft is one who has acquired the skill of archery.
One who has perfected his hand is one whose arrow-releasing is firm and unfailing upon the targets. Such a person, moreover, has attained mastery therein.
"He is called one who has 'done with his hands'"—thus he said, "one who has attained mastery.

"He is one who has performed the act of approaching for a meal in royal families and such"—thus he said, "one who has displayed his craft in royal families and such. "Thus done" means thus made light by means of hollowing out the interior and so forth.
The commentary on the *Lokāyatika-sutta* is finished.
8–9. Commentary on the *Devāsurasaṅgāmasutta*, etc.
39–40. Regarding the eighth [verse], "they overcame": when did they overcome them? It was when they were powerful. Herein is the sequential narrative:
it is said that Sakka, having been a young brahmin named Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, took thirty-three men with him...
While performing wholesome deeds, he fulfilled seven bases of conduct (*vatapada*); having passed away there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.

Seeing him surpassing the other resident deities along with their retinues in ten respects through the power of his potent karma, the residents prepared perfumes and drinks, thinking, "Newly arrived sons of gods have come. Sakka gave a signal to his own assembly.
He gave the order: "Friends, do not drink the scented liquor; merely show the appearance of drinking. They did exactly that.
The resident deities, having drunk as much of the scented liquor as they desired from golden goblets, became intoxicated and fell here and there upon the golden ground to sleep.
Sakka said, "Seize the children of those whose sons have been slain!"
Seizing them by their feet, he hurled them down to the base of Mount Sineru. By the power of Sakka’s merit, all those who followed them also fell right there.
When they regained consciousness at the midpoint of Mount Sineru, they cried out, "Dear ones, we did not drink liquor!
We did not drink liquor! From that time on, they became known as *asuras*. Then, for them, there arose [a state] produced by temperature conditioned by karma.
At the base of Mount Sineru, ten thousand yojanas deep, the realm of the asuras was established.
Sakka stationed a guard there to prevent them from returning, with reference to which it is said:
“Between the two cities of Ayujjha...”
The protection established is fivefold:
the serpent, the skull, the drink-taker,
the one possessed by passion, and the four great beings.
Indeed, because they could not be captured by means of battle, two cities came to be known as "cities of no-war," namely the city of the gods and the city of the asuras.
For when the asuras were powerful, the gods would flee and enter the city of the gods, closing its gates;
then even a hundred thousand asuras would be unable to do anything at all. When the gods—
They become powerful, and then, having fled from the Asuras, even a hundred thousand Sakkas are unable to do anything once the gates of the Asura city have been closed.
Thus, these two cities are called Ayujjhapura.
Between them, at these five locations—among which the Uragas are first—Sakka has established a guard. There, by the term "Uraga," the Nāgas are included.
For they are powerful in the water; therefore, their protection is on the first terrace of Sineru.
By the word *karoṭi*, the *supaṇṇas* are included. It is said that their food and drink is called *karoṭi*; they received that name because of it, and their protection is on the second terrace.
By the word *payassahāri*, the *kumbhaṇḍas* are included; they are said to be *dānavas* and *rakkhasas*, and their protection is on the third terrace.
Their protection is provided by the *madanayuta* spirits; these *yakkhas*, it is said, are of uneven conduct and fond of battle, and their protection is stationed in the fourth gallery.
By the phrase "the four great ones," the Four Great Kings are meant, and their protection is in the fifth gallery;
therefore, if the *asuras*, with minds agitated by anger, approach the city of the gods to wage war—whatever...
The first rampart is made of stone, which the serpents (uraga) guard. Likewise for the others, with their respective guardians.
Those asuras, however, are equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods in terms of lifespan, complexion, glory, and sovereign power;

therefore, not recognizing themselves [as asuras] when they are between [the walls], they think upon seeing a flowering pāṭali tree: "This is not the city of the gods; there, the pāricchattaka tree blooms."
"But here, Cittapāṭalī has been deceived by Jarāsakka after he made us drink liquor, and our city of the gods has been seized.

Let us go; we shall fight with him! Having spoken thus, they mounted elephants, horses, and chariots, took up shields of gold, silver, and jewels, and being prepared for battle, they split the waters of the great ocean in two and emerged while sounding the drums of the asuras.
When those gods have rained down, the anthill-beetles begin to climb Mount Sineru as if it were an anthill.
Then their first battle takes place with the Nāgas. In that battle, however, neither the hide nor the skin of anyone is torn, nor does blood flow;
it is merely like a game of wooden rams played by children.

It is merely a mutual intimidation of one another. Even hundreds of millions or thousands of millions of nāgas, having fought with them, enter back into the city of the asuras themselves and turn back. But when the asuras become powerful, then the nāgas retreat;
they join forces with the supaṇṇas on the second terrace and fight together. This...
The same method applies to the Supaṇṇas and the others as well. However, when the Asuras crush those five places, even those five forces combined together retreat.
Then the Four Great Kings go and report that situation to Sakka.
Having heard their words, Sakka mounts the Vejayanta chariot, which is one hundred and fifty yojanas long.

Either he goes out himself or sends one son. When the gods again defeated the asuras so that they would not return, Sakka, having driven the asuras away, established protection at five locations and placed images of Indra with thunderbolt-hands at the base of Mount Vediyaka.
From time to time, the asuras would rise up, and upon seeing the images, [they would think], "Sakka is vigilant..."
“...he stands,” they say, and turn back from that very place.
But here, this is said with reference to when the asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated: “The devas, O bhikkhus, being defeated, fled toward the north, while the asuras prevailed.
“Facing southward” means facing toward the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. It is said that the asuras, having been defeated by the devas...
Fleeing toward the Cakkavāḷa mountains, they reached the sandy beaches on the surface of the great ocean surrounding the Cakkavāḷa, which were the color of silver plates;

there, having gone to where the seers dwelt in leaf huts, they proceeded along the path to the seers' hermitage, saying, "Sakka, having consulted with these men, is destroying us! Seize the children of those who have killed their own sons!"
When provoked, they destroy the water jars, the walking paths, the leaf huts, and other facilities in the hermitage.
When the seers return from the forest carrying fruits and roots and see [the damage], they restore them with great difficulty;
yet those [asuras], having been defeated time and again, go back and destroy them once more. Therefore it was said: "And the asuras were defeated, monks..."
“They indeed drank facing toward the south. The ninth [sutta] is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Devāsurasaṅgāma-sutta* and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Tapussa-sutta*.

41. “He leaps forward” means he enters. “He becomes confident” means he attains confidence and delight; the meaning is that he establishes himself and is liberated. “The source of conversation” means the root of conversation. For the root is called “pābhata. As it is said:
“Even with a small amount of goods, the wise and discerning man raises himself up, like a tiny fire when fanned.”

For this very reason he said: “‘A source for conversation’ means the root of conversation. By the mention of *vitakka* (applied thought) alone, its concomitant *vicāra* (sustained thought) is also included. For this reason, he stated that the plural designation was used here: “‘In applied thoughts’ means in applied and sustained thoughts.
The commentary on the Tapussa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
5. The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga) 1–10. Commentary on the *Sambādhasutta* and following, 42–51.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], regarding "Udāyī": there are three elders named Udāyī—Kāḷudāyī, Lāḷudāyī, and Mahāudāyī.

"Here, Kāḷudāyī is intended," he said, [explaining] "Udāyī refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. Regarding "the crowded place" (*sambādha*): it means that which is extremely crowded due to the pressure of craving, defilements, and so forth.
