By means of the wisdom of teaching, he perceives accurately the various kinds of teachings to be taught, as well as the differences in the inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, and dispositions of the persons to be enlightened.

"Of enemies" refers to the enemies that are the defilements, or the fivefold Māras, or the adversaries of the Dispensation, namely those of other sects. Their "slaying," however, means overcoming them through the miracles and rendering them speechless.

And [the perfection of] equanimity. Herein, the *Kesīvinaya Sutta* serves as the illustration. Likewise, it was accomplished by one who knows what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) and so forth;
by one who sees beings according to their kamma; by an Arahant through the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) together with their underlying tendencies (*vāsanā*);

and by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*) through the unerring realization of phenomena—such as those to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth—in terms of being directly known and so forth.
Alternatively, he is "the Knower" (*jānatā*) because of his unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times;

"the Seer" (*passatā*) because of his practice of acting with circumspection, due to the conformity of his knowledge to all three types of action—bodily, verbal, and mental; "the Worthy One" (*arahatā*) because of his perfection in abandoning, which establishes the non-existence of lust and the other defilements;

and "the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddhena*) because of his omniscience, which establishes an inexhaustible presence of mind and serves as the cause for the non-decline of zeal and the other faculties.
In this way, the application should also be made by way of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
"Conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhata*) means made by coming together, meeting, and combining with one's own conditions.
This state of being "made" should be understood as being through its production, not through the reconditioning of what has already arisen; thus he says, "produced" (*uppādita*).
To show that for these [formations] volition is the predominant condition, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "that which is conditioned and intended.

Thus, he explains the meaning as "what is intended and fashioned. Furthermore, by way of showing the manifestation of jhāna through the phrase "conditioned and intended," it indicates its nature as something that is being dismantled;
for that which comes into being without having previously existed, [is subject to destruction].

Having offered that, he recites it. Therefore, the text says: "But as for that which... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "established in the states of serenity and insight" (*samatha-vipassanā-dhamme ṭhito*):

here, because he is established in the state of serenity (*samatha*), he is concentrated; having initiated insight (*vipassanā*), while abandoning perceptions of permanence through the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so on, he gradually attains that knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) and [is established] in the states of insight.
It is established. In the phenomena known as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), "lust" (*rāga*) is so called in the sense of coloring;
"delight" (*nandī*) is so called in the sense of rejoicing. Therein, subtle expectation is spoken of, which is called "attachment" (*nikanti*).
"When this is so" means: when the meaning of this sutta passage is to be understood according to the literal expression alone, [regarding] serenity and insight...

"One should cultivate desire-and-lust" means that without having realized the fruit of non-returning, and without having even developed serenity and insight for its sake, one will merely have to cultivate desire-and-lust toward it. Why?
Because by mere desire-and-lust for those states known as serenity and insight, even one who has not yet attained the fruit of non-returning can obtain what is to be obtained by a non-returner.
That being so, the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) must also necessarily be attained by him. Therefore he said: "The fruit of non-returning will be attained.
Because it is to be tasted according to its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), the unerring meaning itself is the "taste of the meaning" (attharasa).
When he says "other various happy destinies," he is referring to the states of ruin (vinipātika). When he says "other various miserable destinies," he is referring to the host of asuras.

Just as a noble person gives much when asked for little, so too, because it was stated that even a single teaching is "this one teaching" when one asks about a single teaching, all eleven teachings came to be called "one teaching" by way of the question, according to the principle of completing the sentence with each individual item. Regarding "by way of the question":
"Venerable Ānanda, was there indeed one teaching [taught] by that... Fully Enlightened One? and so forth.

"Thus it has been rightly proclaimed"—this is by way of the question thus arisen. "In the sense of being the source of the Deathless" means by way of being the cause for the arising of the state of the Deathless;
the meaning is that all meditation subjects, though having a single flavor, are the practice for the attainment of the Deathless.

Thus, in this context, only two stages are mentioned by their specific names: the stage of the supreme fruit (Arahatta) and the stage of the non-returning fruit (Anāgāmi), not because of [the latter's] immediate succession [to the former].
However, it should be understood that the two lower planes are also included here in terms of their actual meaning.
"Worth five hundred" means that its value is five hundred. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Gopāla Sutta 17.
Regarding the seventh [section], "three expositions" (*tisso kathā*) means three commentaries; the meaning is that there are three ways of explaining the meaning of the sutta.
That which has each word as its stalk (*nāḷa*) and root is thus designated "the single-stalked" (*ekanāḷikā*). Alternatively, each word is a stalk, being the path by which the meaning emerges.
*Etissā* means "of this [work], which consists of a single stalk. Therefore he said: "the explanation of the meaning of each individual word.

*Caturassā* means "that which has four corners," that is, four parts (*aṃsa*) or divisions which serve as the means for discerning the meaning. Therefore he said: "the explanation after having tied it into a fourfold [structure].

*Nisinnavattikā* means "that which possesses a sequence of sitting" (*nisinna-vatta*), referring to the fixed order of what was undertaken while seated; [it refers to] the sequence of how it was begun.
The meaning is: "one who brings each point of the matter to its respective conclusion. Therefore he said, "Having shown the wise cowherd," and so forth.

This method of commentary on the meaning of each individual word—by way of showing the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*) of each single word—is found everywhere, rather than stating the meaning of many words together as a whole. "Having bound them into tetrads" refers to the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*).
Having applied this tetrad—consisting of the pair of simile and subject of the simile, as well as "likewise in the bright side"—this is found only in such suttas.

Regarding "reaching the conclusion," some first say: "After showing the simile in the dark side, since a simile is for the purpose of establishing the subject of the simile, the description of the defilement-side is brought forward for the sake of the subject of the simile."

"And for the purpose of elucidating the side of purification" means that even the bright side (sukkapakkha) is brought forward by distinguishing between the simile and the subject of the simile, thereby concluding the meaning of the Sutta.
Having shown the subject of the simile in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), this same method applies to the conclusion, the arrival [at the goal], and so forth.
However, others say: "Having concluded each respective point of the simile and its subject separately for both the dark side and the bright side..."
They say that "the conclusion" refers to the reaching of the end of the discourse. "Ayam" (this) refers to those who follow the sitting posture.

"Iha" (here) means in this *Gopālaka-sutta*. "The practice of all teachers" means that it was practiced and commented upon by all the ancient teachers (*pubbācariya*), and the text (*pāḷi*) proceeds in exactly that manner.
They are called "limbs" (*aṅga*) because they are known as constituent parts; they are sections. Furthermore, these [limbs] here are of a nature that involves fault (*sāvajja*).
Therefore he said: “By means of factors (aṅgāni) means by means of groups of qualities. A “cow-pen” (gomaṇḍala) is a herd of cows. “To tend” (pariharituṃ) means to protect.
That tending, moreover, is wandering about after having enclosed [the herd]; thus he said: “to wander about after having enclosed it.
“Increase” (vaḍḍhi) is the abundance of cows, the growth consisting in the state of having much milk and so forth. It is called “form” (rūpa) because it is manifested as “this is so much.”
Since the delimitation by measure is also a form of the body, he says, "either by way of number or by way of color.

He does not seek [the corpse] because he does not know its state of having perished. In the phrase "blue," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning"; by this, colors such as white, black, and so forth are included.
In the phrase "bow, spear, stake, etc.," this refers to the practice of archery masters who mark their targets with bows when shooting at cattle. [This applies to] the groups of the Kumārabhaṭṭikas.
The mark of the spear made on cows belongs to the groups of the Issaras and Bhattas; this is the construction [of the phrase].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the marks such as the axe and the discus made on the cows of the Rāma, Vāsudeva, and other groups.

"Blue flies" refers to tawny flies or simply small flies. It is called *sāṭikā* because one is struck or afflicted by it; a *sāṭikā* that has increased is an *āsāṭikā*. Therefore he said, "increasing," and so forth. "Hāretā" means a remover.

"By means of a cloth" (*vākena*) means by means of a piece of cloth. "By means of a rag" (*cīrakena*) means by means of a tattered garment. "During the rains" (*antovasse*) means within the period of the rainy season.

"Free from crocodiles" (*niggāhaṃ*) means devoid of crocodiles such as *susumāra* and others. "Drunk" (*pītaṃ*) refers to the state of having been drunk of water. "Dangerous and fearful" (*sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo*) means being full of apprehension and peril due to lions, tigers, and other such threats.
"Five days for one" is *pañcāhika*; that itself is a "turn," thus it is a *pañcāhikavāra*. A *sattāhikavāra* (seven-day turn) should be understood in the same way.

*Ciṇṇaṭṭhānaṃ* means a place frequented, a place where the range [of grazing] has been taken up. *Pitiṭṭhānaṃ* means a place to be done by the father; the meaning is "the task to be performed by the father.
"Taking [them] according to their pleasure" means they go having taken a grazing ground or a river crossing in accordance with the cows' preference. *Gobhattaṃ* means...
The meal to be eaten by the cow is mixed with cotton-seed husks and so forth. By the mention of "meal" (*bhatta*), the rice-gruel (*yāgu*) is also included.
To show the two ways mentioned as "in two ways," it is said: "either by way of enumeration (*gaṇanato*) or by way of origination (*samuṭṭhānato*).
Thus, as they have come down in the Pāḷi, having divided "birth" (*jāti*) into two—namely, "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*)—and not including the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
"The ten bases and fifteen subtle forms"—thus they are presented in the text of the *Rūpakaṇḍa*. "Twenty-five form-components" (*rūpakoṭṭhāsa*):
these are portions of form because, by virtue of their own specific characteristics, they lack mutual confusion;

or alternatively, they are "form-aggregates" (*rūpakalāpa*) because they do not occur individually but occur only as groups. The meaning of "components" (*koṭṭhāsa*) is parts or members. *Koṭṭha* means...
Or, "body" refers to its parts such as hair and so forth; other components are also called "parts" (koṭṭhāsa) because they are like portions. The phrase beginning with "Just as if...
is the application of the simile. Therein, "having discerned form" means having grasped the aforementioned form by means of knowledge according to its specific characteristics.
"Having defined the formless" means, depending upon that form and making it the object [of contemplation].
Having defined the four aggregates—beginning with feeling—as "formless" while they are occurring, and having discerned both form and the formless:
therein, that which has the characteristic of being susceptible to change (ruppana) is form; other than that is the formless.

There is nothing whatsoever apart from these two, whether a self or anything belonging to a self. Having thus discerned both form and the formless, one understands that both of them [arise] through ignorance and the rest.

The construction is as follows: "One who, having observed the condition with its conditions—that is, having applied the characteristics such as impermanence—cannot bring the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to its culmination by means of the sequence beginning with the comprehension of aggregates (kalāpasammasana), does not progress. Such is the meaning.
"This much form has a single origin" refers to the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, and the tongue-base.
The body base (*kāyāyatana*), the female faculty (*itthindriya*), the male faculty (*purisindriya*), and the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—these eight kinds [of matter] arise through kamma;
the two, namely bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) and verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), arise through consciousness. This much is matter with a single origin.

The sound base (*saddāyatana*) alone has a dual origin, arising from both temperature (*utu*) and consciousness. The lightness (*lahutā*), malleability (*mudutā*), and wieldiness (*kammaññatā*) of matter...

This much material form has three origins by way of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment. This much material form—namely, the visible-object base, the odor-base, the taste-base, the tangible-object base, the space element, the water element, and physical nutriment—has four origins by way of temperature, consciousness, nutriment, and kamma.
This much material form—namely, accumulation, continuity, aging, and the impermanence of matter—does not originate from anywhere.

"Arises" means he does not know. Regarding the phrases "not knowing form by way of its origination," and so forth, it should be understood according to the same method explained under the phrases "not knowing form by way of its enumeration," and so forth.
"Characterized by karma" (kammalakkhaṇo) means one for whom the characteristic is the unwholesome action committed by oneself; thus, he is a fool.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool. Which three?
He thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds. These, indeed... are the characteristics.
One who has good conduct as his own performed action as his characteristic is "one characterized by action" (*kammalakkhaṇa*), namely, the wise person. And this too has been said: "These three..."
“Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person. What are the three? He is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds.
These, indeed... [are] the characteristics of a wise person. Therefore it was said: “Wholesome and unwholesome kamma are the characteristics of the wise and the foolish.

Regarding the phrase “having avoided the fool, he does not associate with the wise”: this refers to the association with the wise by one who desires their own welfare, having avoided the foolish person.
One does not do what ought to be done. To show that for one who has become such, this is a disadvantage, it was further stated: "Having avoided fools," and so forth.
In that context, if something conforms to what was permitted by the Blessed One as "this is allowable for you," it is allowable (*kappiya*).
If something conforms to what was prohibited as "this is not allowable for you," it is unallowable (*akappiya*). That which arises from skillfulness—
That which is wholesome is its opposite, the unwholesome. That which is blameworthy is the opposite of the wholesome, which is blameless.

Regarding offenses, the first two classes of offenses are grave; those other than these are light. From the perspective of the nature of phenomena (*dhamma*), that which is greatly blameworthy is grave, while that which is slightly blameworthy is light.
That which is remediable and curable is [light], whereas that which is irremediable and incurable is grave. That which conforms to the natural order of things...

The one is the cause; the other is not the cause. "Not knowing that" means not knowing what is allowable and what is unallowable, what is heavy and what is light, and what is curable and incurable—one who does not know these is unable to guard the precepts even after making them perfectly pure.

One who does not know what is wholesome and unwholesome, what is blameworthy and blameless, and what is a cause and what is not a cause, is unable to perform even the discernment of form and non-form within the aggregates and so forth due to their unwholesomeness.
How could he increase his meditation subject after having taken it up? Therefore he said: "he is unable to increase the meditation subject after having taken it up.

Having arisen in a personal existence that resembles a cow-pen, unwholesome thoughts are like gadflies because they are the cause for the arising of suffering there; thus he said: "having removed the gadfly of unwholesome thought.
Because of the statement: "A boil, monks, is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging," by means of the six...

Just as an abscess with pus oozing from its openings must be covered at those openings with a piece of cloth, so too the wound of one's own person, from which the filth of defilements oozes from the gates of the senses, must be covered by the restraint of mindfulness; yet this person does not do so, and thus it is said:
"Just as that cowherd does not cover the wound, so he does not accomplish restraint."
Just as smoke, arising in dependence upon fuel, being soft and subtle, enters and pervades various openings,
dispels dangers for beings such as gadflies and mosquitoes, and serves as the precursor to the emergence of a mass of flames—
so too, [wisdom] arising in dependence upon the collection of material and immaterial phenomena that serve as the fuel for the knowledge of teaching the Dhamma...
It is smooth and subtle; it enters and pervades various aggregates and bases;
it dispels the dangers of beings' wrong thoughts and the like; and it serves as the precursor for the kindling of the flame of wisdom.
Therefore, because it is "like smoke," it is called "smoke. Thus he said: "The cowherd does not produce the smoke of teaching the Dhamma. [Regarding] himself...
The discourse on the Dhamma appropriate for one who has approached and sat down is the *upanisinnaka-kathā* (the discourse for those sitting nearby).
The discourse of appreciation (*anumodanā*) is the discourse of thanksgiving for the merit already performed, such as giving.

"Because of not performing [these], namely, the discourse on the Dhamma and so forth"—why was this said? Is it not the case that the discourse on the Dhamma and so forth is for the purpose of making oneself known?

"Is it not the case that one should never speak at all? True, one should indeed never speak; however, this was said with reference to the recognition of virtue when the Dhamma is spoken with a pure intention.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"They do not recognize the wise man when he remains silent, for he is mixed among fools."
“May he illuminate and proclaim the Dhamma; may he raise the banner of the seers.
A *tittha* (ford) is so called because beings descend and enter there; it is a place for descending into rivers, ponds, and the like, for the purpose of bathing, drinking, and so forth.
Just as such a place washes away the bodily impurities of beings who have entered the water and dispels their fatigue, [so too does the Dhamma].

They produce purification; in this way, those who have heard much (bahussuta) wash away the defilement of the minds of beings who have approached them with the water of the Dhamma, dispel their weariness, and produce purification.
Therefore, they are like a ford (tittha), and thus they are called a "ford.
Hence he said: "The learned bhikkhus are become a ford. [As for the question: "How, venerable sir, should the phrasing be applied? This—
"How is this word, which is the phonetic form (*byañjana*), to be applied to this meaning? In what manner has it become the designator of this meaning?

Alternatively, there is the reading "nirūpetabbaṃ": the intention is that this natural linguistic expression (*sabhāvanirutti*) must be examined as to how it is established (*nirūḷha*) in this context.
"What is the meaning of this statement?"—thus he asks regarding the meaning of the word (*saddattha*). "In this place... [and so forth].

"In this passage of the text. He asks regarding the meaning of the *bhāva* (the underlying state) when he asks, "What does the text say? Does he ask about the meaning of the *bhāva*, or the meaning of the conventional designation (*saṅketa*)?
"He does not inquire further" means that he does not make any inquiry at all by way of a question intended to sever doubt.
"He does not question thoroughly" means that he does not express or manifest a desire to know [the matter] for himself in every respect.

Therefore he said, "he does not make it known. "Those" refers to the learned bhikkhus. "Explanation" means speaking by analyzing the meaning; thus he said, "they do not teach after having divided [the matter].
"Not made manifest" means that which has not been made clear by knowledge—something secret and concealed.
"They do not make it manifest" means [they do not reveal] the water that supports the earth, like one digging up sand at the foot of Mount Sineru.
And they do not make it plain as if revealing it.
Thus, by virtue of which quality those who are "learned" (bahussuta) are called "ford-makers" (titthiya) in a figurative sense (pariyāyato).

Now, in order to show that very same quality in its non-figurative sense (nippariyāyato) as "ford," the passage beginning with "or just as" (yathā vā) was stated. For [by means of] the Dhamma, they cross over.
One enters into what is called Nibbāna by means of this, and thus it is called a "ford" (tittha). Therefore the Blessed One, having become wise, said:
"When the lake of the Deathless exists, And the stains of defilements have been washed away, If one does not seek that lake, The fault lies not with the lake of the Deathless."
One who does not know the manner of entering the Dhamma—which is like a ford for crossing over to Nibbāna—is said to "not know the Dhamma-ford.

Regarding "drunk and undrunk," he does not know or perceive the state of the cows that have drunk and those that have not drunk among a herd of cattle; for one who does not perceive this, it is said that "he does not find" it.
Having stated, "He does not find the benefit," the text says, "Having gone to the head of the Dhamma-listening," etc., in order to show the manner in which he fails to find it.
He says "noble" (ariya) with reference to the phrase "this is supramundane. For, according to the principle of proximity, there is a negation of what immediately precedes it;
or else, the word *ariya* should be understood as a synonym for "faultless" (*niddosa*).

And as for the term "eightfold," it should be taken both separately and collectively, based on its being eightfold in its components and its predominance. And having done so, even the sevenfold noble path [is included].
The summary is established.
In such passages as "the four foundations of mindfulness," the foundations of mindfulness are stated without distinction.

Among these, those having the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena as their objects are mundane; those that proceed by way of destroying delusion regarding them and have Nibbāna as their object are supramundane.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: "These are mundane; these are supramundane.
"He milks dry" means that, failing to know the proper measure in receiving, he milks dry someone by causing a loss of faith in a donor, and he milks dry someone else by causing a loss of requisites.
"Approaching with speech" is *vācābhihāra*; "approaching with requisites" is *paccayābhihāra*.

By the statement, “These do not show us respect,” he demonstrates the absence of right practice among the junior monks, because they have failed to establish fatherly affection toward their teachers and preceptors. By this indication of a lack of reverence for the training, he shows their unfitness as recipients of support;
and by that, the elders’ lack of concern for them. For it is not through qualities such as virtue...
Having attained stability within the Dispensation, they assist fellow celibates who do not deserve assistance, or they provide assistance that is useless.
Therefore he said, "newly ordained bhikkhus," and so forth. "The bond of Dhamma-talk" refers to the method of miscellaneous Dhamma-talks handed down through the lineage.
It is connected with the truths, the seven rebirth-linkings, and the modes of conditions, and it elucidates emptiness (*suññatā*).

*Guḷhaganthaṃ* (The Hidden Text). "By way of reversing what was stated" means by way of the non-acceptance—that is, the rejection—of the negation stated in such passages as "one who does not know form," etc.

"Having joined [the phrases]" means [joining them] by such statements as "one who knows form knows form either by number or by color," etc., and "his herd of cattle does not diminish, nor is he excluded from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow," etc.
And having thus applied the meaning, it should be understood that the meaning is to be understood in each respective word as appropriate.
The rest is everywhere obvious.
The commentary on the Gopāla Sutta is finished.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Unexplained Meanings in the Commentary on the Section of Elevens within the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
And the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is completed.
Commentary on the Words of Non-Obscure Meaning.
Commentary on the Concluding Discourse:
"The Essence of the Great Commentary" refers to the essence of the *Aṅguttara-mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. "Only fifty-nine" means a small number.

The inclusion of the word "only" (*matta*) is for the purpose of exclusion. By the phrase "the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*," he states that this is precisely the core meaning of the *Aṅguttara-mahā-aṭṭhakathā* mentioned previously, following the sequence of the commentary.
Alternatively, "the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*" refers to the essential meaning within the ancient commentaries.
By this, he shows: having taken the essential meaning of the *Aṅguttara-mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, [he composed] this *Manorathapūraṇī*.
While doing so, he took the essence of the meaning from the commentaries on the root [texts] of the other great schools that was suitable for application here, and thus composed this work.
Furthermore, the phrase "of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra" should be connected with both the preceding and following words:
"proclaiming the system of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra," and "the essence of the root commentaries of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra."
"Taking [it]" means by that merit. "May the whole world be happy": this refers to the entire world of beings, divided into the sense-sphere realm and so forth;

he dedicates his own merit for the sake of the ultimate attainment of happiness for the world including the devas, thinking, "May it be happy, may it be well-off, through the attainment of the three types of enlightenment as appropriate, by means of the bliss of Nibbāna which has been achieved."
To this extent, this entire exposition is complete;
it measures twenty thousand texts in its total extent.
Since the essence of the ancient path of discourse is established herein, [it is thus concluded].
Therefore, it is renowned by the name *Sāratthamañjūsā*.
At the request of that lord of men, Parakkamabāhu—
who desired the endurance of the True Dhamma and sought to illuminate the Dispensation— I [composed this].
In this delightful Jetavana, which was built by him,
adorned with hundreds of palaces, strewn with various groves of trees,
a dwelling-place for those who delight in meditation, and endowed with cool water, he dwelt.
I have composed this work, which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing and is esteemed by the virtuous.
By whatever merit has been accomplished through this, and whatever other merit has been performed by me—
by this meritorious deed, in my second future existence.
Rejoicing in the realm of the Thirty-three, delighting in the virtues of moral conduct and behavior,
unattached to the five sensual pleasures, and having attained the first fruit [of the path],
in his final existence he will see Metteyya, the bull among sages.
Having seen the Lord, the supreme person in the world who delights in the welfare of all beings,
and having heard the teaching of the True Dhamma from that wise one,
may I attain the highest fruit and thus cause the Conqueror’s dispensation to shine.
May kings always protect this people by means of the Dhamma alone;
devoted to meritorious deeds, may they uphold the teaching of the Conqueror.
And may all these living beings be forever free from calamity.
May those who are constantly possessed of noble intentions attain the deathless state.
The Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya is completed.
